News.title: Terrifying moment airliners fly just feet over crowded sports stadium in 'dangerous' stunt
News.content:
Terrifying moment airliners fly just feet over crowded sports stadium in 'dangerous' stunt

Nailbiting new footage shows two Embraer E190 and an Embraer E195 planes coming within just metres of the roof of Cape Town's DHL Stadium during a close flyover

Planes fly dangerously low over stadium in Cape Town

Twin airliners participating in a flyover of a major stadium packed with tens of thousands of people were came within metres of the building's roof, shocking new footage shows.

‌



The two Airlink Embraer E-Jets soared over the DHL Stadium in Cape Town, South Africa, ahead of a rugby game between the country and New Zealand's national teams on Saturday afternoon. Airlink, an official partner of the Rugby's Greatest Rivals series, marked the game by flying the 98-seater jets over the open arena's top.

‌



What was meant to be an electrifying spectacle ended up anxiety inducing as footage showed the planes coming extremely close to the the 55,000-capacity venue.

‌



Jet2 flight from London to Ibiza declares emergency at 35,000ft and diverts to Paris READ MORE :

View 3 Images The planes could already be seen flying low on their approach to the stadium

Footage taken from the roof and posted online showed the Embraer E190 and an Embraer E195 jets zooming within what FlightRadar says was just between 41 and 46 feet (12 and 14 metres) of the stadium. As they came in close, colourful streamers were puffed into the air, which the massive aircraft were seen cutting through.

During one especially alarming part of the manouevre as the jets moved off the other side of the stadium, the jet pitched upwards, pulling its tail even closer to the surface.

‌



The display was welcomed by Airlink, which afterwards praised what it said were "spectacular scenes". But social media users were less enthused, criticising the display for being "absolutely unnecessary and dangerous". One user on Reddit said: "Next level reckless. That is way too small of an envelope for error."

View 3 Images Social media users were shocked to see just how close the planes were to the roof

Another questioned: "Is this like impressively stupid or calculated?" Airlink said in a statement following massive backlash that it "notes the concerns", but pushed back, saying it was a "safe flyby" that followed careful planning.

‌



A spokesperson for the airline said: "Airlink notes the concerns expressed in various social media and online forums regarding yesterday’s formation flyby over Cape Town’s DHL Stadium.

"The flight demanded careful planning and rehearsal, as it required navigating at low altitude, at around 150 knots. The South African Civil Aviation Authority and Air Traffic Navigation Services provided valuable guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby."

View 3 Images Airlink said the display was carefully planned and within aviation regulations

Article continues below

"The two aircraft were flown by highly-experienced crew, with each comprised of three senior captains operating in the roles of commander, co-pilot and safety/technical officer."

The spokesperson added that flight data showed the flyover was performed within the safe altitude set by the SACAA. They said: "The flight data recorded by both aircraft confirms that the flights were performed within the SACAA’s approved and rehearsed safety altitude and speed limits for the flypast."

News.title: Big Church Festival live: Pastor killed by falling sign named and pictured as tributes pour in
News.content:
Pastor Robert Guanco was killed after a sign fell on him at Big Church Festival.

A 41-year-old pastor killed after a sign fell at Big Church Festival has been named and pictured for the first time, as tributes pour in.

Big Church Festival live: Pastor killed by falling sign named and pictured as tributes pour in

A 41-year-old man killed after a huge wooden sign came “crashing down” onto people at Big Church Festival has been named and pictured for the first time.

Robert Guanco, from Eastbourne, was a pastor at Jesus the Living Water Church, which described him as a “faithful servant of God”, loving husband and devoted father.

The sign, which reportedly carried the words “Everything’s Unmissable”, fell near a tented area at the Christian festival in West Sussex on Friday afternoon.

Six other people were injured in the incident, with four taken to hospital for treatment.

One eyewitness said he and his wife were walking just a few paces behind when the sign came down. He said they rushed to help lift it off those underneath and gave first aid alongside others until paramedics arrived.

The festival, which had been due to continue until Sunday, was cancelled by organisers following the incident.

The Archbishop of Canterbury, Dame Sarah Mullally, said she was “sad and shocked” and offered prayers for Mr Guanco’s family, those injured and others affected.

News.title: Kyrenia ferry LIVE: Seven dead as passenger boat capsizes off Cyprus with 267 on board
News.content:
An ambulance arrives at the port of Kyrenia in the Turkish occupied northern part of Cyprus after a ferry overturned off the coast

Seven people have reportedly died after a passenger ferry capsized off northern Cyprus, with a major rescue operation underway.

Kyrenia ferry LIVE: Seven dead as passenger boat capsizes off Cyprus with 267 on board

Seven people have died after a passenger ferry carrying 267 people capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus, according to reports.

Turkish broadcaster TGRT said local leader Ünal Üstel had confirmed seven fatalities following the disaster off Kyrenia.

A major search and rescue operation remains underway. Girne Mayor Murat Şenkul earlier told Turkish broadcaster A Haber that around 200 people had been reached, with between 60 and 70 still unaccounted for at that stage.

The vessel capsized early on Sunday afternoon around two kilometres off the coast of Kyrenia after departing for the Turkish port of Tasucu.

Turkish Cypriot and Turkish coastguard crews have been deployed, along with rescue helicopters and other vessels, as efforts continue.

News.title: Gareth Gates stuns fans with Pride performance in tiny trunks and bottomless pink chaps
News.content:
Gareth Gates stuns fans with Pride performance in tiny trunks and bottomless pink chaps

Pop Idol star, Gareth Gates, sent fans into a frenzy at Manchester Pride this weekend when he rocked up on stage belting out his greatest hits and showing off his buff body

View 5 Images Pop Idol finalist, Gareth Gates, looked a world away from his squeaky clean debut on the ITV show (Image: FARRELL / BACKGRID)

Pop Idol finalist, Gareth Gates, looked a world away from his squeaky clean debut on the ITV show 25 years ago at Manchester Pride this weekend.

‌



The singer, 42, who was only 17 when he shot to fame with show winner, Will Young, on the iconic talent series, sent fans into a frenzy when he rocked up on stage showing off his ultra buff body.

‌



Singing his heart out, sporting in a number of revealing outfits, including a pair of tiny trunks - as well as an eye-popping pair of bottomless pink chaps - the dad-of-one looked like he was having the time of his life.

‌



5 View 5 Images Pop Idol star, Gareth Gates, sent fans into a frenzy at Manchester Pride (Image: FARRELL / BACKGRID) 5 View 5 Images He whipped off his jeans to reveal his tiny trunks (Image: FARRELL / BACKGRID)

With slick choreography, Gareth had the crowd on their feet as he whipped off his jeans to reveal a pair of tiny sequin-strewn underpants. As fans whooped and cheered the Bradford-born star had a smile a mile wide as his audience screamed with excitement.

Gareth shot to fame on Pop Idol as a spiky haired teenager with a stutter when he lost out to Will Young in the first-ever offering of the show back in 2002.

‌



Then an overnight success, the star found himself mixing with a whole host of famous faces, including Katie Price.

Katie, then known as glamour model, Jordan, claims she took Gareth's virginity in news which hit all the headlines. Setting the story straight on Jamie Laing's podcast recently, the singer said: "I'll just say I was extremely inexperienced with a girl who was extremely experienced. I could see why she thought that.

5 View 5 Images Cheeky! (Image: FARRELL / BACKGRID) 5 View 5 Images Gareth shot to fame on Pop Idol at the age of 17 (Image: Getty Images)

‌



"I haven't ever spoken about relationships. I believe that relationships are between two people and I couldn't believe that somebody else was selling stories about very, very intimate details."

Admitting the story being splashed all over the newspapers was a "real learning curve" he added: "And I was shocked and I learned a lot about that - about people and about the industry, and about trust I guess. I would never have ever done that to her or to anybody else, and so it was a real learning curve for me."

Despite losing out to Will on Pop Idol, Gareth was finally crowned victorious when he won Celebrity SAS: Who Dares Wins in 2023.

Article continues below

Speaking to the Mirror about the gruelling experience, he said: "It actually felt like I’d been preparing for this my whole life. The struggle with my speech and having to be mentally strong to hear them say [I had passed]. I was like, ‘Wow, this is incredible’.

"I thought at last, I’ve actually won a talent TV show and not came second this time. It was a massive weight off my shoulders. I’ve finally redeemed myself from being the biggest loser in the UK back in 2002."

News.title: Nepal floods teacher saves more than 1,600 lives with alarm calls as death toll tops 700 and thousands missing
News.content:
Nepal floods teacher saves more than 1,600 lives with alarm calls as death toll tops 700 and thousands missing

A teacher at a school directly in the path of the horror torrent that crushed buildings along the Trishuli river has been credited with saving every child and all but two staff

People trapped on balcony in Nepal floods

A quick-thinking teacher who sounded the alarm as a wall of water came crashing down a major river in Nepal has been credited with saving more than 1,600 lives.

‌



Principal Rajendra Dawadi, 47, had already welcomed 900 children to his school, the Tribhuvan Trishuli secondary school in the Trishuli valley of north-central Nepal, when he received an urgent phonecall from a friend on Wednesday, August 26. The friend informed him that the school five miles up river had been taken in the devastating floodwaters that would go on to kill 752 people in Nepal alone, and 16 in Tibet, and leave more than 2,500 others missing.

‌



The impending doom rushing down the Trishuli river to Mr Dawadi's school could have killed another 1,643 people, but they were saved thanks to his quick thinking.

‌



Final happy photo of Brits on Nepal tour - then they were gone READ MORE :

View 7 Images The Tribhuvan Trishuli secondary school was swept away in the floods (Image: FACEBOOK)

The Times reports that floodwaters put every single one of the 900 children already at school and 700 more arriving by bus in the path of a deadly torrent of water, with the Tribhuvan Trishuli secondary school located just 200 feet - 60 metres - from the river's banks.

As the severe floods tore through the Himalayan river system, Mr Dawadi sounded the school bell and told teachers to get the children out of their classrooms.

‌



The teacher then called the drivers of approaching school buses, asking them to turn back moments before they crossed the bridge to their campus. With the warning extended, some of the children had started to panic as they realised the danger.

View 7 Images Principal Rajendra Dawadi saved all his students from the flood

Mr Dawadi followed people rushing away on foot, and after finding shelter under a bodhi tree watched the floodwaters sweep away their school buildings.

‌



Every child and all but two staff members were saved by the principal's quick thinking. Santos Pariyar, 32, was sadly washed away after he returned to his rented room beside the rapidly rising river to cook breakfast that morning. Sultan Lama, the janitor, was killed as a returned to close the doors.

The children saved by Mr Dawadi were lucky not to have been impacted by the water, but others were only rescued after becoming caught in the deadly deluge.

View 7 Images Photos show hollowed out buildings in flood-hit areas (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Urgent rescue operations launched

One five-year-old girl, Manisha, was rescued two days after the floods by emergency teams in Syabrubesi, in Nepal's Ruswa district. She was reunited with her parents at the Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu, the BBC reports, and is in stable condition after emergency workers were alerted to what they thought was a cat miaowing under rubble.

Police officer Sanju Khatri, with Nepal's Armed Police Force, said teams found Manisha trapped after they started moving debris, and it took them two hours to free her.

Other rescuers have been attempting to reach hydropower workers believed to have been trapped in tunnels on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites which have been clogged by flood debris. On Sunday, they deployed heavy machinery as rain and rising river waters hampered their earlier efforts.

‌



View 7 Images People were seen desperately scrambling for safety both before and after the disaster (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Nepal's energy ministry said in a statement: "Drilling of four holes has been completed... preparations are now underway to enter the tunnel directly... and proceed with search and rescue operations."

Also rescued were Laxmi Pandey Pyakurel and her family, who were trapped on a balcony at their home as they were surrounded by floodwaters. Now viral footage showed the family looking down onto the grey waters with seemingly nowhere to run. Laxmi, 42, told the Daily Telegraph: “We saw death very closely. Death was staring at every one of us. We thought these were our final moments. I told everyone that if we had to die, we would die together.”

‌



Brits missing following disaster

As well as local residents swept up in the horror, hundreds of tourists, including 33 Brits, have been reported as missing. Among them is former Mrs India UK Surabhi Manmath Padhy and her husband, Santosh Sahu, who were in the country with their 18-year-old son Spandan and 13-year-old daughter Saina, when the floods hit.

They had reportedly travelled to Nepal en route to Kailash Mansarovar, but have not been heard from since communications were wiped out by the floods.

Spandan had just finished his A-levels at Royal Grammar School, Guildford, and according to his Linkedin page was preparing for a degree in philosophy, politics and economics. A spokesperson for his school said they have been "reported missing" in Nepal.

‌



View 7 Images Satellite footage shows where the massive torrent of water burst the banks of the Himalayan rivers (Image: 2026 Planet Labs PBC/AFP via Getty Images)

They said: "It is with great concern that we have been informed that a former student, along with members of his family, have been reported missing in Nepal.

"Whilst we are hoping for positive news, we do not have any further information at this time. Our thoughts, love and deepest sympathies are with all of the families and loved ones of anyone affected by this tragedy in Nepal at this incredibly difficult time."

‌



The brother of another missing Brit, Neetu Goyal Tiwari, has pleaded "help us find her" after revealing she had not been seen since Wednesday.

View 7 Images Rescuers are digging through a mass of dirt carried down river by the flooding (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

He said his family has " called every helpline given by the Indian government and reached out to the British Embassy in Kathmandu" as they are "very scared" while worrying about what may have happened. Newlywed food truck owner Pramod Poudel said his wife Sumitra went missing following the floods and started his own search for her.

‌



He told The Sun that her last words to him were "I love you so much", saying: “When I last spoke to her, she said to me, ‘How are you? I love you so much.’

“I have not had contact with her since then. It’s devastating — I don’t even know how to explain how I’m feeling right now. I’m so worried about her, and all my family. I work so hard for them and they are my whole world. I’m very hopeful of finding them but I’m also praying to God.”

More flood warnings

Flood warning notices were sent to people's phones early Sunday as rescue crews worked to clear a major highway connecting Kathmandu to one of the areas worst hit by Wednesday's catastrophic floods, as some residents began returning to ruined homes to see what can be salvaged.

‌



Residents sat in homes with walls washed away by the floods, shovelling sludge-like mud and rubble off balconies or window frames.

The latest warnings came after Chinese authorities informed their Nepalese counterparts of increased water flow upstream, according to Dharam Raj Uprety, chief executive of Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

View 7 Images Footage taken on the ground shows people stuck in mud and slush following the disaster (Image: Nepalese Army/AFP via Getty Images)

Article continues below

But residents of the flood-hit villages said they were struggling to make sense of near-constant alarms they've received since the initial floods.

"Sometimes they say a flood is coming, then we have to run again to higher ground, even at night. There is also rain," said Govind Shreshta, a resident. "It's really difficult for me. I have a 72-year-old father and 70-year-old mom. I must carry them and I am exhausted. It's going on like this for those who are still alive."

News.title: 'I'm a sleep expert, this is how to stay cool in bed during a heatwave''
News.content:
'I'm a sleep expert, this is how to stay cool in bed during a heatwave''

As summers warm up, cooling sleep tech and simple hacks like breathable bedding and light duvets are replacing high togs to help you stay comfortable all night.

View 3 Images Hotter summers are becoming the new normal, but there are plenty of ways to cool down before sleep (Image: Getty Images)

With hotter summers becoming the new normal, we're starting to think about our bedrooms differently. "For decades we've focused on keeping warm in winter. Now we're having to think about keeping cool instead," says Simba sleep expert UK Lisa Artis. "Breathable bedding, lighter duvets and mattresses designed to regulate temperature are becoming just as important as high tog ratings once were.

‌



"There's no single miracle solution to sleeping through a heatwave. But combining a few simple cooling hacks with sleep technology that's designed to disperse heat will give you the best chance of staying comfortable until morning." Lisa shares her three cooling sleep hacks actually worth trying...

‌



Skip the freezing shower

"It sounds like the obvious answer, but an ice-cold shower isn't actually the best way to cool down before bed," says Lisa. "It can trigger your body to conserve heat, meaning you may end up feeling warmer afterwards. A lukewarm shower is much more effective because it allows your body temperature to fall naturally as you cool after stepping out."

‌



View 3 Images 'An ice-cold shower isn't actually the best way to cool down before bed," says Lisa (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Yes... fridge socks really can work

"It sounds bizarre, but cooling your feet can genuinely help," says Lisa. "Your feet are packed with blood vessels close to the skin's surface, making them one of the quickest places for your body to release heat. Pop a clean pair of socks into the fridge for around 30 minutes before bed. The cooling effect is gentle but often enough to help your body switch into sleep mode."

Chill the pillowcase, not the pillow

"Your head and neck are major heat-loss zones, so cooling them can make falling asleep much easier," says Lisa. "Rather than freezing the entire pillow, place just the pillowcase in a sealed bag in the fridge for around 20 minutes. You'll get that instant cooling sensation without ending up with a damp pillow later in the night."

‌



Choose clever bedding

While these tricks may help you fall asleep, Lisa says they won't keep you cool if your mattress and bedding are trapping heat for the next eight hours. "Cooling hacks only last for a few minutes. Your mattress, duvet and bedding affect your body temperature all night long. If they're holding onto heat, there's only so much frozen socks can do."

View 3 Images With hotter summers becoming the new normal, Lisa believes we're starting to think about our bedrooms differently. (Image: Simba)

Instead, she recommends treating your summer sleep set-up like cooling technology rather than simply bedding. "Choose lightweight, breathable fabrics that allow air to circulate and moisture to escape. And if you're investing in a mattress, look for one that's specifically engineered to promote airflow rather than trap heat.

‌



“Simba's Hybrid® mattresses combine patented Aerocoil® springs with Simbatex®, an open-structured, graphite-infused foam engineered with thousands of tiny perforations. The result is more than five times the airflow of standard memory foam*, allowing excess body heat to escape while fresh air circulates through the mattress throughout the night."

With hotter summers becoming the new normal, Lisa believes we're starting to think about our bedrooms differently. "For decades we've focused on keeping warm in winter.

"Now we're having to think about keeping cool instead. Breathable bedding, lighter duvets and mattresses designed to regulate temperature are becoming just as important as high tog ratings once were. There's no single miracle solution to sleeping through a heatwave. But combining a few simple cooling hacks with sleep technology that's designed to disperse heat will give you the best chance of staying comfortable until morning."

News.title: Freddie Mercury's 'only friend' Mary Austin reveals devastating detail about relationship
News.content:
Freddie Mercury's 'only friend' Mary Austin reveals devastating detail about relationship

Freddie Mercury's best friend, Mary Austin, who almost married the Queen icon, has spoken out about the troubled star, including the moment he told her he had HIV

View 7 Images Freddie Mercury will forever be remembered as one of the world's most prolific performers (Image: Popperfoto via Getty Images)

Mary Austin remembers first meeting Freddie Mercury at a time when Queen didn’t even have a name; a young man with a 'halo' of thick brown hair who spoke with confidence and conviction.

‌



Within just a few years, Freddie had gone from being a young graduate asking Biba receptionist Mary on a first date in Soho, and months later inviting her move into a £5-a-week flat, to becoming the frontman of one of the biggest bands in rock history.

‌



Born Farrokh Bulsara, Freddie - together with his Queen bandmates Brian May, and Roger Taylor - produced some of the most enduring songs in music history, with timeless hits including Bohemian Rhapsody and We Are the Champions.

‌



But behind the flamboyant stage persona was a complicated private life. Freddie struggled with his sexuality and, later, a devastating HIV diagnosis. Throughout it all, Mary remained one of the most important people in his life - his former fiancée, closest friend and confidante, standing by him until his death in 1991, aged 45.

Praising Mary, Freddie once said: "All my lovers asked me why they couldn’t replace Mary, but it’s simply impossible. The only friend I’ve got is Mary, and I don’t want anybody else. To me, she was my common-law wife. To me, it was a marriage."

View 7 Images Freddie Mercury with his lifelong friend and one-time partner, Mary Austin and John Reid, music manager (Image: Mirrorpix)

‌



The couple were so close, that the singer asked her to marry him, and he also left Mary half of his £75 million estate, including the keys to his £25 million Georgian mansion in Kensington, in his will.

Mary, played by Lucy Boynton, in the film Bohemian Rhapsody, which stars Rami Malek as Freddie, is widely considered to be one of the most important people in the singer's life and now she's opened up about their relationship in heartbreaking detail.

Speaking about the moment he proposed on Christmas Day in 1973, after being introduced to Freddie by Queen guitarist, Brian May, she told The Times: “Freddie handed me a large square box. When I tore away the paper, there was another box inside. It was so like him. I opened the second box and found another, then another. Finally, I reached a small jewellery box with a silver ring inside."

‌



Revealing the charasmatic singer "looked as nervous as I’d ever known him" before popping the question, Mary continued: "We hadn’t talked about marriage. Even so, I didn’t need to think. “Yes,” I said. “I will.” I was 22; he, 27.”

View 7 Images The couple were so close, that at one stage the singer asked her to marry him (Image: Popperfoto via Getty Images)

Despite their romantic engagement, Mary said cracks began to show and she could tell Freddie was "struggling" with an internal conflict. "Emotionally, he was sincere with me, but physically he was moving somewhere else."

‌



Claiming she believes his song Lily of the Valley was written about her, she cited the lyrics: 'I lie in wait with open eyes, I carry on through stormy skies …But the Lily of the Valley doesn’t know', explaining: "I didn’t find out for some time what the Lily of the Valley didn’t know. There was so much change happening around us, uncertainty felt almost normal."

In early 1977 Freddie told Mary he was bisexual, to which she replied: “No, you’re gay.” Insisting she didn't mean to hurt him with her response she says: "He didn’t reply to that. It wasn’t said to wound him, nor to deny him anything, just that I knew immediately what his proclamation meant for me."

7 View 7 Images They were introduced by Queen guitarist Brian May (Image: PA) 7 View 7 Images Despite their romantic engagement, Mary said Freddie soon began to 'struggle' (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Mary went on to have two sons with the painter Piers Cameron, who she separated from in 1991.

She says she did think about distancing herself from Freddie entirely after their split and was offered a job at CBS Records in London. However, she decided to turn it down and continued to work as the star's PA.

Their relationship evolved, with Mary revealing Freddie even introduced her to his boyfriends. "It still hurt, but things were better", she said.

‌



7 View 7 Images Mary supported Freddie throughout his life (Image: Mirrorpix) 7 View 7 Images Mary at Freddie's funeral (Image: Mirrorpix)

As Queen's fame continued to rise with sold-out shows and Number One hits, Freddie was battling a private hell.

‌



On the outside, his band reached a career high with their show-stealing performance at Live Aid followed by a run of stadium shows across Europe, culminating in a concert at Knebworth in 1986 in front of 120,000 fans.

It would become Freddie’s final performance with Queen.

Mary said her best friend in the world revealed his HIV diagnosis to her in the spring of 1987, but the pair kept it private.

‌



They both knew that performing would soon become impossible, with Freddie telling Mary 'how physically painful it was becoming.'

Five years later, Freddie died, leaving the world - and Mary - in mourning.

Freddie never forgot his “wife”, leaving her a piece of his world forever. “He left me his cherished home. His sanctuary became mine,” Mary said.

‌



This year, Freddie would have celebrated his 80th birthday on September 5. To mark the milestone, Mary has worked with the V&A to launch a free temporary trail, Freddie Mercury: Splendid Things, showcasing costumes and accessories from throughout his extraordinary career.

The collection takes its name from a quote the flamboyant frontman gave in 1978: “I like to be surrounded by splendid things. I want to lead a Victorian life surrounded by exquisite clutter.”

It is a fitting description of a man whose love of flamboyance and fashion. And one that takes on an especially poignant meaning when remembering one of the last times Mary saw Freddie at his usual bombastic self before his illness took hold, at a “silly hat-themed” party held to celebrate his 40th birthday.

News.title: Pistachio Green named hottest colour of the year - and it's everywhere
News.content:
Pistachio Green named hottest colour of the year - and it's everywhere

The soft green hue has been dubbed the trendiest colour of 2026 so far

View 2 Images The colour is used for everything; from food to fashion (Image: Getty Images)

Pistachio has been crowned the most fashionable colour of 2026, new research has revealed. A survey of 2,000 adults discovered the delicate green shade triumphed over contenders including sage green, chocolate brown, and butter yellow to claim the top spot amongst tones that best reflect the mood of the year so far.

‌



More than six in 10 (62%) reported spotting the trendy shade cropping up increasingly throughout their everyday lives, from food and beverages to clothing, home décor and social media content.

‌



The pistachio phenomenon seems particularly pronounced amongst younger age groups, with 89% of Gen Z and 77% of Millennials having observed the colour featuring more prominently in 2026.

‌



The research was commissioned by Samsung to coincide with the launch of the Galaxy S26 FE, which is available in pistachio, blueberry and graphite.

Colour trends also appear to influence taste and behaviour, as 66% of Gen Z and 55% of Millennials have found themselves liking a shade more after seeing it repeatedly in fashion.

It also emerged that colours can act as an instant time machine, with 46% saying certain hues can transport them back to a specific stage in their lives.

‌



View 2 Images Pistachio beat sage green and chocolate brown to the top spot

Annika Bizon, from the tech firm, said: “Colour has an incredible ability to capture a moment.

“We remember the shades of the clothes we wore, the interiors we loved and even the technology we carried, and together they become part of how we picture an era.”

‌



The study also found colour has a surprisingly powerful ability to date our memories, as 28% said a particular one reminds them of their childhood.

While 23% associate certain hues with their teenage years and 50% say shades can bring back memories of a particular decade. Others find themselves transported back through colours connected to fashion movements (28%), food and beverages (23%), films and telly (17%), or gadgets (10%).

Some shades have become so synonymous with their moment that they now risk instantly dating whatever they appear on, according to 63%.

‌



Avocado green was named the colour most likely to make something look like it belongs to another era, followed by mustard yellow, chocolate brown, and burnt orange.

The importance of colour is especially clear in technology, as 61% believe an unusual colour makes a tech product stand out.

While 52% think the right colour can make technology feel more fashionable and 51% said it can make a tech product feel more personal.

‌



Younger adults are even more likely to see device colour as part of their identity, with 61% of Gen Z and 57% of Millennials seeing this as part of their personal style, compared with just 20% of over 60s.

Annika Bizon, from Samsung UK & Ireland, whose new Galaxy S26 FE boasts upgraded camera features and AI-driven functions including My FanCam, Horizontal Lock and Photo Assist, commented: "Pistachio feels particularly right for 2026 because we're seeing this fresh, expressive shade move beyond one trend or category and into so many different parts of culture, from food and fashion to interiors and design.

"Technology is increasingly an extension of personal style too. We carry our phones everywhere, so people understandably want a device that doesn't just perform brilliantly but feels personal to them."

News.title: PC Harper's killers to stay in jail as PM announces changes to early release scheme
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told the BBC that PC Andrew Harper's killers will remain behind bars as he announced changes to the early release scheme aimed at easing prison overcrowding.

In an exclusive interview with BBC Breakfast, Burnham said anyone convicted of unlawful killing, including all forms of manslaughter, would be excluded from the scheme, which would have made two of the officer's killers eligible for early release.

Burnham said extra prison space would be created by deporting foreign prisoners and releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences.

It follows months of campaigning from PC Harper's family and former colleagues to block the release of his killers.

The 28-year-old was responding to a burglary in Berkshire in 2019 when he was dragged along a road by a vehicle as three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft.

When it emerged that two of the killers, Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, could be released early, there were passionate calls for the government to intervene and block those convicted of manslaughter from early release.

"I heard obviously what Andrew Harper's family were saying, I mean who couldn't? Nobody would want a position to arise where those guilty of killing a police officer are let out early from prison," Burnham told the BBC.

He conceded the announcement would mean "hundreds" more people stay in prison, meaning additional space will need to be found in a system that is more than 97% full in England and Wales.

News.title: Burnham gets the early prison release changes he wanted - but at what cost?
News.content:
The prime minister's announcement that he will keep hundreds of criminals behind bars who would otherwise have been released early is one he has wanted to make for weeks.

Andy Burnham had already expanded the list of people ineligible for early release and had consistently said he wanted to go further.

What is not clear is exactly what has changed to allow him to do so.

Earlier this month, the Ministry of Justice warned that exempting any more prisoners risked "prisons reaching capacity and collapsing".

The prime minister himself previously said he had "pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do".

In his exclusive interview with BBC Breakfast, Burnham picked out the release of people on controversial indefinite sentences and the deportation of foreign criminals as measures that had made his latest intervention possible.

It is understood extra capacity will also be created by immediately beginning work to create new cells in existing prisons.

But none of these are short-term solutions.

Ending indefinite sentences will require new legislation, meaning it could be years before space is freed up.

Previous governments have struggled to quickly deport foreign offenders and there are not thought to be any new returns agreements with other countries. The case of grooming gang ringleader Shabir Ahmed, who Pakistan has resisted attempts to deport, is one example.

Retrofitting prisons to create more cells is also expected to take months.

People in government concede that in the short-term, Burnham will only be able to follow through on today's announcement by making prisons even more full.

With the adult male prison estate already running at 98% capacity, it is a move that could worry some in the sector.

But in the end, the prime minister believed he simply had to act.

The extra exemptions Burnham has announced are being described within government as a "political decision".

That is not surprising given the intense pressure that had built up, especially around the potential for PC Andrew Harper's killers to be released early.

Burnham's inner circle are mindful that political misjudgements at the start of Sir Keir Starmer's premiership caused long-lasting damage.

They believe Sir Keir never recovered from early rows over freebies and winter fuel payments, and point to a lack of major mishaps in Burnham's first six weeks in office as evidence of a more slick political operation.

There was some surprise in Downing Street about how much media attention the issue of early release received over the summer.

That is one reason why the prime minister's aides are relishing the new parliamentary term, when news stories come along at a faster rate and so are less likely to linger in the headlines.

After the initial flip-flopping on whether the government would be able to exempt more prisoners, the mother of PC Harper told BBC Breakfast that the handling of the situation had been a "hash".

Government officials working on the plans have spoken to the families of victims, who made it clear they did not want the new measures to be dripped out in leaks to the media.

Instead it was decided one big announcement would be the neatest option.

It had seemed likely that would come in the form of a parliamentary statement on Tuesday from the justice secretary.

Instead, the prime minister decided to make the announcement himself in an interview with BBC Breakfast.

It is understood Burnham was mindful of mounting speculation and wanted to give victims and the public as much certainty at the earliest possible opportunity.

In doing so, he may have risked the ire of the Speaker Sir Lindsay Hoyle, who is generally disdainful of governments that make major announcements outside of Parliament.

He may also have offered up ammunition to the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, who has already accused Burnham of being a "people pleaser" who finds it difficult to say no to people.

That characterisation is likely to be tested again when more stories inevitably appear about the victims of prisoners who will still be released early.

It already started on Sunday morning, when the domestic abuse commissioner said she remained "deeply concerned about the number of abusers" still set to be freed.

While this is not the first time Burnham has said he has pushed the system to the limit, Whitehall sources are now adamant there will be no more additional exemptions.

News.title: British woman killed in stabbing at German railway station
News.content:
A British woman has died after being stabbed at a railway station in southern Germany in the early hours of Sunday morning, police have said.

The 31-year-old woman was attacked at the station in Rosenheim, Bavaria, shortly before 01:00 local time (00:00BST). She was taken to hospital where she died as a result of "severe" injuries, the Bavarian Police said in a statement.

Officers arrested a 27-year-old German man at the scene immediately after the incident. The background and motive for the attack is under investigation, the statement added.

Police have asked anyone who may have witnessed "an argument or physical altercation" at the station late on Saturday or early on Sunday to contact them.

The suspect, from the FÃ¼rstenfeldbruck district, will be brought before magistrates later on Sunday, according to German news agency DPA.

It is not known if the two knew each other or what the woman was doing in Bavaria, DPA also reported.

Rosenheim is one of the largest cities in Upper Bavaria and is a busy rail hub for passengers travelling to Austrian cities including Vienna, Salzburg and Innsbruck.

The Rosenheimer Herbstfest - an event similar to the Oktoberfest beer festival - is currently taking place in the area.

News.title: Church names pastor killed by falling sign at Christian festival
News.content:
The man killed at a Christian festival in West Sussex on Friday has been named by his church as Robert Guanco, 41.

He was a pastor at Jesus the Living Water Church in Eastbourne, East Sussex.

Six other people were injured at the event by a falling sign at the Big Church Festival, near Steyning, four of whom were taken to hospital for treatment.

In a statement, his church said: "Pastor Robert was a faithful servant of God, a loving husband to Isay, a devoted and caring father to Ellie, and a blessing to so many people whose lives he touched. His life, his faith, his love, and his service to God will never be forgotten."

On a fundraising page for Guanco's family, pastor Norman Ponce from Jesus the Living Water Worldwide Church, said he was a "faithful servant of God".

"What was meant to be a time of worship, fellowship, and celebration became an unimaginable tragedy," he added.

Ponce said Guanco was a "beloved son, cherished brother, loving husband" and "great father".

"He was also a good friend, mentor, and a blessing to so many people whose lives he touched," Ponce said.

"His life reflected humility, faith, love, compassion, and service. Through his ministry, kindness, prayers, and encouragement, he touched many lives."

News.title: China censors videos showing deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border
News.content:
Dramatic footage showing flash floods tearing through the main border crossing between Nepal and Tibet has been widely shared around the world.

But the footage has become almost impossible to find on China's heavily censored internet service, with only a single image broadcast by state media.

Hundreds of people are feared dead, and thousands remain missing as a major rescue operation continues into the weekend.

On Saturday, Chinese state media shared videos of rescue teams searching through mud and debris, but there has been little footage of the floods themselves, or accounts from survivors or anxious families.

Tibet remains a highly sensitive subject for China following its annexation in the 1950s. The region has long demanded greater autonomy and is one of the most strictly controlled regions in the country, with access for foreign media tightly restricted.

Read more on this story.

News.title: 97-year-old woman rescued after Nepali floods looked like 'a warrior'
News.content:
A 97-year-old woman pulled from flood debris in Nepal is recovering in hospital, according to her doctors.

Guna Maya Bohara's great-nephew, Dipak Bohara, has told BBC Nepali she looked like "a warrior" who had returned victorious from battle.

The operation to pull Bohara out of the rubble of her care home took four hours.

Bohara travelled from Kathmandu to help rescue his great-aunt.

Hundreds of people have been confirmed dead after Wednesday's flash floods, which scientists believe were triggered by a glacier collapsing in the Himalayan border region with Tibet.

Video produced by Mansi Kapur and Kamal Pariyar. Video edited by Suneth Perera, Jasmin Dyer and Andrew Webb.

More on this story here.

News.title: What we know about the 33 British nationals missing in Nepal
News.content:
Families are flying out to Nepal to help the ongoing search for 33 British nationals still missing after deadly floods hit the country.

The brother of Neetu Goyal Tiwari, one of the missing Brits who has not been seen since Wednesday, has appealed to officials to locate his sister.

"Please help us find her", Naresh Goyal told the BBC as he struggled to hold back his emotions.

On Friday, Nepalese authorities named 573 tourists who are still missing in the country and despite fears of a second wave of flooding, search efforts have continued.

To help, the UK is deploying a rapid deployment team to Nepal to support British nationals affected in the region.

The specially-trained crisis response team is expected to arrive in Kathmandu on Saturday, a move that follows Prime Minister Andy Burnham's pledge of Â£5m worth of humanitarian support for relief and recovery efforts.

And as rescue efforts continue in the aftermath of the disaster which killed at least 538 people, details of the missing are slowly emerging.

News.title: We all share a 15-acre Georgian mansion for the price of a two-bed house
News.content:
Residents range in age from seven to 70. This summer, however, the balance will shift towards a younger demographic, as two older residents are leaving and two families with three children aged from six to 12 will be moving in.

There is a four-stage application process to become a community member.

"We know that the more effort we put into the application process, the better chance it's going to work and it's going to be a good fit," says Louise.

Jenny Kincova, 64, the longest current resident of nine years' standing, is one of those moving on to live in Llanidloes itself, like a number of previous residents.

She says of her move to Dol-llys: "I was on my own. My girls had left home. I didn't just want to move to a place and not know anyone. Once I moved here, I was really excited by the prospect of communal decision-making and cooperative community living."

Although she still enjoys the communal living, she has started to find the "emotional energy" needed for decision-making and keeping a group together tiring.

"I don't want to lose contact with here at all," she said.

"As you can see, we still get on, it's not about that at all. It's just about change again.

"I'm not going to have all this space and I'm not going to live in a listed building."

The hall offers free allotments to locals in exchange for some help on their work days, holds open days, lets groups use its communal rooms for things like yoga classes, and will be holding its first board games weekend this summer.

Its residents even gave the hall to friends for free to use as their wedding venue.

It has recently hosted volunteer workers from the Wwoof (Worldwide Opportunities on Organic Farms) organisation, where people get free board and lodging for two weeks while helping out with projects in the grounds and learning skills.

News.title: Two missing as French fishing boat sinks in Channel
News.content:
Searches are continuing for two crew members after a French fishing boat sank in the English Channel, the Maritime and Coastguard Agency said.

A coastguard rescue helicopter, fixed-wing plane and two RNLI lifeboats began searching an area south-west of Eddystone Lighthouse off Plymouth after the crew released a distress call at 18:00 BST on Saturday.

HM Coastguard in Falmouth said three people were rescued from the boat and have been taken to hospital.

A large number of civilian vessels are assisting the "intensive search" for the two remaining crew members, an HM Coastguard spokesperson added.

They also confirmed that an intensive search was maintained during the night.

"It is continuing today with multiple assets sent to help," they said.

Lifeboat crews from Newlyn and Salcombe have taken over the search from the Plymouth and Falmouth RNLI crews, who worked through the night.

News.title: Man Utd pay tribute to 'proud Red' officer who died in A66 crash
News.content:
The two sons of a police officer killed in a crash on Teesside will lead out the Manchester United team as mascots for Sunday's Premier League match against Ipswich at Old Trafford.

PC Matthew Blades, described as a "proud Red" by United, was a regular at Old Trafford. The club have paid tribute to him in Sunday's match programme. His widow will attend the game with their children.

PC Blades and his colleague PC Tom Clough died in a head-on collision between their police car and a vehicle going the wrong way on the A66 near Middlesbrough early on 22 August. Five people in the other vehicle also died.

United said they learned of the deaths of the two officers "with great sadness".

"Matthew was a proud Red, a devoted family man and a police officer who dedicated his life to helping others," said the club, in a tribute in the programme.

On Saturday, there was a minute's applause in memory of PC Blades and PC Clough before Middlesbrough's Championship encounter with West Brom at Riverside Stadium. Pictures of the two men were displayed on a screen.

People also gathered to pay tribute at Seaton Carew FC's game against FC Hartlepool. PC Blades had been a junior football coach at both teams.

Earlier this week, 17 people were arrested in connection with the investigation into the crash bringing the total number of arrests to 24.

The occupants of the other vehicle, a Passat - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17, also died.

News.title: Girl faces six-month recovery after 'freak accident' bus crash on holiday
News.content:
After eight days in hospital, Greta was transported back to the UK for treatment with Williams in an air ambulance which their Â£106 travel insurance policy covered.

"They [the pilots and medics] told me it cost â¬50,000 just for the flight. That was quite scary, Â£106 paid for that. Anything can happen."

Williams said Jet2, which sold them the package holiday, waived the cost of changing Len and Eiry-ana's flights back to the UK.

Greta was admitted to The Grange University Hospital in Cwmbran and had physiotherapy, and will find out on 2 September whether she can return to school.

"We can't do anything until that assessment. It's strict bedrest at the minute.

"She's not allowed to do much, she's not allowed to walk loads or do much which is a massive shame. Her friends have been fantastic."

Williams added: "She was petrified when it happened. All she wanted was reassurance from me. We tried to keep it as positive as we could in the circumstances.

"She was phenomenally strong. I'm so proud of how she coped."

"This is something that's going to haunt us forever," added Williams.

"It's going to take a long time to get over it all. We need normality to hit first, as we're in the summer holidays, before we can process it properly.

"You can see the accident has impacted them, and being in a foreign country has escalated their fears.

"We were trying to fill it in with so many experiences and memories as possible to make it fun-filled.

"They don't want to go on holiday ever again. We're going to try and take them somewhere - probably not on an excursion - to ease their mind. It was a one-off freak accident, and these things don't generally happen."

Graeme Buck from the Association of British Travel Agents said travel insurance was "one of the must-haves whenever you travel overseas".

"While most holidays go ahead without any problems, accidents and unexpected events can happen, and the costs of medical treatment and getting home can be significant.

"Cheap isn't always the best, and it's important not to choose a policy based on price alone. Holidaymakers should check what their policy covers and make sure they have comprehensive cover that is appropriate for their trip, including any activities they plan to take part in, such as winter sports."

News.title: Two murder arrests after balcony fall man dies
News.content:
Two men have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a man who fell from a balcony died.

Officers were called to reports that the man had fallen at flats on Liverpool Street in Salford shortly after midnight on Saturday, Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said.

The force said the man died later that night. A man arrested on suspicion of attempted murder has now been arrested on suspicion of murder.

A second man has also been arrested on suspicion of murder.

The incident has been referred to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) because the men had earlier contact with police, GMP said.

An IOPC spokesperson said: "After being notified by the Greater Manchester Police of the previous police contact with the parties involved in this incident, we sent investigators to the police post-incident procedures in Manchester in assessment mode to gather further information.

"We continue to remain in assessment mode and will assess a GMP referral in due course."

News.title: Dementia patient's deportation from Sweden delayed
News.content:
A man with dementia will be able to remain in Sweden while a legal bid to delay his deportation is considered.

The Swedish authorities said they wanted George Mason, originally from Hinckley in Leicestershire, to leave the country by midnight on 20 August, after his application for permanent residency was rejected.

Mason's daughter, Michelle Torossian, said the family had been told an injunction to halt his deportation would be decided by Swedish authorities in a timeframe of two weeks to six months.

Torossian said she was told by the British Embassy in Stockholm that the original deportation decision would not be enforced by the authorities while the injunction order was considered.

The BBC has contacted the Swedish Migration Agency, which said it was unable to comment on individual cases.

News.title: Heavyweight Itauma handed harsh world-title lesson
News.content:
It would be too simplistic - and unfair - to say Hrgovic won the fight purely through mind games, but the 34-year-old had succeeded in making the build-up uncomfortable.

Hrgovic spent fight week repeatedly attacking Itauma's age, dismissing him as "just a kid". As the week wore on, Itauma looked increasingly irritated and eventually lost his composure at the weigh-in, shoving Hrgovic before the Croatian responded with a slap.

Itauma prides himself on being unusually cerebral for a heavyweight. He reads psychology and self-help books, talks openly about sharpening his mind and appears to spend far more time analysing himself than most 21-year-olds.

But there is always a danger that deep thinking becomes overthinking, something Anthony Joshua has been accused of repeatedly during the latter stages of his career.

Whether the pre-fight barbs played any part or not, Itauma's gameplan once the bell rang was clear; he wanted to end the night early.

"Someone said to me he doesn't feel like he'd win a world title unless he knocks him out. I didn't like that," Warren said.

That mindset was understandable because it had served Itauma extraordinarily well until now. But perhaps Hrgovic had been underestimated by almost everybody - Itauma, the media, pundits, former fighters and bookmakers who installed the Briton as a heavy favourite.

Hrgovic is an Olympic bronze medallist who went 12 hard rounds with the giant Zhilei Zhang, while against Daniel Dubois - the only defeat on his record - he was leading on two of the three scorecards before the fight was stopped because of cuts.

'El Animal' knew what it felt like to be hurt, to become tired and to remain in a fight when things were going badly. Itauma did not.

News.title: Swimmers told to avoid beauty spot as 'hidden hazards' revealed by drought and fires
News.content:
People have been warned to stay away from a popular beauty spot pond used for swimming and other water sports due to "hidden hazards" exposed by reduced water levels.

Keepers Pond in Abergavenny poses "serious safety risks" with levels dangerously low, according to Bannau Brycheiniog National Park, also known as the Brecon Beacons.

It said that along with the prolonged dry spell, the water had been used to tackle recent wildfires.

"As the water has receded, previously hidden hazards and unknown objects have been exposed on the pond bed, creating serious safety risks. For your own safety, you must not enter the water under any circumstances," the park authority said in a Facebook post, external.

News.title: 'Click, don't pick' warning as fungi posts mushroom
News.content:
Social media posts showcasing fungi picking is affecting a forest's ecosystem, according to officials.

Picking wild mushrooms from Epping Forest in Essex is banned under by-laws but fungi-related content has surged in popularity online.

Foragers risk getting fined or prosecuted for picking the mushrooms, but they can also be poisonous if eaten.

Caroline Haines, the chair of the City Corporation's Epping Forest and Commons Committee, said posts showing mushrooms being collected "can encourage others to follow suit" and urged people to "click, don't pick".

Picking the fungi can disrupt the forest's ecosystem, which helps recycle nutrients, support wildlife, and preserve some 55,000 ancient trees.

However, fungi-related content continues to grow in popularity on social media, with posts showcasing unusual mushrooms and foraging finds attracting large audiences.

Every year, the August bank holiday has an absurdly frenetic energy – a last hoorah type of party that sees even those begging for the mercy of autumn pulled back onto the dancefloor by those who refuse to accept the warmer weather’s jig is almost up. Soon, it’ll be long nights and (whisper it) Christmas – but it’s not all over yet: free day parties in Hackney, the 60th anniversary of Notting Hill Carnival, a double-billing of Tyler, the Creator at All Points East and Maribou State at Lido festival are reigniting the summer spirit in London alone.

As such, the final bank holiday until December is always accompanied by something else, too: warning messages about drugs, each year seemingly more supersonic than the last. This year’s highlights include: pink cocaine (a mixture of ketamine, MDMA and pink colouring), a new-ish form of ketamine, called 2-Fluorodeschloroketamine, and high-potency ecstasy.

open image in gallery A tablet marked ‘It’s Coming Home’, which was among a large quantity of Class A, B and C drugs found by police buried in the grounds of the Creamfields 2026 festival ( Cheshire Police )

Ahead of this year’s Creamfields festival in Cheshire, police dug up 204 canisters of laughing gas, MDMA and ketamine while searching the grounds. The superintendent in charge of the operation said he expected to find more drugs below ground as the dig continued, adding dealers would be “very disappointed” to find their products had vanished from the site.

So, are party drugs getting stronger year on year? Dr Caroline Copeland, senior lecturer in Pharmacology and Toxicology at King’s College London, and director of the UK’s National Programme on Substance Use Mortality (NPSUM), says not exactly. “MDMA is like alcohol. So, the potency doesn’t change, but a tablet can have more MDMA in it than usual.”

Instead, substances are hitting harder due to the increasing number of ingredients frequently mixed into party drugs. “On the database I run, we’ve seen the average number of substances detected increase from two or three in the mid-2000s to five or six substances on average today. So, polydrug use is definitely going up, which is more dangerous.”

open image in gallery Pink cocaine is a strawberry-flavoured polydrug that commonly contains MDMA and ketamine ( AFP/Getty )

“You just don’t know what’s in it” is a common cry from parents attempting to dissuade young people from recreational drug use. From her research, Copeland has some idea: she’s seen cocaine commonly cut with the anti-worming agent levamisole, which has been linked to cancer, and illicit vapes laced with anaesthetics, which can cause abnormal heart rhythms.

A new, particularly troubling, rumour is that nitazenes – a class of synthetic opioid 500 times stronger than heroin– could find their way into party drugs, thus potentially leading naive users, unaware they’re ingesting a substance far stronger than fentanyl, towards a fatal overdose.

“It’s a huge concern for the sector,” says Ruth Squires, who oversees the youth drug and alcohol harm reduction service, 1625 Outreach, for the social charity Change Grow Live.

MDMA is like alcohol. So, the potency doesn’t change but a tablet can have more MDMA in it than usual Dr Caroline Copeland, director of the National Programme on Substance Use Mortality

“Currently, synthetic opioids like nitazines are being found more in opiate use, like heroin. However, there is a fear in the field that this will start to impact the wider market. We’re not seeing too much of that on the ground yet, but I think the risk is a real concern.”

Synthetics are increasingly appealing to drug gangs – and Copeland concurs the market is about to see much more of them. “Cartels are realising that, for naturally occurring products like the opium poppy, cocoa plants, cannabis, you need land, good weather, cultivation techniques, farming equipment and the products themselves are very bulky, so if you’re trying to traffic them, they’re much more difficult to hide.”

open image in gallery ‘A huge concern’: Nitazenes are a synthetic opioid that are 500 times stronger than heroin ( DEA )

As synthetic substances are astronomically more potent, gangs don’t need to make as much, which is cheaper. “You also don’t have as large a quantity to smuggle,” Copeland notes. “You could put one gram in 100 greeting cards, and if 99 of them get intercepted at the border, even if only one gets through, that gram could be diluted into 1,000 doses. When you have a change like that in the market, combined with higher demand, that can lead to bad mixing on behalf of the drug gangs.” Next thing you know, supersonic tablets.

When it comes to the end user mixing substances, Copeland says there are broadly three scenarios that are “very bad”: Taking multiple depressants together, which can cause respiratory depression; taking multiple stimulants together, which can cause serotonin syndrome or cardiac toxicity; and taking a mix of uppers and downers. “Then you’re hitting the brake and accelerator at the same time,” she says. “If you did that to a car, you’d break it. So, if you’re making both systems go, that’s a recipe for a physiological crisis.”

People are buying one substance and it’s actually something else entirely Ruth Squires, 1625 Outreach

Alongside the challenge of this synthetic cocktail comes the issue of marketing. Much like how colourful, fruit-flavoured vapes have been declared the “kiddification” of smoking, drug gangs have worked out that if you dye these party powders pink and scent them strawberry, then they’re much more likely to reel in the otherwise health-conscious next generation of ravers.

“Pink cocaine is very Instagram-ready,” says Copeland of the polydrug reportedly found in One Direction singer Liam Payne’s system after he fell to his death from a third-floor balcony in Argentina in 2024. “Its core components would only cost around £20-£30 a gram, but they’re selling it for £130-£150. So, it’s being marketed as more expensive – and a fun product.”

“There was apple-flavoured ketamine at a festival we worked at,” adds Squires, of the novelty products making their way into dealers’ offerings to attract a new audience. “Then you’ve got the edibles area of the drug market, which is absolutely aimed towards children and young people: sweets, crisps, all kinds of things have been laced with synthetic cannabinoids.”

open image in gallery Wiltshire Police seized cannabis-laced gummies which were made to look like Fruit Pastilles earlier this year ( Wiltshire Police )

This August, scientists from the University of Bristol found that weed gummies sold on social media contained a potentially fatal quantity of the synthetic cannabinoid spice. Following testing for the substance, which police said they ordinarily encountered in prisons, up to 20 times the average spice dose was found in the colourfully packaged gummies.

In the last year on record, 5,565 people died from drug poisoning in England and Wales – the highest number since records began in 1993, with drug experts branding the figures a “national scandal”. This included 195 people who died after taking nitazenes, including 21-year-old musician Dylan Rocha, who received drugs laced with the opioid in the post.

“People are buying one substance, and it’s actually something else entirely – that’s the main issue we’re seeing in the festival scene and beyond right now,” concludes Squires of this year’s warnings. Additionally, as the number of substances in a dose goes up, certainty over how to treat overdoses in the event something goes wrong inevitably comes down.

Many people taking drugs at UK festivals across the country this coming weekend will be doing so for the first time. Much like with alcohol, the effects on so-called naive users are markedly more impactful than a seasoned user. “Visit your harm reduction service at the festival site,” urges Squires. “You’re not going to be criminalised – it’s just transparent advice… Start low, go slow. Check in with your friends. If you’re concerned, follow your gut and get help.”

If you or someone you know is suffering from drug addiction, you can seek confidential help and support 24-7 from Frank by calling 0300 123 6600, texting 82111, sending an email or visiting their website here.

More than thousand people are feared missing, including UK tourists, after devastating flash floods tore through villages on the Nepal-Tibet border, killing 752 people.

Authorities in Nepal warned of possible fresh flooding, urging residents in already devastated districts to remain on high alert. The combined death toll in Nepal and Tibet has risen to 768, with more than 3,000 people still missing, authorities said on Sunday.

The mountainous area is popular with hikers and trekkers from around the world as well as pilgrims who cross the Himalayas on journeys to sacred sites such as Mount Kailash and Lake Mansarovar in Tibet.

As rescuers continue to search for survivors and drop off emergency supplies to isolated communities, the UK government says it will do “everything it can” to help British nationals affected by the flash flooding.

open image in gallery ( AFP/Getty )

As the death toll is expected to rise, here is what to know about travel to Nepal and Tibet.



What has happened?

On 26 August, major flooding in Nepal’s Rasuwa district and the border with Tibet has devastated communities living in the mountainous region, with at least 800 foreigners still missing.

Widespread destruction has been caused, with buildings, roads, other transport and communications infrastructure severely damaged.

Videos have shown a wall of water crashing through river banks, collapsing bridges, tearing through homes and other infrastructure in villages along the Bhotekoshi River.

Similar footage from the opposite side of the Nepal-Tibet border also showed people fleeing before a deluge of rock, mud and water engulfed the area.

open image in gallery ( AP )

How many tourists have been affected?

The latest update from the Nepal Tourism Board says 752 tourists are still missing, according to various trekking and travel companies.

Indian nationals make up the highest missing persons count, with 178 unaccounted for, followed by 127 domestic Nepalese tourists. Many of the Indian nationals are believed to be Hindu pilgrims who were trekking towards the sacred site of Mount Kailash in Tibet.

The Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing on the Tibetan side of the border, including more than 100 Nepalis and people from over a dozen other countries.

Additionally, 53 Ukrainians, 51 Malaysians, 65 Americans, 35 Australians and 33 UK nationals remain out of contact, the notice says.

open image in gallery A person looks through the lists of survivors outside Maithili Barrack army training centre, in the aftermath of flash floods and mudslide, Nuwakot district, Nepal ( Reuters )

Sunil Sharma, a spokesperson for the board, said: “We are coordinating with the relevant authorities for their search and rescue.”

The Nepal Tourist Police also told BBC News that they are continuing to collect information from tour operators about the tourists who had travelled in the area.

Some tourists have been rescued, the national police and army have said, although not all their nationalities have been confirmed.

open image in gallery ( AFP/Getty )

Around two dozen tourists had been rescued and brought back from the Rasuwa district to the neighbouring Nuwakot district on Thursday, while 21 Indian nationals were also being brought back to Kathmandu.



What does the UK government say?

The UK’s Foreign Office (FCDO) said on its online advice page that the “situation may change rapidly”.

“If you are travelling in the region, follow the advice of the Nepalese government and local authorities and be alert to the changing situation. The Nepalese government has established a toll-free emergency Nepalese language number, 1234, and a dedicated hotline 1144 accessible in Nepal.”

If you are affected and need assistance from the UK government, call:

from Nepal +977 (0)14237100

from the UK +44 (0) 207 008 5000

It also advises British nationals in Nepal to sign up to get email notifications for updated information.

If you are in the UK, but are concerned about someone in Nepal, the FCDO helpline for information is 020 7008 5000 (24 hours).

open image in gallery ( AFP/Getty )

The FCDO also warns of heavy flooding and landslides in Gyirong County in Shigatse, Tibet, near the Nepal border.

“There is an ongoing risk to life from flooding, landslides and infrastructure damage. Roads, power supplies and telecommunications have also been disrupted.

“Exercise caution and follow the advice of local authorities,” it said.

open image in gallery ( AFP/Getty )

Can I cancel and get money back on my holiday?

As the FCDO has not warned against non-essential travel to Nepal, there will be no special circumstances in place to be able to cancel a trip for a full refund.

The conditions for cancelling your trip will be dependent on your holiday provider, so it’s best to contact them if you’re looking to postpone.

There is no obligation for companies to refund bookings if you want to cancel, and you will not be able to claim on your travel insurance due to safety concerns unless government advice changes.

If you do have travel insurance, some policies include natural disaster cover for an event that prevents you from reaching your holiday destination. Check your insurance policies and speak to your insurer to see where you stand.

Beer-guzzling bandits made off with over 50,000 cans of Pabst Blue Ribbon, prompting the brand to beg for the truckload’s return, “no questions asked.”

A truck carrying 1,602 cases of PBR — equaling 50,000 cans, or 40,000 pounds of beer — disappeared from an Anheuser-Busch distribution center in Montclair, California, on August 17.

The company issued a plea for the beer’s return in an August 21 Instagram post, writing, “To the thief: we don’t fault you for wanting to brag to your friends how much PBR you have, we just wish you obtained it the honorable way.

“Pabst is officially starting the clock now — you have exactly 18 days and 44 minutes to return our truckload of beer, no questions asked. Leading up to that time, we will be offering a reward to anyone who can help us solve this mystery.”

“This is real and we are deadly serious,” the company added.

open image in gallery Some 50,000 cans of beer are missing ( Getty )

The company did not explain its unusual countdown window for the missing shipment’s return, but it may be a nod to 1844, the year Pabst was founded. It was also unclear what kind of reward would be provided for information.

The company said they filed a police report.

In a statement, the Montclair Police Department said it is investigating two cargo thefts reported August 17 at the Anheuser-Busch distribution center, which investigators believe may be related.

The first theft occurred around 10 a.m., when a shipment destined for Tucson, Arizona, was picked up for delivery but never arrived at its intended location.

Authorities said the shipment was valued at approximately $45,000.

open image in gallery Police are investigating two cargo thefts reported August 17 ( Pabst Blue Ribbon )

About an hour later, police said that someone claiming to be a subcontractor used phony paperwork to arrange the pickup of about $25,000 worth of Anheuser-Busch and Pabst Blue Ribbon products.

“Investigators identified similarities between the two incidents and are investigating whether they were committed as part of the same fraudulent cargo-theft operation,” police said.

The incident is under investigation, police said.

Beer enthusiasts in Pabst’s comment section were quick to make jokes about the theft.

“It’s a missing truck of empties and it’s in my driveway,” one user commented on the Instagram post.

“IT WASN’T ME (party at my house tomorrow night 10:00 p.m.,” another user quipped.

“God forbid men have hobbies,” another commenter joked.

A white rice recall has been expanded by the FDA.

The recall of white jasmine rice from Lundberg Family Farms was first announced in April.

Lundberg Family Farms confirmed to The Independent at the time that 4,500 cases of the two-pound bags of white rice sold at Wegmans were affected by the recall over potential foreign material contamination concerns.

Now, the FDA has updated the recall notice to note that over 27,000 two-pound bags of the rice have been affected. The product is often sold at stores including Wegmans, Target, Walmart, Giant, and Whole Foods.

The updated notice also stated that the rice was sold in 13 states: California, Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Louisiana, North Carolina, New Hampshire, New York, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin.

open image in gallery White rice has been recalled in 13 states ( Getty/iStock )

The recalled product can be identified with the UPC 073416-040281. Some packages have the Lot Number 260201MA and Best Before date of February 1, 2027, and others have the Lot Number 260202MA and Best Before date of February 2, 2027.

In a statement to People, Lundberg Family Farms said: “The affected product was removed from store shelves several months ago.

“The incident was isolated to a single production run, and no illnesses were reported from consumption of the affected product.”

The white rice recall is the latest plaguing consumers.

A recall affecting 19 million eggs was recently elevated to Class I, meaning “a situation in which there is a reasonable probability that the use of or exposure to a violative product will cause serious adverse health consequences or death.”

Nearly 100 people have fallen ill, with 26 hospitalized. There have not yet been any confirmed deaths.

open image in gallery 19 million eggs have been affected by another recent recall ( Getty )

The recall applies to eggs sold under the Country Morning, Cal-Maine Sunups, Brookshire’s, Simple Truth, and Kroger brand names. They will have sell-by or best-by dates between July 20, 2026 and August 17, 2026.

A pet food recall also has consumers on high-alert.

Fromm Family Foods has recalled two types of its wet canned dog food following complaints about metal contamination.

The affected products are the Fromm Turkey Pâté Wet Dog Food 12.2-ounce can, with a best before date of March 20, 2029 and the lot code EP2A3306 551006, and the Fromm Diner Classics Milo’s Meatloaf Pâté Wet Dog Food 12.5-ounce can, with a best before date of March 20, 2029 and a lot code of EP2A3306 551029.

Oma’s Pride has also recalled 639 6lb bags of its Woof Complete Canine Chicken Recipe after testing found salmonella contamination.

The affected product has a best before date of January 27, 2029 and a lot code of BB012729.

News.title: UK travellers are still being caught out by this Brexit passport rule
News.content:

Just back from a trip to Croatia, this week Independent Travel writer Amelia Neath told me about a woman who was meant to be on her flight to Split, but was turned away at the gate. On presenting her travel documents, the unfortunate traveller was told that her passport was not valid for travel to Croatia – despite the fact that it had yet to reach its expiry date.

This woman had sadly been caught out by the ‘10-year issue rule’ that applies to Brits travelling to the European Union (as well as Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein) since Brexit. This rule stipulates that “third country” nationals (which includes the UK since we left the EU on 31 January 2020) must present a travel document that has been issued within the previous 10 years the day you enter the EU. The other stipulation is that the passport should be valid until the end of the traveller’s stay plus an additional three months.

While her husband and four children went ahead and boarded the flight, this poor woman would have had to go back home and likely miss her holiday. It is possible to apply for an urgent passport with the “1 day premium” service, but the earliest you can get an appointment is in two days, with the passport being ready to collect four hours later, at a cost of £239.50. Add to this the cost of a new flight and it becomes an incredibly pricey (not to mention stressful) business to get the holiday back on track.

Sign up to the free Travel Insider newsletter here

Being turned away from your flight at the boarding gate – after booking (and paying for) a trip, packing, preparing, travelling to the airport and checking in – must be devastating. Previously on Independent Travel, we have extensively covered the ‘10-year issue rule’ as we heard of case after case of travellers falling foul and being denied boarding – and I’m sad to see it’s still happening. This week we spoke with Celia Jenkins who wasn’t aware that her passport was invalid for travel to the EU until she was at Bristol airport waiting to board her Jet2 flight to Kefalonia in Greece, where her family has a second home. Celia, 78, and her husband Rees, 82, were told by staff that their passports were 10 years and three days old, meaning they would be denied entry into Greece. Celia estimated that this mistake cost her and Rees £500 in bus and taxi fares, along with a night at an airport hotel and flights, plus the opportunity to spend a week with their children and grandchildren in Greece.

Although it is a passenger’s responsibility to make sure that their travel documents are valid, I do feel incredibly sorry for travellers like Celia and the many others who have been caught out by this rule. Beyond the frustration that becoming “third party nationals” was a consequence of Brexit, I also appreciate that for many travellers there is no reason why they should be aware that the passport rules had changed. Despite the fact I should certainly know better, I have personally been very nearly caught out by not having the right travel documents – including a last-minute panic when I realised I hadn’t secured my Canadian Electronic Travel Authorization the day before I flew to Alberta (thankfully it was granted immediately), and a memorable afternoon spent frantically rummaging through drawers to find a yellow fever certificate I needed for a trip to Uganda. My recommendation is – no matter where you are travelling, whether you’ve been there before, and how well you think you know the destination – check country entry requirements carefully on the UK Foreign Office website as soon as you book your trip, and ensure you have all documents in order well ahead of travel.
