View image in fullscreen Kieran McKenna’s relentless coaching at Ipswich was exhausting so it was no surprise he needed a break following their third promotion in five years. Photograph: Cat Goryn/Action Images/Reuters

During 11 v 11 practice games, McKenna would be the only one who coached. Over his five years at Ipswich, no drill was ever repeated in exactly the same form; repetition and possible staleness were to be avoided at all costs. Little wonder that after a third promotion in five seasons at the club, he felt exhausted, in need of a break rather than taking on an uneven fight in an ungrateful Premier League that could only sap his reserves further.

Brian Clough would take holidays during the season. He would turn up only infrequently at training. His input was sharp, erratic, impressionistic. Four decades on, a top-level manager is running a team of coaches and analysts that probably outnumbers the players with whom he has direct contact.

He cannot simply ignore the board until he needs money for a signing but has to manage up to whatever structure of sporting directors exists above him. He often will have little autonomy, although the success of Mikel Arteta, who has a more traditional role and seems to micromanage everything at Arsenal, may change that. And he is liable to be sacked after a month of poor form. The pressure is enormous, the margin for error minute.

That perhaps explains why so many top managers are now drifting into international football. Management, it’s commonly said, is a drug, but perhaps that fix is more palatable when it is delivered in five doses spread over a season, plus a major tournament every other year, rather than in the relentless drudgery of the club game. Carlo Ancelotti took his break from the club game at 66, Jürgen Klopp at 56, Tuchel at 50. None have demonstrated any great desire to return to the remorselessness of the league.

The Premier League may be the greatest stage in management. It may be where the best salaries are paid. It may be where every manager wishes to test himself. But it is an exhausting and capricious world that requires extraordinary reserves of energy, physical and mental. It is no theatre for old men.

Sports.title: ‘I’ve had a very hectic career’: Mario Balotelli on Italian football’s troubles and his future
Sports.content:
Whenever the name Mario Balotelli is brought up, particularly in Italy, the conversation is almost inevitably laced with a sense of regret. There is that lingering “What if?”, a collective sigh over a player who possessed the raw, undeniable potential to be one of the best in the world, if only things had been different.

Yet being in front of him, with a smile on his face, it becomes clear the 36-year-old striker has reached an unexpected level of wisdom and maturity, traits that shine through in his lucid analysis of Italian football’s current struggles and the vanishing street culture of the sport. As Balotelli reflects on what he would tell his adolescent self, there is also a distinct feeling that he has finally made peace with his own turbulent narrative, that he isn’t chasing the ghosts of unfulfilled expectations.

Balotelli joined Al Ittifaq in the United Arab Emirates simply to enjoy the game, to find pure joy on the pitch, and to realise a long-held family dream of playing alongside his brother, Enock Barwuah. “To tell you the truth, it was an idea that came up more or less at the last minute,” he says. “The president wanted to meet me, and we talked. The project interested me. Everyone always says: ‘You go to Dubai for the money,’ but thank God, I’m not short of that. So, money wasn’t the only goal. The project was actually nice and competitive. I grew fond of the idea and decided to give it a try.”

View image in fullscreen Mario Balotelli signed for Al-Ittifaq in January 2026 on a two-and-a-half-year contract. Photograph: Al-Ittifaq

The realities of playing in the Middle East present a stark contrast to Balotelli’s past experiences. “Infrastructure-wise, it’s very good. The stadiums are beautiful. The problem is the public: there’s no crowd, which is a bit sad,” he says. “The organisation is also lacking a bit, but I think they’ll improve on that with time. I’m talking about all the teams across the board.” On linking up with his sibling, he says: “It’s beautiful. Ever since we were little, we always said we’d play together one day. He’d always ask me: ‘If you play for Inter, Milan, or [Manchester] City, how can I play with you?’ I used to tell him that when I got older, I might play in a team of a slightly lower level and maybe they’d give us that opportunity. It’s always been a dream, and now it’s coming true.”

Despite his new surroundings, Balotelli remains acutely aware of the deep-rooted problems plaguing football back home, particularly after Italy’s failure to qualify for three successive World Cups. “The problems, in my opinion, are very simple,” he says. “I prefer to give practical explanations rather than technical ones, based on everyday life and what I see in Italy.

“When we were little, we played hours and hours of football. I remember my mum getting mad at me because I’d stay out until it was too dark to see the ball. They’d threaten you that you couldn’t go out to play the next day. Now, when I walk around cities like Brescia, though I see it in other Italian cities too, the parks are empty. There’s no one around.”

Balotelli continues: “Computers, phones, and PlayStations have ruined a lot. Above all, the parents’ mentality has changed. A seven‑year-old kid today might play football for two hours every three days. We had the same structured training sessions, plus three hours of playing at the park every day, which felt like fun but was actually extra training. I truly believe talents were born on the street and in the parks. You played a lot, learned a lot, and tested yourself against older kids. If you were good, they didn’t let you play with kids your age; they made you play with the older ones. Those were tests that served me well in the long run. Playing with people older than me has always been one of the most important things in my career.

“Today, kids are on their phones. They feel like Ronaldinho because they watch his videos. I felt like Ronaldo because I could actually pull off the same tricks at the park. It’s very different.”

Despite his pessimism over the state of Italian football, Balotelli, who earned 36 caps for the Azzurri, scoring 14 goals, remains confident of a bright future. “Yes, I think so for the upcoming generations,” he predicts. “Maybe not right away, but in the next two or three generations. It’s normal for a country to have downturns but then you bounce back. Spain, France, and Germany have all had them.”

View image in fullscreen Mario Balotelli has won 36 caps for the Italian national team – the last in September 2018 – scoring 14 goals. Photograph: Luca Bruno/AP

When it comes to the national team, it’s impossible to ignore Roberto Mancini, reappointed as head coach and someone who acted as a mentor for Balotelli, as well as a defining figure throughout his most successful years. “He texted me to wish me a happy birthday, and I joked with him, saying: ‘Look, I can still play!’” Balotelli reveals. “I’m very happy he’s back with the national team; I’m very fond of him and I wish him the best. In Italy, people tend to blame the coaches a lot but, honestly, the system should take more of the blame. It’s the truth that nobody wants to say.”

As a curious footnote, the last time Balotelli played for Italy was on 7 September 2018, against Poland in Bologna. It also happened to be Mancini’s first competitive game in his first spell in charge of the national team. So, could Balotelli play for Italy under Mancini again? “If I keep scoring, yes,” he replies emphatically.

Balotelli’s time in England remains a standout chapter in a career filled with highs and lows, especially the three years he had at Manchester City when he won the Premier League and FA Cup – under Mancini. “It remains one of the best memories of my career,” he says. “At that time, City wasn’t as renowned as it is today. We joined the team that took the first steps for City to become what it is today. That gives you a special feeling. It means a lot more, actually.”

View image in fullscreen Mario Balotelli had an eventful three years at Manchester City, where he won the Premier League and FA Cup. Photograph: Matthew Peters/Manchester United/Getty Images

As he navigates the twilight of his career, Balotelli’s focus is clear. “I’m feeling good,” he states. “I’m recovering from a slight leg issue but I’m training, and it’s going well. It’s hot, which makes it a bit difficult to give 100%, but if you pace yourself and use your head, you can manage to play quite well. The heat is definitely a drawback, however.

“On the pitch I want to play as long as I feel good. Playing is what I love doing, so as long as my body doesn’t say: ‘Enough,’ I’ll keep going. Off the pitch, once I finish my career, I definitely want to manage my businesses and focus on my kids. I’d prefer tranquillity, though. I’ve had a very hectic career, so a sedentary lifestyle wouldn’t be a bad thing.”

If Balotelli could offer one piece of advice to his 16-year-old self, what would it be? “I’d tell him not to make certain choices,” he says, “and to listen to certain people at specific times.”

Sports.title: Lavish spending fails to fix Tottenham’s big issue – the lack of soul and spine | Jonathan Liew
Sports.content:
Time for Tottenham to start panicking? This is, of course, a subtle trick question. Tottenham is one of those clubs that never actually stops panicking. They panic when they concede and they panic when they score. They panic when they have the ball and they panic when someone else does. They have a coach in Roberto De Zerbi whose face evokes a state of permanent alarm, the expression of a man perpetually having a toilet door opened on him. One year they even managed to panic their way to the Europa League. For the ever-rattled Spurs fan, this club is less a treasured devotion and more a lifelong haunting, broken up by occasional panic substitutions.

You could intuit that sense of encrusted resignation pretty much from the moment Anthony Elanga’s improvised shot kissed the post and trickled over the line to give Newcastle the lead. Since beating Aston Villa 4-1 in late 2024, Tottenham have gone behind 44 times in all competitions and come back to win precisely zero of them. There is something innate and endemic here, a chronic case of Long Tottenham for which – despite the new coach, the new leadership structure and more than a third of a billion pounds in transfer fees – there remains no proven cure. Yoane Wissa’s clincher was of zero surprise to anyone.

Allow Instagram content? This article includes content provided by Instagram . We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'. Allow and continue

And so welcome back to the temple of pain, the Theatre of Everyone Else’s Dreams, a stadium that fittingly still has no naming rights because pretty much every visiting side gets to own the place. Over the past 12 months, Aston Villa have won the same number of domestic fixtures at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium (two) as Tottenham. Unai Emery’s men may well get the chance to retake their lead here in three weeks’ time. In the meantime it was Newcastle, with one clean sheet in their last 18 matches, who feasted on Tottenham’s neuroses, stayed tight and stayed patient, waited for the train that always arrives.

Perhaps as Matthias Jaissle’s team climbed all over the duels and the second balls there was also a certain reassuring symbolism here: a lesson in the enduring value of culture over commerce. Newcastle have lost half a team but kept their soul; Tottenham have bought half a team and are still searching for theirs. There were inevitable boos for Sandro Tonali, who was actually fine: one of those rare Tottenham players who actually treasures the ball and wants to do interesting things with it. Alongside him Mateus Fernandes was restless, classy, excellent. Omar Marmoush on his debut looked fit and sharp. But of course the individuals were never the problem here.

The problem was the little things: the lost headers, the fractional pauses on the ball that kill momentum, the rushed shots, the extra touches, the tackles not quite committed to, the barely perceptible signs of a deep-rooted softness. Take Elanga’s goal, which sprang from an unpressed Nico González long ball, a poorly challenged Amar Dedic header, a cool turn and finish. Three very simple things in a row, at least two of which should probably have been prevented. No screaming howler or smoking gun here. Just a run of lost battles, a sum of marginal flaws, a team that for all its moments of promise and competence has not yet been welded together into a coherent whole.

View image in fullscreen Sandro Tonali tussles with Anthony Elanga. Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA

How De Zerbi fixes this is anyone’s guess. It feels increasingly clear that for all the new blood there is still a kind of generational trauma here, perhaps dating back to the injury crisis of 2024-25, when a threadbare squad was pushed beyond the boundaries of wellness and sanity. For the veterans of that campaign, your Archie Grays and Micky van de Vens, your Destiny Udogies and Rodrigo Bentancurs, you occasionally glimpse that accumulated tension in the 50-50 tackles and big physical clashes, the sense of players still not quite trusting their bodies. And oppositions really do pick up on this stuff. Right now there is a clear blueprint for beating Tottenham: compete, do the simple things well, and eventually bully them into playing your game.

How much worse does this get before it gets better? Are Spurs fans ultimately in for another season of discontent and disgruntlement, of taking an unhealthy interest in the latest score from the Coventry Building Society Arena? The instinct here is still to be patient and wait for the required chemistry to develop. But what if two defeats become four, or six? What if it’s November and the top scorer is still somehow Richarlison with two? How does a club so medicinally addicted to panic possibly avoid it?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Quietly, there is now some ridiculous creative talent at this club. The signings of Marmoush and Sávio, the new-look midfield, the return of Mohammed Kudus and Dominic Solanke, the prospect of James Maddison and Dejan Kulusevski and Xavi Simons to come. A World Cup finalist in Marcos Senesi sitting unused on the bench. It feels inconceivable that Tottenham could be in relegation trouble again. But as with so many clubs before them, Tottenham are discovering that buying new footballers is the easy part. Growing a spine will take considerably longer.

Sports.title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 9: Liverpool
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 8th (NB: this is not necessarily Tom Garry’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 11th

Prospects

After a disappointing 2025-26 campaign, there is renewed positivity at Liverpool. A strong summer transfer window, coupled with encouraging results in pre-season, suggests they will significantly improve on their 11th-place finish, continuing the good run they had in the second half of last season.

Gareth Taylor did not take charge until quite late last summer and the squad needed something of a rebuild. This time around, the former Manchester City head coach has been able to spend a full pre-season with his team. The managing director, Andy O’Boyle, has also had three transfer windows since starting his job to try to evolve the squad. The arrival of Germany forward Vivien Endemann, from Wolfsburg, is a very promising signing, while goalkeeper Khiara Keating has been reunited with Taylor, albeit she is not as experienced as Sweden’s Jennifer Falk. Falk was tremendous during a loan spell with Liverpool in the second half of last season, but opted not to make her stay permanent because she wanted to be closer to family.

There were other notable losses, including the centre-back Gemma Bonner. Nonetheless, Liverpool appear to have a squad that is more than capable of staying up although they still look a long way off challenging for Europe and their budget is dwarfed by the big spenders.

It took Liverpool until late January to record their first league win last season and this time around they will want to make an immediate impact. It should help that they begin away to promoted Charlton.

Off-field picture

The women’s team have never really benefited from the type of cash injections from their owners, Fenway Sports Group (FSG), that Arsenal, Chelsea and Manchester City’s women’s sides have from theirs. Liverpool have recorded an overall profit of more than £500,000 when the past eight seasons are combined and consistently break even. They also boast top-class facilities at their Melwood training base..

The manager

Taylor will want to see the team look more accustomed to his style of play. The 53-year-old has yet to win over the fanbase, but he does have a strong CV, winning the Women’s FA Cup and the League Cup with Manchester City in 2020 and 2022 respectively, and very nearly a league title, too. A former Wales international striker, Taylor represented a broad range of clubs, from Bristol Rovers to Nottingham Forest and Wrexham, with spells at Sheffield United and Manchester City in between.

Star signing

Liverpool were delighted that Endemann decided to make the switch from Wolfsburg. The 25-year-old had a good record in the Bundesliga, as well as 17 caps for Germany, whom she helped finish third at the 2024 Olympics. Endemann won a German Cup with Wolfsburg in 2024 and has Women’s Champions League experience, too.

View image in fullscreen Vivien Endemann will give Liverpool more threat in front of goal. Photograph: Nick Taylor/Liverpool FC/Getty Images

Stat attack

Liverpool improved after a very slow start to the last campaign. They earned 11 points more in the second half of the season than in the first, the widest margin of improvement in the Women’s Super League. Doubling their tally from the second batch of 11 games would have given them 28 points, enough for sixth.

Set for a breakthrough

The 20-year-old Japan youth international Mao Itamura has been signed from Feyenoord. She was named as the Eredivisie player of the year last season and is a versatile forward with great dribbling skills. She should add a fresh and exciting dimension to Liverpool’s attack.

What they say

“We want to be in the first half of the table because we have really good players and I think we can show what we are capable of. I believe in every single person in this team. We have good chances to have a great season. And we all have this good feeling; I can feel it in the training” – Liverpool and Switzerland forward Aurélie Csillag

Where are they playing their home games?

Liverpool play the vast majority of their home matches at St Helens Stadium, which they share with the rugby league side. It has a modern feel and a capacity of about 18,000. They have announced they will be playing three times at Anfield this season; the first of those games being a derby against Everton in September.

Sports.title: Carrick dismisses ‘lazy’ Manchester United criticism and defends Fernandes’ leadership
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick has said it was “lazy and easy” to say everything was wrong with Manchester United after the opening-day defeat at Hull.

United lost 2-0 in a tame display and the manager was asked whether his captain, Bruno Fernandes, and Youri Tielemans, Belgium’s captain, had shown the leadership that might have affected the performance and result.

“It’s one game,” Carrick said. “I think there’s enough leadership in our dressing room that we’ll have it throughout the season. Just because we lose a game doesn’t just mean leadership [is the reason]. I got ‘passion’ thrown at me after the game; it’s not just that. You lose two set plays like we did [for the goals], it changes the game.”

Carrick was asked what the reason was for the performance. “You’ve watched football a long time, right? Teams lose games and win games, and it’s not just because you try or you don’t try. There’s all sorts of different reasons. I don’t have to give you the total reason, because we know what we’re trying to improve on.”

The 45-year-old was pressed to offer one factor why the defeat occurred. “I think it’s so easy and lazy to just … a team loses a game, everything’s wrong: this is wrong, this is wrong, not trying enough, not enough passion,” Carrick said. “It’s like the obvious answer. So, there’s a lot that goes into a game of football that can take [the result away] from [you].

“We’ve probably played like that and won games, and everyone goes: ‘What a great team, what a great coach, what a great load of players’ – when we find a way to win 1-0. So, from my perspective, when you’re analysing it, it’s not the feeling [that the inverse is true]. We’ve got to dig deeper than that and understand the details of it. And we don’t get carried away when we win certain games because we know it’s not been perfect.”

United host Ipswich on Sunday without Carlos Baleba, who signed on Tuesday for £70m from Brighton but has an ankle injury that may rule him out for three or more weeks. This means the midfielder may not make his debut until Tottenham’s visit on 10 October, after the international break.

United have admired the Cameroon international since last summer so Carrick was asked why the 22-year-old was signed so late in the window. He said: “It’s not always straightforward, and things have got to drop. So we’ve been patient. We wanted to get the right players in, that fit the group, that will take us forward, and Carlos is definitely one of them.”

Sports.title: Liverpool’s Andoni Iraola angered by substitution delay before Forest penalty
Sports.content:
Andoni Iraola bemoaned a poor first-half display plus a broken electronic board for Liverpool’s disappointing 2-2 draw with Nottingham Forest in the first home game of his Anfield reign. Forest led twice, but were denied a third successive Premier League win at Liverpool by Víctor Muñoz’s emphatic 82nd-minute equaliser.

The visitors’ second goal, from a penalty converted by Morgan Gibbs-White, stemmed from a throw-in taken quickly by Liam Delap while Iraola was attempting to make a triple substitution.

He was prevented from doing so because the fourth official was unable to flash up the substitutes’ numbers due to a malfunctioning electronic board. “I cannot explain because I don’t have an explanation,” said the exasperated Liverpool head coach.

“I wanted to make those substitutions about three minutes before. It was two, three, four times the ball had gone out. He [the fourth official] was having some problems with the board. The penalty wouldn’t have happened if I had made the subs.

“I had complained the previous time. The supporters were shouting and they were aware of the situation. I’ll leave you to decide whether it was a penalty or not.”

Despite his annoyance over the buildup to Forest’s penalty, Iraola conceded that Liverpool created their own problems for the second week in succession with a sluggish start.

He said: “The first half was poor, it was not good enough. We haven’t controlled the game and after we improved a lot in the second half. We were much more intense, quicker on the ball and had more urgency, but it hasn’t been enough to win the game and we have to blame the first half.

“I am frustrated because we want to win, especially at home. It’s not a good result. We have come back from two results where we were losing and I like what we have done in the second half, but we haven’t been able to complete the comeback.

“In the first half we were too passive without the ball. Afterwards we improved this and intensity gives you the chance to win duels and attack quicker and better. But in the first half there was a lack of intensity and we had issues with throw-ins today.”

Sports.title: Enzo Fernandez LEFT OUT of Chelsea squad to face Brighton: Wantaway star dropped by Xabi Alonso for second-straight match - as Blues boss insists he is doing what's 'best for the club' amid Man City's £100m interest
Sports.content:
Enzo Fernandez LEFT OUT of Chelsea squad to face Brighton: Wantaway star dropped by Xabi Alonso for second-straight match - as Blues boss insists he is doing what's 'best for the club' amid Man City's £100m interest

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Enzo Fernandez has been omitted from Chelsea's matchday squad for the second time in just four days, as speculation over his future at Stamford Bridge intensifies amid Manchester City's interest with transfer deadline day looming.

The 25-year-old is wanted by City before the transfer window closes on September 1 - with the Etihad outfit preparing a £100million bid, as reported by Daily Mail Sport. Even if that offer does come it is set to be rejected, with Chelsea wanting £120m.

And with Fernandez's future remaining uncertain, Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has opted not to include the midfielder for Sunday's Premier League clash at home to Brighton and Hove Albion.

Asked pre-match about his decision to not include the Argentina international, the Spaniard told Sky Sports: 'We think what is best for the team and the club. Sometimes we need to make tough calls; we don't know what will happen in the future.

'But today it was better that we have this squad, and in the future we don't know what is going to happen.'

Fernandez's exclusion comes days after he was dealt the same fate during Thursday's League Cup second-round 2-0 win over Luton Town.

Enzo Fernandez has been left out of Chelsea's matchday squad for a second-straight match - with Premier League rivals Manchester City keen to sign him in a £100million transfer

Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso says the midfielder's omission is what is 'best for the club' currently

In the build-up to that tie, which Chelsea won courtesy of Danny Welbeck and a Hakeem Odoffin own goal, Alonso insisted that Fernandez would be involved against their League One opponents.

However, when the team news came out on Thursday evening, Fernandez's name was nowhere to be seen in the 20-man squad.

Asked about Fernandez's absence from the squad against Luton, Alonso said pre-match: 'We assessed situations, individual and collective and we have decided he is not in the squad for today.'

However, speaking post-match the Spaniard was a lot more open, revealing that the decision was made by himself and the club hierarchy.

'It was a decision from myself and from the club,' Alonso said. 'We had other players that needed minutes and it was that way. It's a decision that I took. He's a good professional. He's training well. I have nothing to say about him.

'It was just a decision that we had to take, thinking about the game that we're playing tonight and we'll see for (Brighton on) Sunday.'

Speaking on Wednesday, Alonso was adamant to see his No 8 involved, saying: 'Yes, so we expect that he's involved.

'He's trained, he's training really well, he's a good professional and he will be involved.'

When pressed on whether he wants Fernandez to remain a Chelsea player after this window, Alonso added: 'We want to have the best team possible. We know his qualities. He has shown it. We have to wait, but we will think about tomorrow and let's see how things develop.

'We assess the whole squad as a unit and in that squad, we want good balance in terms of quality, in terms of positions, in terms of personalities, so we are aware of everything and we are prepared for whatever.'

Sports.title: NFL star and six-time Pro Bowler arrested on drink-driving charges to throw his career into jeopardy just days before the start of the season
Sports.content:
NFL wide receiver Keenan Allen has thrown his Indianapolis Colts career into jeopardy after being arrested on drink-driving charges just 11 days on from signing with the team.

Allen, 34, is a six-time Pro Bowler and former Comeback Player of the Year, who is preparing for his 14th season in the NFL - and first in Indianapolis after leaving the Los Angeles Chargers.

But on Sunday morning the NFL star - who has earned just under $140million in his career to date - was behind bars and facing two misdemeanor charges after being arrested by police in the early hours of the morning.

According to an IMPD police report and jail booking, as first reported by Fox59, Allen was arrested at around 1am on preliminary charges of DWI and DWI endangering a person.

In a statement on Sunday morning, a spokesperson for the Colts said: 'We are aware of the incident involving Keenan Allen last night. We are in the process of gathering more information and have no further comment at this time.'

He was picked up by cops on the 100 block of S. Meridian Street, just hours after he had played for the Colts in the preseason game against the Detroit Lions at the Lucas Oil Stadium.

Keenan Allen is facing multiple drink-driving charges after being arrested in Indianapolis

Just hours before his arrest, Allen was playing for his new team against the Detroit Lions

No further details have yet been made available about the circumstances surrounding the arrest, and it is understood the player is still being held at the Marion County Arrestee Processing Center.

Allen's arrest comes just two weeks ahead of the start of the 2026 season, with Indianapolis preparing to host the Baltimore Ravens in Week 1.

He only signed for the team earlier this month after being released by the Chargers at the end of the 2025 season, bringing to an end his second stint with the team.

Allen has spent 12 of his 13 NFL seasons with the Chargers organization, after first being selected by San Diego in the third round of the 2013 NFL Draft.

Allen has played 13 of his 14 seasons for the Chargers organization after being drafted in 2013

Allen attends a charity event in Los Angeles earlier this month, before signing for the Colts

He then moved with the team to LA ahead of the 2017 season, in which he went on to enjoy his most productive season off the back of an ACL tear which limited his 2016 season to just a single game.

In 2017 he recorded 1,393 receiving yards, third of anyone in the NFL, going on to win the Comeback Player of the Year.

In March 2024 he was traded to the Chicago Bears, but after just a year away from the team he agreed a return to the Chargers for the 2025 season.

Last year he signed a one-year, $8.5m deal and played a part in all 18 games, including the Wild Card playoff loss to the New England Patriots.

Sports.content:

Sports.title: Chelsea complete £7.5m Emiliano Martinez signing: Argentina star handed immediate START as he vows to help the Blues 'win titles' after sealing move from Aston Villa
Sports.content:
Emiliano Martinez was handed an immediate start by Xabi Alonso after his £7.5m move from Aston Villa was announced.

The Blues confirmed the arrival of the 33-year-old on Sunday morning, with Martinez signing a three-year deal.

Daily Mail Sport reported that Martinez was understood to be eligible to immediately represent Chelsea against Brighton, with sources saying that the goalkeeper was registered before the deadline.

Martinez had to be officially signed before 12pm on Friday. Though the club only announced his arrival on Sunday morning, his registration was secured in time.

Despite rumours of an injury, Martinez also said in his unveiling that he is fit and ready to go.

'We always had the plan to get the best possible squad, and now that we have Emi [Martinez] we are bringing in a goalkeeper of world stature, winning mentality. He is ready to play and here we go,' Alonso said.

Emi Martinez was handed an immediate start for Chelsea after his move from Aston Villa

The Blues confirmed the arrival of the 33-year-old on Sunday morning on a three-year deal

Martinez had been registered in time to be available to feature against Brighton

'Yesterday he was in practice; everything was already arranged. And for sure, he is one of those players that doesn't need that much to adapt. I'm sure he can have an impact.'

Martinez's arrival is expected to see Robert Sanchez leave the club, with the Spaniard conceding two avoidable goals against Fulham on Monday.

Sanchez was not named in the Chelsea squad, with Mike Penders named as substitute goalkeeper by Alonso.

Martinez, speaking ahead of the match, vowed to help Chelsea to win titles.

'I’m delighted to be at this football club,' Martinez said.

'Coming to Chelsea, for me and my family, was an easy decision to make and I’m just over the moon - I can’t wait to get started.

'I want to be successful here. I'm someone who wants to win at everything I do and I want to bring that here to this football club because it’s a football club that wins titles, so I think it’s a good match.

'I’m all passion and I play with my heart. I will give 100 per cent every game, every training session to make the club, my teammates and the supporters proud.'

Martinez has been surplus to requirements at Aston Villa since the club signed Zion Suzuki from Parma earlier this month.

Martinez saw a move to Juventus collapse earlier this month despite an initial £6million offer, with Unai Emery happy to press ahead with Suzuki and Marco Bizot as his goalkeeping options.

Sports.title: How Arsenal overhauled their academy to produce a new wave of world-class Hale End talent: The two experts leading aggressive recruitment, the Folarin Balogun template and fighting back when rivals poach their top young stars
Sports.content:
It’s all change in the Arsenal academy after a period of flux.

Per Mertesacker left the top job over the summer after eight years to become the German FA's managing director, a role he starts in January. Following the former Arsenal captain out of the door was Under 21s head coach Max Porter, who was appointed Stoke City assistant manager.

That left a void in the heart of Hale End, at a time when academy production lines are more important than ever in a world of pure profit and homegrown talent.

But now, with a new hierarchy in place headed up by Mertesacker's replacement Pascal de Maesschalck, the Gunners are looking to reassert their status as an academy goldmine.

Hale End’s proud history stands strong, having produced the likes of Tony Adams, Ashley Cole and Jack Wilshere over the years.

The most recent gems, Ethan Nwaneri, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Max Dowman, have all shone in Mikel Arteta's first team, where they join the jewel in Hale End's crown, Bukayo Saka.

New Arsenal academy director Pascal De Maesschalck with academy operations manager Lee Herron

Arsenal are looking for the next gem off their production line, which has recently produced Max Dowman, Ethan Nwaneri and Myles Lewis-Skelly

But the output masked problems within. The Under 21s won just eight of their 21 matches last season in the Premier League 2 competition, including a 7-0 thrashing at the hands of Liverpool in January.

When the Under 19s beat Bayern Munich 4-2 in the UEFA Youth League in November 2025 – helped by Dowman dropping back down to that level and scoring twice after already making a handful of first-team appearances – it snapped a 16-game winless streak across the Under 18s, 19s and 21s.

And while the academy teams foundered with uncertainty over who would replace Mertesacker, rivals took advantage.

First, Manchester City hijacked a move for promising Leicester City winger Jeremy Monga, whom Arsenal had been close to signing. Then, Tottenham beat the Gunners to West Ham’s Under 15s midfield star Isaac Allen. Talented youngsters such as Kyran Thompson and Mishel Nduka chose to continue their careers elsewhere, at Newcastle United and Manchester City respectively.

But in recent weeks, the balance has been wrestled back under new academy director De Maesschalck, the 52-year-old Belgian who was previously technical director at Chelsea's sister club Strasbourg, following ten years as Club Brugge academy head and three years leading Monaco's youth development.

Each of those clubs is renowned across the continent for producing world-class talents. At Brugge he became highly regarded for making academy players ready for the first team, while at Monaco he brought through golden boys such as Eliesse Ben Seghir, Maghnes Akliouche and Soungoutou Magassa, who all became first-team stars before earning the club sizeable sums when joining Bayer Leverkusen, Paris Saint-Germain and West Ham respectively.

And it’s understood that he’s been tasked at Arsenal to make the academy more aggressive in recruitment and recoup more money in player sales.

That drive is already in effect. Arsenal have previously brought in players under 18 from Scotland and Ireland, like Callan Hamill, Evan Mooney and Ceadach O’Neill.

Arsenal lost two of their top talents this summer in Mishel Nduka (left, to Manchester City) and Kyran Thompson (right, to Newcastle United)

Defender Elijah Upson, 18, the son of ex-Arsenal centre back Matt, joined from Spurs

And of late, there’s been a push to raid other clubs across England for their best talent. Arsenal sporting director Andrea Berta hinted towards this in his quotes around the appointment, praising De Maesschalck's knack for ‘identifying the best emerging talent to join Arsenal on a journey towards professional football’.

Defender Elijah Upson, 18, the son of ex-Arsenal centre-back Matt, joined from Spurs. Midfielder Axel Donczew, 16, has signed from Cardiff City, while Crystal Palace’s Mylo Bernard, 16, has also joined, and Arsenal are also set to beat multiple clubs to the signature of highly rated Blackburn Rovers striker Igor Tyjon, 18.

And then on the selling front, there’s been a move under Pascal to have produce more cases like Mika Biereth and Folarin Balogun who, while not quite good enough for an Arsenal team pushing to be the best in Europe, help out on the financial side.

London-born Denmark striker Biereth was snapped up from Fulham's academy in 20212 and sold to Sturm Graz for £4million three years later. The Austrian side then sold Biereth to Monaco in January 2025 for £12.8million, earning Arsenal more money as a result of their 30 per cent sell-on clause.

Balogun, meanwhile, was sold to Monaco for £34.3million in August 2023 after not quite making it in Arteta's first team. After a breakout World Cup with the US national team, he has been linked to the likes of Tottenham, and has a 17.5 per cent sell-on clause. Arsenal want more of this to continue during De Maesschalck's reign.

There’s been change in the coaching setup, too. David Horseman has stepped up from his roles as Under 19s manager and Under 21s assistant to replace Porter as Under 21s head coach, in an appointment overseen by Arteta, assistant manager Albert Stuivenberg and De Maesschalck.

It’s understood they liked Horseman's balance of having extensive academy experience, as well as both managing and coaching in the Football League, specialising in player development.

Just two years younger than Arteta, Horseman has already spent nearly 15 years working in professional academies. He started at Bristol City, spending eight years across different positions including Under 18 manager, head of academy coaching and academy manager.

‹ Slide me › Arsenal poached Mika Biereth from Fulham's academy in 2021 and three years later without making a first-team appearance, he was shipped off to Sturm Graz and then Monaco

‹ Slide me › Folarin Balogun couldn't quite make the grade at Arsenal but after a breakout World Cup, his 17.5 per cent sell-on fee in the £34.3m deal that took him to Monaco could pay dividends

Under 21s head coach David Horseman leads his team through pre-season training

His forays into senior management and coaching have been more challenging. In July 2023, Horseman was appointed head coach of Forest Green Rovers but lasted just six months, winning only two of his first seven matches. He returned to Bristol City as caretaker manager alongside Lee Cattermole after Matt Taylor was sacked in December 2024, but the team were relegated at the end of the season and Horseman left.

But it’s academy expertise which the Gunners are tapping into. Before joining Arsenal in September, he had a short spell at Manchester United as a professional development phase coach. That gave him an insight into how another enormous academy operates from the inside.

For Arsenal, the overall aim is clear: produce more first-team players by raiding their English rivals, while ensuring those who don’t make the first-team grade are of the quality to be sold for worthwhile sums.

After a period of uncertainty, the academy is entering a new era under De Maesschalck with the Gunners determined to stand above the rest.

Sports.title: Moses Itauma LOSES IBF world heavyweight title clash in huge upset: British star leaves arena on a stretcher after being stopped by Filip Hrgovic in ninth round
Sports.content:
Moses rose to the mountain summit and was left there as a brother Christian climbed over him and walked on to the promised land.

There was a hugely significant difference from his biblical namesake.

Itauma was flattened in a fight against Filip Hrgovic the Croatian Iron Man of such astonishing violence that it was frightening.

A fight so brutal that the most trumpeted UK boxing prodigy for decades had to be carried out of the ring on a stretcher - make that his shield - and on to hospital.

The other promise - that of becoming the second youngest world heavyweight champion of all time behind Mike Tyson - went unfulfilled.

Hopefully not for good.

Moses Itauma has suffered his first pro defeat at the hands of Croatian star Filip Hrgovic

Itauma, 21, was taken away from the ring on a stretcher after a brutal contest

But not the prediction of a fight across their ages to remember for years to come.

Twenty-one played 34 and the kid lost - after flooring and pounding Hrgovic for eight rounds.

By his own admission Hrgovic did ‘not know where I found the strength and energy to beat him to the ground in the ninth.

But he did venture to add: ‘ I knew he would tire at some point.'

As Itauma was submerged by a torrent of punches the towel fluttered in from his corner.

He lived to fight. Maybe only just.

Prior to the showdown, questions had hung over London’s 02.

Was Moses too young to fulfil all the prophesies?

Was Fil the Croat too late in life to seize the Holy Grail?

Hrgovic claimed the vacant IBF world heavyweight title after surviving plenty of heavy punches - and dealing his own

Had Itauma lost his cool at the very last with that schoolboy shove at the weigh-in. Or had he been asked to help sell the last few tickets somewhat surprisingly still for sale on Friday evening?

Had Hrgovic — who was fighting a British boxer for the fifth consecutive time — eventually succeeded in getting under the skin of the lad whose face he threatened to smash?

Would we be treated to the promised slugfest and brutal knockout? Which of them might be launched to stardom?

As they say, anything can happen in heavyweight boxing — and Itauma was to find that out to his cost later.

Among those who were looking most keenly for answers were potential future opponents for Itauma. Daniel Dubois, another big-hitting English heavyweight prodigy who already wears the WBO world championship belt, and white collar puncher Fabio Wardley.

Those two meet this October in a rematch of their midsummer slugfest in which Dubois prevailed by brute force and willpower in the 11th round — and the pair squared up to each other in the ring before the main event, which was scheduled for 12 rounds.

That will all have to wait for now. Itauma, who was born in Kezmarok, Slovakia, but raised in Kent after moving at eight years old, stormed out of the blocks.

Both had pledged to go for a quick kill in the fervent 02. Itauma was as good as his word. His first five big shots won the first but Hrgovic’s chin proved resilient.

Itauma is the most trumpeted British heavyweight prodigy for decades, but this is a setback

Moses tested it to better effect at the onset of the second and scored a flash knockdown. But the Croat rallied and slowly came into the fight, shaking Itauma three times in the third.

In the fourth, there were worrying signs for the man from Zagreb as a cut appeared above his right eye. Itauma kept examining the Hrgovic chin but he could not land the early finish.

To his credit, Hrgovic was giving as good as he got as he traded blows with Itauma in the fifth during some brutal exchanges.

It was pretty much the same story in an astonishing sixth that tested the resilience of both to the limit as they tried to land a killer blow. By now, both fighters appeared to be struggling as the gas tank appeared to empty.

It was new ground for Itauma in the seventh as he had never gone beyond six rounds.

In his impatience, some of his swings became wild. But not all. By the end of the round, Hrgovic was being treated for a swelling above his left eye.

It looked all over in the eighth as Itauma unleashed a flurry of big shots. But Hrgovic refused to down tools and found a second wind in the ninth as he put paid to Itauma’s hopes of a historic victory.

Other men were brave beyond the call. But the most rousing salute of all must go Croatia's first world heavyweight champion.

Filip Hrgovic. What a man.

Sports.title: Are you watching Joe Cole? High-flying Hull win second straight Premier League game with victory at Coventry after being written off by pundit - as jubilant fans joke about winning the title following perfect start
Sports.content:
Two games, two wins, joint-top of the Premier League with Manchester City. Not bad for a club mocked openly by Joe Cole and written off by most as relegation certainties.

Hull City famously surprised everyone by riding high in the early part of the 2008-09 season and they are threatening to do so again.

‘To say we are the worst team in Premier League history… it’s not a bad start from the boys,’ smiled forward Oli McBurnie, who was excellent.

‘Joe Cole has been a professional for however many years and knows what it’s like. I know he’s just saying it for banter and he’s probably got carried away – I’ve done it before. His photo wasn’t put up in the dressing room or anything like that!’

What a story Hull are becoming. Their colourful chairman Acun Ilicali shares transfer updates with supporters on social media and much of their XI here looked like a Championship tribute act, featuring players like Semi Ajayi, John Egan, Cody Drameh, Ryan Giles and Oli McBurnie.

But they are Premier League players, all right. Even at this early stage, Hull look more equipped for this level than Coventry, who had most of the ball but lacked the speed or guile to break their opponents down.

After losing at Arsenal on the opening day and with Manchester City to come next weekend, this was a fabulous chance for Frank Lampard’s team to put a win on the board against a team who finished 22 points below them in the Championship last season. But it was not to be as substitute Liam Millar outpaced the Coventry back line eight minutes from time to finish a swift counter-attack.

Already owner Doug King, who belted out the club’s anthem from the posh seats before kick-off, will be wondering where his club’s first win will come from.

Hull City look better equipped for the Premier League than Coventry City - Liam Millar gave them the victory on Saturday afternoon

With a trip to Manchester City next, Coventry may fear a long wait before their first win

Hull’s unlikely lads

Man of the match Ajayi was released by West Bromwich Albion in May 2025. Egan has played at this level before with Sheffield United but joined Hull in winter 2025 when on the fringes at Burnley.

Apart from half a season with Luton in 2023-24, Ryan Giles has bounced around the EFL: Hull is the eighth club he has represented after failing to make the grade at Wolves. This is the 30-year-old McBurnie’s ninth club, having joined on a free transfer a year ago. Before joining Hull four years ago, Regan Slater played for Carlisle and Scunthorpe.

While they are still likely to be battling the drop this term, they have the raw material to give them a fighting chance. McBurnie held the ball up superbly. Mohamed Belloumi is a lightweight by modern Premier League standards but he is the sort of lock-picker Coventry lacked and supplied the pass for Millar to run in for the winner.

Millar was a youth player at Liverpool and has since played for Kilmarnock, Charlton, Basel and Preston, and his future at Hull is uncertain despite his goal. He has rare pace, though, and could have scored shortly before he did, following another rapid break. ‘We knew the centre-backs struggle with balls behind them,’ said boss Sergej Jakirovic. ‘It was an excellent win, unbelievable.’

Sergej Jakirovic has done a fine job to get his Hull players up to speed with elite football

Tough autumn for Coventry

Coventry have worked hard through the summer to improve the squad while trying to keep faith with some of the players who brought them up. It did not work here, though, as Lampard acknowledged.

‘It depends how we want to react to defeat,’ said Lampard. ‘Two games gone, 36 left. We can’t expect anything in the Premier League. When we had chances to play forward, we played safe. That’s not us.’

Coventry are unlikely to face many teams here who are happy to sit deep and defend. They will play more conservatively themselves and when summer signing Sidiki Cherif is fit, they will have pace on the counter-attack themselves.

Yet when you’ve lost your first two and you’ve yet to score, none of that feels very comforting. The Sky Blues have been out of the top flight for a quarter of a century. They have their work cut out to make sure it is not just a one-year stay.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan
