Wednesday's flash floods started after a glacial collapse high in the Himalayan region. Scientists who studied satellite images said bedrock underneath a glacier high in the Himalayan region had collapsed, taking part of the glacier with it. The rockfall was so extreme that it registered as magnitude 5.2.

Sponsor Message

The rocks and melted water then swelled the rivers in the valleys below, causing a torrent of water that swept buildings, bridges and earth downstream in Tibet and Nepal.

Homes and businesses left intact after the flooding were still without electricity on Sunday, as twisted power line poles and wires lay tangled in the mud.

Prithivi Highway is a crucial supply route for food, fuel and other goods entering Kathmandu from other parts of the country. While most of the highway is operational, other parts still face repair challenges.

Meanwhile, Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Sunday his country will send a specialized disaster search-and-rescue team to Nepal to assist with relief efforts and help evacuate Malaysians affected by the disaster,

Malaysia has also pledged $1 million in financial aid to Nepal, he said in a statement.

World.title: Medicare's pilot GLP-1 discount program has a catch. Some sick patients don't qualify
World.content:
Medicare's pilot GLP-1 discount program has a catch. Some sick patients don't qualify

toggle caption Erica S. Lee/KFF Health News

In January, Jeff La Marca got a prescription for the popular weight loss drug Zepbound. But he couldn't afford the $750 monthly price tag.

This story was produced in partnership with KFF Health News.

Then Medicare launched an 18-month pilot program that offers GLP-1 medications to some enrollees for only $50 a month. La Marca thought he might finally be able to afford the drug.

"I thought, 'Thank God, there's a path,'" said La Marca, who lives in Basking Ridge, N.J., and has tried numerous diets and exercise regimes.

But the 68-year-old's celebration was short-lived.

His application to the pilot program was denied.

La Marca has severe obstructive sleep apnea, one of several diagnoses that exclude patients from the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program's $50 monthly price.

Sponsor Message

The notification didn't say why he was rejected. He thinks that if he didn't have that diagnosis, he would qualify due to his weight.

"I'm obese, morbidly obese, BMI 42. I had quadruple heart bypass surgery. I'm at risk for stroke. I'm prediabetic. And yet I can't get it. I'm livid," he said.

A temporary patch for a long-standing gap

About 1 in 5 American adults has taken a GLP-1 medication, and most of them, including those with health insurance, say the drugs are difficult to afford. Federal law has long barred Medicare from covering drugs prescribed solely for weight loss, which is why the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program made a big splash when it launched in July.

It's a short-term pilot program in which Medicare is offering coverage of three GLP-1s for weight loss and management, to see whether that would save Medicare money later. Eligible patients must be enrolled in Medicare Part D, a prescription drug coverage add-on to Medicare.

Even though people must have Part D insurance to qualify, the preauthorization request doesn't go through the insurer; it's instead submitted to a separate system run by a contractor for the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.

The pilot includes Wegovy, the KwikPen formulation of Zepbound and the oral medication Foundayo.

Sponsor Message

Under the pilot, many Medicare beneficiaries with a body mass index of 35 or higher — the upper range of obesity — qualify for coverage of one of those drugs, if prescribed. Those otherwise eligible who have a BMI of 27 to 34 can qualify if they also have certain health conditions, such as prediabetes or cardiovascular disease.

But buried in the fine print is a distinction that's tripping up patients like La Marca: The $50 price under Bridge applies only to people using the drug solely for weight loss.

Anyone who has a qualifying medical condition that the Food and Drug Administration has approved GLP-1s to treat, such as Type 2 diabetes or moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea, is instead routed back to their Medicare Part D prescription drug plan, which can require copays of hundreds of dollars a month for GLP-1s.

"The Bridge program was designed to target those people who can't get GLP-1 coverage through Part D but would benefit from taking one for weight loss," said Juliette Cubanski, who directs the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News.

toggle caption Erica S. Lee/KFF Health News



The cost to Medicare of subsidizing the drugs will depend largely on how many people use the program, and the federal government hasn't released an estimate.

Cubanski has estimated that 3.8 million people qualify and that, if a quarter of them enroll in Bridge and remain on treatment for the program's full 18 months, it will cost Medicare about $3.3 billion. If three-quarters enroll, costs could rise to $10 billion.

If the government expanded the program to include the additional 5.9 million people who are overweight and already eligible for GLP-1 coverage through Medicare Part D, it would add billions of dollars more to the program's cost.

The demonstration's initial weeks have been positive, and most prior authorization requests have been completed in under 12 hours, CMS spokesperson Timothy Foster said.

Sponsor Message

"This has allowed thousands of eligible beneficiaries to access GLP-1 medications for weight loss at pharmacies nationwide," Foster said.

When GLP-1s aren't affordable

Patients like La Marca are left in a tough spot, qualifying for Part D coverage of a GLP-1 but facing much higher cost sharing.

"'Coverage' doesn't always mean 'affordable,'" said primary care physician Taylor Lacy, who describes herself as a "big proponent" of GLP-1s and practices at Sunflower Medical Group in Roeland Park, Kansas.

The Bridge program is leaving behind patients with the greatest medical need, she said.

She noted that many Medicare patients already must navigate prior authorization and spend months trying alternate, often cheaper treatments, a process known as step therapy, before finally getting approval — only to arrive at the pharmacy counter and discover that their GLP-1 copays will run them $200 to $600 a month, if not more.

toggle caption Erica S. Lee/KFF Health News



Researchers studying how Medicare insurers cover GLP-1s have found that recipients have faced increases in out-of-pocket costs and that almost all plans now require prior authorization, which can make getting the drugs more difficult.

Chris Bond, a spokesperson for insurance industry trade group AHIP blamed drugmakers' prices, "which they alone set and they alone can lower."

La Marca's insurer declined to answer specific questions about La Marca's case.

Patients and prescriptions left waiting

For now, La Marca's GLP-1 prescription remains unfilled. The severe sleep apnea diagnosis that helps establish his medical need is also what excludes him from the discount program that would bring the cost within his reach.

As he reflected on his appeals and the dead ends, La Marca paused, his eyes filling with tears of frustration.

"This is now my quest, because it's my only chance to improve my health," he said. "It's the only thing left. I've tried everything."

This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with KFF Health News, a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues. KFF Health News is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling and journalism.

World.title: Trump administration deports relative of Afghans who helped US military to Central African Republic
World.content:
Trump administration deports relative of Afghans who helped US military to Central African Republic

toggle caption Sam Mednick/AP

DAKAR, Senegal — The United States on Saturday deported dozens of people to the Central African Republic, including an Afghan whose brothers collaborated with the U.S. military, his lawyer and an advocacy group said.

The Afghan man, who is in his early twenties, was granted protection against deportation to Afghanistan by a U.S. judge due to fears of persecution by the Taliban, his lawyer Alma David said.

His family in Afghanistan had received threats from the Taliban because of the work performed by the brothers in support of the U.S. military, according to court documents seen by The Associated Press.

Sponsor Message

One of the Afghan man's brothers lives in the United States and served in the Afghan National Army, which collaborated with the U.S military before the Taliban seized power in 2021, David said.

Another one of his brothers was a pilot trained by the U.S. and was killed by the Taliban, she added.

The deportation flight which landed in Central African Republic's capital Bangui on Saturday, included 12 Afghans and eight Iranians, as well as several people from Nepal and Nicaragua, said Savi Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First.

Under a series of often secret agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to two dozen countries that aren't their own as it pushes ahead with its immigration crackdown, advocates say. Immigration lawyers say the practice is being used as a legal loophole to indirectly return some asylum seekers to countries they fled. The flight on Saturday is the second to the Central African Republic since June, which carried two dozen migrants, including an Iranian woman facing persecution in her home country.

World.title: Canada has leverage in this trade fight, but economists warn it comes with a cost
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With the Trump administration's promise to impose more tariffs on us in January, many Canadians are asking: What leverage should we use to get them to change course?

The question suggests that there are actually real things we can do to change U.S. President Donald Trump's mind — that if Canada hits back hard enough, or demonstrates its willingness to suffer enough, we will get that policy change.

Christopher Ragan, the founding director of McGill University's Max Bell School of Public Policy and former chair of Canada’s Ecofiscal Commission put it this way: "Canada is in a set of negotiations with a party that appears to be unpredictable, volatile, so I don't think anybody really knows what's going to work here."

Don Drummond, former chief economist for TD Bank, said if Canadians are willing to suffer the consequences, there are plenty of ways to punch back at the U.S.

WATCH | Carney says U.S. tariffs designed to ‘hurt and divide us’: Carney says U.S. tariffs designed to ‘hurt and divide us’ | Duration 0:38 Prime Minister Mark Carney called U.S. President Donald Trump's new 50 per cent tariffs a 'miscalculation' because Canadians are united and 'masters of our destiny.'

"You first strike the things they've said are the most important to them," Drummond said. "They made it painfully clear that the only thing they want or need from Canada is oil, and maybe for a while electricity.

"We've had an export tax on oil and natural gas before and we could introduce that. We could also introduce quotas," he said.

Canada's leverage is significant when it comes to energy and fertilizer. In 2025 Canadian comodities accounted for 63 per cent of oil imported into the U.S., 81.3 per cent of imported electricity, almost 100 per cent of imported natural gas and 80 per cent of imported potash.

A number of non-tariff options

And while there's still a long way to go before Canada fully develops its critical mineral reserves, Drummond says we could notify the U.S. that they won't get preferential access when those reserves come online.

"We could also restrict American access to Canada," Drummond said. "In the extreme we could require a visa and we could be very stingy with them."

Canada could also refuse to buy the F-35 fighter jets from the U.S. and choose instead to go with the Gripen from Sweden, he said.

Canadian banks, governments, pension funds and others currently hold about $459.6 billion US in U.S. treasury bonds.

"Given that the U.S. is tormented at the moment trying to get their long-term bond yields down, if we said we were going to divest ourselves of those, or at least not buy any more, that would tick them off," Drummond said.

Drummond also said that Canada's CPP fund could divest itself of all U.S. assets (51 per cent of the $864-billion fund is invested in the U.S., compared to just 12 per cent in Canada), but that would open the door to using Canadians' retirement as a political tool and placing retirees at risk — a step he said the country should avoid taking.

"You could put back the digital services tax, for example. Why the hell did we give it away? We got absolutely nothing for giving it away," Drummond said.

He says we could also eliminate the Canadian Film or Video Production Tax Credit, which he says results in lost tax revenue of about $500 million annually, with little economic benefit for Canada.

"So it could be fairly broad-based, it could be export restrictions or export taxes, it could be any number of things," Drummond said.

Some economists warn that while employing these non-tariff measures might feel good and would certainly harm the U.S. economy, they would hurt Canada's economy more.

Long-term, short-term pain

"I think emotions are pretty high and there's just a desire to lash out, but cooler heads require us to take a moment to think about what it is we're trying to achieve," said Trevor Tombe, director of fiscal and economic policy at the University of Calgary's School of Public Policy.

Tombe says the 50 per cent tariffs on about $27 billion of Canadian goods represent a hit to Canadian GDP of about 0.4 or 0.5 per cent, and taking retaliatory action that costs Canada more than that doesn't make economic sense unless it changes U.S. behaviour.

"That's a lot easier said than done," Tombe said. "And if we do things that increase costs in the United States, that might very well play into the hands of the U.S. administration by allowing them to blame Canada."

Beyond hurting Canada's economy in the short term, there's another negative side effect: hurting it in the long term.

WATCH | Canada won't accept being 'subsidiary' of the U.S.: Carney: Canada won't accept being 'subsidiary' of the U.S.: Carney | Duration 0:57 When asked by the Globe and Mail when Ottawa will come back to the table to hammer out a trade deal with Washington, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his delegation won’t accept attitudes that see Canada as a 'subsidiary' of the U.S. Carney's comments come after U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Canada would come back to the table due to its dependence on the U.S. for security.

"Maybe we have a lot of leverage, a lot of ability to impose pain, but it comes at a huge cost for us because we are both losing revenue and we are potentially severing relationships with our best customer," said Wolfgang Alschner, the Hyman Soloway Chair in Business and Trade Law at the University of Ottawa.

What if, for example, the U.S. replaced all Canadian oil with Venezuelan oil in a decade?

By way of example, Alschner says, China's export controls on critical minerals have prompted the U.S. to try to strike new deals, find new customers and build new critical mineral supply chains. Perhaps the best example of this is Canada's push to diversify in the face of the Trump administration's trade war.

"Even if you do it for a short period of time, you're sending a signal that this can be turned on and off. And so maybe the United States will not have time to mitigate that particular disruption at that moment, but it will then put measures in place to mitigate it in the future," he said.

Alschner also said bringing back concessions such as reimposing the Digital Services Tax or cancelling tax credits would be a direct provocation with an unclear dividend.

Sometimes there is only the fight

Ragan from McGill University says the U.S. would likely react strongly to export controls or taxes that drive up U.S. gas prices. That would risk turning energy scarcity caused by Canada into something that unites Americans against this country.

"That move escalates the trade war a few notches at once," Ragan said. "I say this half jokingly, but I wonder if you restricted electricity sales or oil sales or natural gas sales, whether that would lead Donald Trump to calling the troops. I'm not so sure."

Some economists say that rather than take actions that cost the Canadian economy in the short and long term, Canada should focus on how it can make up the difference with trade expansion and diversification abroad while building at home.

"Another way to think about the U.S. right now that I find kind of helpful is that they are flailing around in increasingly irrational ways and we are getting hit in the face," Tombe said.

"To the extent that their moves are crazy and not grounded in economic rationale, the best option might be to step back, try to weather the storm, and hopefully they work out their own issues domestically."

Tombe says that aside from the broader move to diversify our exports, sign new trade deals and build at home, Canada still hasn't liberalized internal trade, an opportunity he calls low-hanging fruit.

He says that by simply recognizing credentials across the country, Canada could boost productivity enough to offset a 25 per cent across-the-board tariff.

Alschner says the advantage Canada has right now is that the EU and other global trading partners are locked in similar trade disputes with the United States, which means they may be highly motivated to work with Canada.

"We should really use this as an opportunity to forcibly substitute U.S. imports with strategically selected non-U.S. imports," Alschner said. "We should say to the European Union, 'All right, what are the things that you can sell to us that the United States used to sell to us?'"

WATCH | Canada hits back at U.S. with $28B worth of retaliatory tariffs: Canada hits back at U.S. with $28B worth of retaliatory tariffs | Duration 1:42:33 Industry Minister Mélanie Joly tells Power & Politics that Canada is 'fighting back' against U.S. tariffs by introducing retaliatory tariffs on nearly $28 billion worth of U.S. goods. Economist Trevor Tombe lays out how these tariffs could affect Canadians. And NDP Leader Avi Lewis shares details about his recent meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Tombe notes that while there are plenty of economic reasons to avoid employing non-tariff retaliatory measures in this trade fight, Canada's battle with the U.S. isn't entirely economic.

The U.S., as Prime Minister Mark Carney has said, wants to break us so it can own us, and some say a threat to our sovereignty requires an un-economic response.

"I'm getting a little tired, mainly, with fellow economists who point out that it's harmful to Canada to retaliate. I think that's pretty narrow-minded," Drummond said.

"I'd like to give that advice to the kid in the schoolyard who's getting bullied, [because] it's not much more complicated than that: If you want to stop a bully you have to be prepared to get your nose bloodied. It just eggs them on otherwise."

World.title: Stressed out about politics? It could be impacting your health
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Following too much political news, including the ongoing Canada-U.S. trade war, could have significant mental and physical health impacts, researchers say. Recent studies linked excessive political news with insomnia, anxiety, loss of appetite and depression.

In downtown Toronto, it doesn't take long to find people with politics on their minds.



"I think everyone is pretty stressed about politics right now. It's hard not to be," said Tonya Facey when stopped by CBC News. "Politics is a part of everyday life and there's a lot going on, politically."

Jamie Haynes, visiting from St. John's, said he too worries about politics.

"Especially with the war on the go with Donald Trump and Canada — it's quite concerning," he said.

The trade war with the U.S., an Alberta referendum and Quebec election this fall, global conflicts: these are the kinds of political events that can trigger stress, researchers say. Political decisions that impact people's daily lives, and political disagreements that cause conflict with others are also sources of worry.

Political stress is now an entire field of study that gained traction in the U.S. around the 2016 presidential election. Here in Canada, political scientists, psychologists and mental health experts are also investigating the toll this form of stress can take on someone's health.

"There has been a lot of documented evidence, particularly over the past 10 years, in looking at things like loss of sleep, loss of appetite, negative emotions, periodic depression — these sorts of things that people can tie to things like a major election or maybe a particular conflict that's happening in the world,” said Amanda Friesen, a Canada Research Chair in Political Psychology.

The professor of political science at Western University in London, Ont., launched the Body Politics Lab in 2022, where her team carries out studies investigating how people's bodies and minds react to politics.

Political stress is a field of study that gained traction around the 2016 U.S. presidential election. Political science professor Amanda Friesen founded the Body Politics Lab at Western University to measure how people feel, emotionally and physically, about politics. (Meagan Fitzpatrick/CBC)

One study gave 81 undergraduate students a ring-like device that measured their temperature, pulse and sweat level as they scrolled their TikTok accounts. Western University PhD student Samantha Jones said a key takeaway from the results was not so much the physical reactions to viewing political content, but the emotional ones.

"They were more likely to report feeling negatively afterwards, compared to other types of content," said Jones.

They were also more likely to engage with it — by sharing it and viewing the comments — and that informs the algorithm.

"So despite this content making them feel negatively," said Jones, "they are inadvertently saying they want more."

Finding a healthy balance

Friesen said these kinds of studies are aimed at understanding what stresses people out when it comes to politics, and what that stress can mean for their health — and the health of democracy.

"One of our projects right now is balancing democratic and personal health," she said.

If something is shown to harm someone's well-being, they're usually advised to avoid it. But politics trickles into people's everyday lives, and with social media and the 24/7 news cycle, it's hard to avoid. Plus, people need to stay engaged in politics in order to have a thriving democracy, said Friesen.

Noah Vanderhoeven, one of the Body Politics researchers, said he thinks a balance between staying informed and maintaining healthy habits can be struck.

Some people even respond to the stress in ways that are good for democracy, he said.

"These kinds of anxieties about politics in the world can also be addressed through political action and being involved and engaged as a citizen," said Vanderhoeven.

He's leading a study this fall tied to the Alberta referendum, which he said could be a stressful event for some.

One study gave undergraduate students a ring-like device that measured their temperature, pulse and sweat level as they scrolled their TikTok accounts. University of Western Ontario PhD student Samantha Jones, seen with colleague Cole Stevenson, said people reported feeling badly after seeing political content. (Meagan Fitzpatrick/CBC)

Staying informed about politics in a healthy way can be a challenge for some Canadians, according to Dr. Allison Crawford, a psychiatrist at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health who leads Canada's national 9-8-8 suicide crisis hotline.

She said people are reaching out because of political stress.

"When political worry causes uncertainty in general, especially related to finances or people's sense of security or the safety of the world, we do often see that in our texters and callers," said Crawford.

People report losing sleep, feeling unsettled, overwhelmed and helpless, she said.

'I think everyone is pretty stressed about politics right now,' says Tonya Facey in Toronto. Crisis line callers report losing sleep, feeling unsettled, overwhelmed and helpless due to political stress. (Meagan Fitzpatrick/CBC)

Recognizing symptoms is a good first step, said Crawford, then people should reach out to someone they trust for support.

"We do want people involved in our democracy and we want people to not disengage but there are things that we can control and things that we can't control," she said.

Time spent consuming news and social media is something that can be controlled, Crawford advised, and could be limited as a way to de-stress.

Trade war stress 'spike'

Recent news headlines in Canada are dominated by the trade war with the U.S. and Friesen said she believes Canadians’ political stress levels have "spiked" since U.S. President Donald Trump took office a second time and took aim at Canada.

"Suddenly there was this sort of external 'enemy' that pulled Canadians together but increased this stress," said Friesen. "I think there's this kind of element of uncertainty. Is this all posturing? What does this mean? And anytime there's uncertainty, that is going to cause anxiety.”

That’s exactly what Amélie Valois said she’s feeling.

"Politics do stress me out especially what's going on with the U.S. right now, and how it's going to impact our grocery bills, and business, and everything going forward," she told CBC News as she walked towards the Rogers Centre to take in a Blue Jays game. "It's stressful."

World.title: As Germany's far right gains ground, coded symbols are hiding in plain sight
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Germany's far right gains political ground in some parts of the country, researchers say some supporters are getting more comfortable showing their views in public — albeit sometimes without displaying an explicitly political symbol.

At recent rallies for the Alternative for Germany, or AfD, that coded language was visible on things as ordinary as a pair of sneakers or a T-shirt.

Researchers say logos for brands including New Balance and Lonsdale are increasingly used as dog whistles for nationalist and Nazi symbolism — something that is especially significant in Germany, where the display of Nazi symbols is restricted by law.

"What we noticed in the last couple of years is that frequently at these events, you see a lot of people who have different signs which relate to the extreme right," said Gideon Botsch, head of the Emil Julius Gumbel Research Unit on Antisemitism and Right-Wing Extremism at Potsdam University.

"Some are clear and open right-wing and neo-Nazi symbols ... others are opaque or playing the game a little bit."

New Balance sneakers are seen on attendees at the AfD rally. Some on the far-right have also adopted that brand as a symbol of their political beliefs. (Lisa Mayor/CBC)

Some have co-opted New Balance, taking the large "N" on the side of its sneakers to mean "nationalist" and "NB" for Nationale Bewegung, or "national movement," Botsch said.

Likewise, Lonsdale has seen renewed use of its sportswear by the far right in part because, he says, when worn a certain way the logo spells out NSDA — the abbreviation for Germany's National Socialist Party.

"Those who know will know; those who don't know will think this is harmless," Botsch said.

The ambiguity is significant because Germany's law against Nazi symbols "expressly covers flags, badges, uniform items, slogans and forms of greeting,” said Sophie Scheuble, digital policy and counter-extremism manager at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue.

This marketing image from German online retailer Spartoo.de shows the Lonsdale brand being half-covered to reveal the letters NSDA. Spartoo has no affiliation with the far right. (Spartoo.de)

So "most of what is worn at far-right events is therefore lawful, and this distinction is well understood within right-wing extremist scenes.”

Those restrictions have led to an increase in the use of symbols recognizable only to those who know what they mean, without crossing legal lines.

When the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt's domestic intelligence service updated its handbook on far-right symbols in May, Scheuble said, its director noted that most extremists avoid prosecutable symbols and instead rely on codes and catchwords.

What has changed, researchers say, is the political environment where those styles are appearing.

Changing political climate

The Alternative for Germany, or AfD, has grown from a fringe party in 2013 into the likely winner of an upcoming state election in Saxony-Anhalt. The party has been legally designated a far-right extremist group in the state.

If it wins, it would mark the first time a far-right party has had an absolute state majority in Germany since the Second World War.

AfD Leader Ulrich Siegmund appears on stage at the rally, which drew more than 4,000 people, on Aug. 23. The party is expected to win an upcoming state election in Saxony-Anhalt. (Malte Broyer/CBC)

Fabian Wichmann, an expert at the EU Knowledge Hub on Preventing Radicalization, said there is a growing "grey zone" between Germany's hardcore neo-Nazi movement and the broader populist right.

Members of neo-Nazi groups attend AfD rallies and meetings and have encouraged their supporters to vote for the party, he says, seeing its success as a step toward their own political goals.

"The AfD has a widespread and diverse group of followers," Wichmann said. At its election events and marches, "you will see people who look very normal in their clothing," wearing things like New Balance and Lonsdale.

He said not everyone wearing those brands is a neo-Nazi, but there are "also a lot of neo-Nazis who wear this kind of stuff because they have some typical symbols, some typical narratives they share."

A rally attendee is seen wearing a Thor Steinar belt. The brand has gained popularity in some far-right circles for its use of Nordic runes. (Malte Broyer/CBC)

But the bigger change researchers say they're seeing isn't in the clothing itself. It's in the willingness to display those signals openly.

Wichmann says that shift matches the growing strength of Germany's far right and the AfD.

"They feel like ... the culture, the temperature of a society is changing. And now it's possible to wear something like this without getting into conflict,” he said.

"There's a feeling of, 'OK, we are on the winner's side right now,' and that's the reason why they are so openly wearing it."

Lonsdale's decades-long battle

New Balance has no affiliation with Germany's far-right movement. The company did not respond to requests for comment, but in the past has said it "does not tolerate bigotry or hate in any form."

Likewise, Lonsdale has spent decades fighting its appropriation by the far right with anti-racism initiatives since it became popular among German skinhead and neo-Nazi subcultures in the 1980s and '90s.

But the British boxing and sportswear company says the phenomenon is returning.

"We have noticed that since around summer 2024, the Lonsdale brand has once again been increasingly worn by far-right extremists,” spokesperson Ralf Elfering said. "This earlier misuse of the Lonsdale brand — and the fact that we are seeing it again today — is very frustrating.”

Elfering said the company stops supplying retailers when it discovers Lonsdale is being sold in a clearly extremist context.

Other brands, however, carry considerably less ambiguity, according to experts.

Botsch points to Thor Steinar, a brand known for Nordic and runic imagery that has long been associated with Germany's far-right scene.

"Thor Steinar … maybe is a clearer sign than New Balance or Lonsdale that somebody is part of the scene," he said.

The company's original rune logo prompted police seizures after German authorities argued it resembled banned SS symbolism. Higher courts ruled in 2008 that displaying the logo was not punishable, according to Scheuble, and the company had by then introduced a replacement logo.

World.title: FIBA Women's World Cup begins without Canada. Is it a setback for national team, or a reset for LA28?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It was a cruel twist of fate.

Just three days before the WNBA and its players landed on a new collective bargaining agreement — one that would officialize Canada’s first WNBA team’s inaugural season — the country’s national team was dealt a blow.

It was eliminated from World Cup contention. And by Toronto Tempo head coach Sandy Brondello’s Australian team, no less.

“I felt like, they’re going to kick me out now. And in the end I had to remember what hat I’m wearing and what name I have across the front of my chest,” Brondello said, citing a bit of awkwardness at her conflicting roles.

“It was a hard-fought game. I feel sorry for Canada. I think they’re a really strong team and they’ve got some great young players coming through, so they’re gonna be strong for years and sometimes you need a little reset to get back up. We did the same thing after Tokyo.”

“Canada’s going to be fine. I know they’ve got the Swords [sisters] and got some great players from the college system and they get their hands on them and add to that, I think they’re going to be in a good spot.”

On Monday, the WNBA will break for two-and-a-half weeks to allow its players to compete at the World Cup, which begins in Berlin Sept. 4. Canada, thanks to that 82-76 loss to an already-qualified Australian squad in March, won’t be there, even despite a fourth-place finish at the 2022 edition of the event.

Despite losing to her Australian team, Toronto Tempo head coach Sandy Brondello is confident 'Canada is going to be fine.’ (Michael Chisholm/Getty Images)

Canada wins pre-qualifying tournament

Some better news arrived Sunday, when Canada crushed Mexico 83-53 to complete a 5-0 pre-qualifying tournament in Guadalajara and book its spot in a 2028 Olympic qualifier set for that February.

Syla Swords, the 20-year-old mentioned by Brondello as one of Canada’s bright young stars alongside sister Savvy, won tournament MVP after averaging 14.8 points, 3.6 rebounds, 2.2 assists and one steal per game.

It sets Canada up with a relatively low-stakes next 17 months and a prime opportunity to build chemistry, lay groundwork and allow next-generation players like Swords to continue maturing and evolving as basketball players.

The team that ran through Mexico was made up of six veterans (think Kayla Alexander, Sami Hill) and six younger players, including NCAAers Syla Swords (Michigan), Agot Makeer (South Carolina), Delaney Gibb (BYU) and others. Head coach Nell Fortner called it a perfect mix — and was especially impressed by the latter contingent.

“They're built a little differently. I don't know if that makes any sense, but their commitment is so strong to the sport of basketball and to their country,” Fortner said.

Swords, especially, continued to show that she could be Canada’s next basketball star.

“She played fearless. I tell you what, she showed us all and anybody watching what an extraordinary shooter she is, from her quick release to her accuracy to her consistency. And she's just already a pro, she carries herself like a pro and it was really fun to coach her,” Fortner said.

Still, there’s no denying that giving Swords and her peers the World Cup stage to grow on would have been ideal. Canada, now ranked seventh by FIBA and with its WNBA players on board, lost three of five games in the March tournament in a pool with just one team ranked higher.

“Do I wish we were at the World Cup? Heck yeah,” Fortner said. “But we did the next best thing. And that was important for us to do that. We committed to it. Everybody dug into it, from players to coaching staff. And we accomplished it. And that's very encouraging moving forward.”

The group of six young NCAAers also featured Avery Howell (Washington), Cearah Parchment (Illinois) and Jasmine Bascoe (Villanova). Meanwhile, Michigan’s Mila Holloway was in camp with the team but missed the tournament due to injury, per Fortner. Duke star Toby Fournier was not with the team during the summer, per Fortner, who added that “we surely would have loved to have had her.”

While disappointed Canada won't be competing at the World Cup, head coach Nell Fortner, centre, believes winning the pre-qualification tournament is the next best thing, (Burak Basturk/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)

Canadian talent at NCAA level

It is hard, if not impossible, to recall a time when there has been this much Canadian talent at the NCAA level — in line with the explosion of the sport during this decade.

Fortner, the 67-year-old from Jackson, Miss., watched a similar thing happen in her home country as head coach and general manager of the expansion Indiana Fever in 1999.

“All of a sudden, you're looking at players, little girls growing up, knowing that they want to be a professional basketball player. Oh my gosh, that's phenomenal. And the number of young women playing basketball, it'll explode very soon in Canada, and that's exciting,” Fortner said.

In an interview with select media just before the Tempo tipped off their regular season, WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert also mused on how impactful the Tempo could be for the national program.

“Especially on the grassroots. For young girls to be able to come into Toronto no matter where they're from in Canada — obviously we're doing a couple games in Montreal and Vancouver — and see professional basketball players, I think it'll inspire a bunch of girls, as I said, to pick up a basketball who probably wouldn't have otherwise picked up a basketball, especially if they see someone who looks like them, plays like them, is like them,” Engelbert said.

For now, Canada has those 17 months to prepare for its one shot to compete at the Los Angeles Olympics.

Fortner said she hopes to gather the team, including its WNBAers, for a training camp next February. Canada’s biggest tournament ahead of the Olympic qualifier will be the FIBA AmeriCup next July in El Salvador.

“They're not learning something new every time they come to a training camp. We're just building, continuing to grow what we do offensively and defensively,” Fortner said.

After Brondello’s Team Australia “reset” in the wake of an eighth-place finish at Tokyo 2020, it went on to beat Canada for bronze at the 2022 World Cup before claiming another third-place finish at the 2024 Olympics.

Success may not be quite so swift for the Canadians, but the building blocks appear in place to turn the World Cup step backward into two forward.

World.title: Ferry carrying more than 260 passengers capsizes off northern Cyprus
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A ferry carrying more than 260 passengers capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday, Turkish media reported.

The catamaran-style ferry was travelling from the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, in the breakaway north of ethnically divided Cyprus, to the Turkish port of Tasucu in Mersin province.

There are no reports of casualties so far.

The ferry started taking in water a few kilometres off the coast, the Turkish state-run TRT news channel reported.

Northern Cyprus Transportation Minister Erhan Arikli told TRT that the ship had overturned and that rescue crews were already on the scene.

Several companies run ferries on the busy route between Kyrenia and Tasucu. It is not yet known which company was operating the ferry that capsized.

Video footage from the scene shows people with life-vests floating in the waters around the capsized vessel.

World.title: Nepal warns of possible fresh flooding as communities grapple with devastation
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Authorities in Nepal warned of possible fresh flooding on Sunday and urged residents in flood-affected districts to remain on high alert after water levels rose in the Bhotekoshi River.

Flood warning notices were sent to people's phones early Sunday as rescue crews worked to clear a major highway connecting Kathmandu to one of the areas worst hit by Wednesday's catastrophic floods, which killed at least 800 people and left more than 3,000 missing in Nepal and Tibet.

In Dhading, one of the worst-hit regions in Nepal, some residents began returning to ruined homes to see what can be salvaged.

Residents sat in homes with walls washed away by the floods, shovelling sludge-like mud and rubble off balconies. Others scanned the ground for items they could pick out of the mud and rinse off. One man had returned for his chickens, which he found alive. He tied them up and put them in the cabin of his truck.

"Everything is finished. Nothing is left. Not even our home," Sharmila Tamang, a Dhading resident who was trying to salvage items from her home, told The Associated Press.

At a key power plant that was severely damaged by the floods, workers started inspecting the facilities Sunday to survey the destruction. The plant serves more than 20,000 people across four districts.

In the town of Galchhi, a group of residents sought higher ground on a nearby bridge and watched as the river roared by. Some pointed to enormous rocks washed downriver during the earlier floods, while others standing on a suspension bridge were warned off with whistles.

Along the river, homes, vehicles and farm tractors could be seen jutting from the thick grey-brown sediment that enveloped entire villages in some areas. Parts of rice terraces along the riverside had dropped into the river after landslides hit them.

WATCH | Nepal-Tibet flash flood death toll continues to climb: Nepal-Tibet flash flood death toll climbs as fears of 2nd flood grow | Duration 2:21 CBC News is on the ground in Nepal, where fears are growing that a swollen artificial lake formed by this week's massive flash flood along the Tibet border could cause another flooding disaster. So far at least 579 people have been confirmed dead, while almost 2,000 are still missing.

Nepal's disaster agency said Sunday the death toll had climbed to 788 with 2,502 missing, while Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing on the Chinese side of the border.

The missing include hundreds of people from over a dozen countries who were in the region to work, visit the mountains or make a pilgrimage to a sacred peak. On Sunday, Chinese state media said 261 foreigners were missing in Tibet, including over 100 Nepalis and others from around the world.

Residents are receiving constant flood warnings

Homes and businesses left intact after the flooding were still without electricity on Sunday, as twisted power line poles and wires lay tangled in the mud.

Prithivi Highway is a crucial supply route for food, fuel and other goods entering Kathmandu from other parts of the country. While most of the highway is operational, other parts still face repair challenges.

The latest warnings came after Chinese authorities informed their Nepalese counterparts of increased water flow upstream, according to Dharam Raj Uprety, chief executive of Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

Residents look at the swollen Trishuli River from a higher area on Sunday. (Niranjan Shrestha/The Associated Press)

But residents of the flood-hit villages said they were struggling to make sense of near-constant alarms they've received since the initial floods.

"Sometimes they say a flood is coming, then we have to run again to higher ground, even at night. There is also rain," said Govind Shreshta, a resident. "It's really difficult for me. I have a 72-year-old father and 70-year-old mom. I must carry them and I am exhausted. It's going on like this for those who are still alive."

Large concrete and smaller suspension bridges were destroyed, leaving communities on the other side of the river with less easy access.

"Those who are there are now stuck there. Those who are here are stuck here. It's going to be very difficult," said Sattan Singh Tamang, 47, who was working near a bridge when Wednesday's floods came.

Nepalis have become victims of climate change: minister

Wednesday's flash floods started after a glacial collapse high in the Himalayan region. Scientists who studied satellite images said bedrock underneath a glacier high in the Himalayan region had collapsed, taking part of the glacier with it. The rockfall was so extreme that it registered as magnitude 5.2.

A young boy is helped by a women to put up a photograph of her missing relative on a wall alongside photographs of missing and deceased people displayed outside a government hospital in Kathmandu on Sunday. (Dar Yasin/The Associated Press)

The rocks and melted water then swelled the rivers in the valleys below, causing a torrent of water that swept buildings, bridges and earth downstream in Tibet and Nepal.

Nepal's foreign minister called for a global response to climate change, saying Nepal was bearing a disproportionate share of its impact.

"Despite having only 0.1 per cent contribution to the global emissions, people of Nepal have become major victims of climate change," Shisir Khanal said Saturday.

Scientists have said it is too early to draw a direct connection between global warming and Wednesday's catastrophe. However, they said that as Earth's temperature rises because of human activities such as burning oil, gas and coal, the chances of such disasters increase, especially in the Himalayan mountains, which are warming considerably faster than many other parts of the world.

World.title: An island mysteriously appeared — then disappeared — on B.C.'s largest reservoir
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

No one knows where it came from or where it went, but a massive new island might be floating out somewhere in the Williston Reservoir in northern B.C.

The forested land mass caught the attention of B.C. Hydro and local residents earlier this month after it was spotted bobbing in the massive man-made lake north of Mackenzie.

Rocky Avery says video and pictures of the island were taken by a boater and later shared with him. He posted them on social media, and they quickly went viral.

"It was a pretty amazing sight to see, never seen anything like that in my 40 years in this country," said Avery.

"There was a big fishing derby coming up, so I wanted to make sure everybody was aware of what was going on. And I wanted B.C. Hydro to know too that it was out there, just in case it was floating down their way."

The discovery left a B.C. Hydro spokesperson incredulous when CBC News first inquired about the island's origins.

Bob Gammer says he was first skeptical about the origins of the video because of the rise of generative AI technology. Not everything posted online can be trusted as being credible at first glance, he said.

"It's certainly something we've not heard of before," said Gammer. "And with not very many people reporting it, it was difficult to locate."

LISTEN | Floating island on Williston Reservoir: Radio West 3:57 A floating island in northern B.C.'s Williston Reservoir

But satellite imagery dated July 21 confirmed the island was in fact real, and floating in the main body of the reservoir west of Finlay Bay, about 100 kilometres west of the W.A.C. Bennett Dam.

Gammer says the island was estimated around 70 metres wide and 140 metres long, or about 9,800 square metres in area.

According to those estimates, that's roughly the size of two NFL football fields.

By Aug. 5, the island was no longer showing up in satellite data.

"We've been taking more updated snapshots and we can't see the object anymore. So it's disappeared now," Gammer said.

"It doesn't mean it's gone to the bottom of the reservoir. It may have returned to a more sheltered area along the shoreline."

Gammer says no operational impacts are expected, though B.C. Hydro is monitoring for the island's possible reappearance.

Satellite data provided by B.C. Hydro shows the location and size of a floating island found in the Williston Lake reservoir in northern B.C., about 100 kilometres west of the W.A.C. Bennett Dam. (B.C. Hydro)

First full reservoir in 14 years

The Williston reservoir, impounded behind the W.A.C. Bennett Dam in 1968, is the seventh-largest reservoir in the world and visible from space.

High winter snowpacks and steady summer rains have filled it to the brim, forcing B.C. Hydro to open the dam's spillways in June and July to release water.

Gammer says it's likely the island formed over many years somewhere along the shore where driftwood accumulated, allowing plants and trees to take root in the decomposing debris.

As reservoir levels rose, it broke free, and winds carried it out into open water.

"We haven't had a full reservoir in 14 years," Gammer said. "We can't pinpoint the origin of this floating island [but that's] one explanation that seems reasonable."

Avery says this year's high water has washed out shoreline sand dunes popular for quad-biking, and pulled more trees and debris out into the lake than usual.

"There's areas we would never even drive a boat on before, and now we're going up over top of it," said Avery.

High water levels in the Williston Lake reservoir in northern B.C. prompted B.C. Hydro to open the W.A.C. Bennett Dam spillways in June and July to release water. (Matt Preprost/CBC)

Phenomenon seen across the world

While a rare sight in Williston Lake, floating islands are a rather common phenomenon seen in dam building.

In Wisconsin, massive chunks of peat bog broke off from the bottom of Lake Chippewa after it was flooded for the Winter Dam.

One of them, called the "Forty Acre Bog," has to be pushed by boat every year to prevent it from drifting into a local bridge.

In Africa, researchers are investigating how floating islands in Lake Victoria are impacting transportation, fisheries and water quality. The world's second-largest freshwater lake spans across three countries.

Mackenzie, a town north of Prince George, is one of numerous communities along Williston Lake. (Chris Corday/CBC)

Lake needs public help to monitor

Gammer says the power utility relies on public reports in monitoring its reservoirs.

Because the Williston reservoir is so huge, he says it's not feasible to surveil it by water, and that B.C. Hydro will keep an eye out for sightings of the island via satellite.

Avery says local tugboat crews do a good job pulling what logs they can out of the lake, but says people need to be careful boating on the waters.

"When it's calm, it's fine. You can usually see them, but you get a little bit of choppy waves and it's really hard to see them until you're right on top," he said.

"Some are full-size trees and it'll do a lot of damage to your boat. So you got to be super careful."

Subscribe to CBC's Fort St. John Weekly for a roundup of the best news and stories from B.C.'s Peace and Northern Rockies.

World.title: Icelanders vote to stay out of EU in close-fought referendum
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Icelanders voted to stay out of the European Union, referendum results showed on Sunday, as they rejected a government push to reopen membership talks and sided with those who said Iceland's fishing waters were too important to risk.

The Arctic island of 400,000 people has debated whether to join the EU for well over a decade and had initially been expected to narrowly back holding membership talks, but opinion polls this month showed views had changed.

In Saturday's referendum, 52.8 per cent of ballots cast were against the government's proposal to hold negotiations with Brussels, 47.2 per cent were in favour, and 82.5 per cent of eligible voters took part, public broadcaster RUV and other Icelandic media reported.

Out of six constituencies, only the two in central Reykjavik had a majority that voted in favour, while the rural areas and the Reykjavik suburbs voted against.

The government framed membership as a shield against trade wars and Arctic rivalry and presented the referendum as a "now or never" moment. Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir said a "no" would end the debate for as long as her centre-left coalition was in power.

Decades of membership debate

In Brussels, some officials had voiced hope that a vote to join from Iceland could ease skepticism toward EU enlargement and strategically strengthen the bloc when Arctic security is in focus.

Iceland, a NATO member state but with no standing army of its own, also debated whether EU membership could boost the country's security when U.S. President Donald Trump has cast doubt on the U.S. commitment to the military alliance.

Iceland Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir votes in the national referendum on resuming EU membership talks, at a polling station in Reykjavik on Saturday. (Leonhard Foeger/Reuters)

Trump has also repeatedly said he wants to acquire Greenland, another Arctic island.

But for some Icelanders, fishing was a sharper focus than security.

The industry is one of Iceland's biggest, making up 15 per cent of gross domestic product in direct and indirect contributions, and some 40 per cent of export revenue, data shows.

Interest rates and the cost of living

The island nation first applied to join the EU in 2009 when a financial crisis hit the country's small, exposed economy. The government ended talks in 2013.

Ahead of Saturday's referendum, finances were again a central issue as Iceland has grappled with high inflation and interest rates.

Supporters of a "yes" vote said EU membership, and possibly adopting the euro, could bring relief. Iceland's central bank interest rate is eight per cent, compared with 2.25 per cent at the European Central Bank.

"It would not solve Iceland's structural faults, but it could become a catalyst to a more healthy economy," said chief economist Vilhjalmur Hilmarsson at Viska, one of Iceland's largest labour unions.

WATCH | Trump's interests in the Arctic: Why Trump wants Greenland | Duration 4:22 The Trump administration has made it clear it wants to take control of Greenland and it isn’t ruling out using military force. For The National, CBC’s Eli Glasner breaks down why the U.S. has labelled annexing the sparsely-populated island a ‘national security priority.’

Opposition leader Gudrun Hafsteinsdottir, who led the "no" campaign, said the economic case is overstated. "These are not problems that Brussels will solve for us. These are problems that Icelandic politicians must solve," she said.

Voter Ragnhildur Skarphedinsdottir, 70, said Iceland was managing well on its own and that she was voting "no."

"By staying independent as we are, we look brightly to the future," she said before casting her ballot in Reykjavik.

Under EU rules, fishing quotas are based on historical fishing patterns, among other factors. Some Icelandic officials have said Iceland would therefore retain control of its waters, since no EU country has fished there for decades.

Hafsteinsdottir disputed that. "I know that the European Union will come up with some promises of some flexibility, especially in the beginning, but we know that it will not be for good," she said.

World.title: Finance minister presents Colombia’s $203B budget proposal
World.content:
Colombia’s Finance Minister Miguel Gomez presented a budget proposal of COP634.9 trillion ($203 billion) for the coming year, a 14% increase compared to last year.

Much of the increase is due to the government’s debt obligations, which went up 55% to 155.4 trillion ($49.8 billion), almost a quarter of the entire budget.

At a presentation, Gomez told press that an earthquake that left tens of thousands homeless in western Colombia earlier this month also forced the administration of Abelardo de la Espriella to increase spending.

In a video, the finance minister also said that the government “has taken deci

The budget bill, a revision of the one that was presented by the former government of former President Gustavo Petro, will have to be approved by Congress before October 20 or be issued as a decree.

The government will also present a Finance Bill, which determines how the government plans to pay for its spending, before December.

World.title: Colombia claims killing eight suspected EMBF guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella said Thursday that Colombia’s armed forces killed eight guerrillas of FARC dissident group EMBF in a joint operation.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella said that the military offensive targeted “camps used by structures of the Jorge Suarez Briceño Block,” a unit of the EMBF, in a rural part of El Retorno in the Guaviare province.

In a precision airstrike followed by an operation carried out by our commandos, the preliminary tally shows that 8 terrorists have been killed so far, 11 rifles and 5 machine guns have been seized, along with a large amount of logistical supplies. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that “Colombia must know we are going on the offensive” against organized crime and illegal armed groups that are all deemed “narco-terrorist” organizations by the government.

“Major ringleaders and their criminal organizations will find no hiding place or sanctuary anywhere in the country,” the president added.

De la Espriella took office earlier this month, vowing to end peace negotiations with illegal armed groups and go on a military offensive with the help of the US military instead.

One of the groups that was negotiating peace with the administration of former President Gustavo Petro was the EMBF, led by former FARC commander “Calarca.”

The group, together with FARC dissident group EMC, controls large swathe of territory in southern Colombia and along the border with Venezuela.

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: De la Espriella claims 123,700 barrels stolen monthly from Colombia’s state oil company
World.content:
Oil thieves from north Colombia would be stealing at least 123,700 barrel of gasoline, diesel and naphtha, a month, claimed President Abelardo de la Espriella.

According to De la Espriella, the theft of the refined oil products that wee imported or produced by state-owned oil company Ecopetrol “is utterly alarming, and demands an immediate and forceful response from the State.”

Every month, approximately 123,700 barrels of refined products—gasoline, diesel, and naphtha—imported or produced by Ecopetrol would be stolen. This would occur solely on a 14-inch pipeline that connects Pozos Colorados, in Santa Marta, to the interior of the country, and the losses are concentrated mainly in Cesar and Magdalena. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“We would be talking about more than 1.5 million barrels a year, with losses exceeding $500,000 million for Ecopetrol and, therefore, for the nation,” the president said in a post on social media platform X.

De la Espriella added that “these fuels are used as raw materials in the illicit processing of cocaine” by illegal armed groups that operate in the country’s periphery.

If we confirm that a large portion of this fuel is being used to power cocaine production facilities, then we are not only dealing with a massive theft from Ecopetrol: we are dealing with a criminal network that may be linking the theft of hydrocarbons to drug trafficking and the financing of armed terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president ordered a “joint operation” of the military, police, prosecution and administrative authorities “to comprehensively combat this criminal economy” led by Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora.

“I want results and periodic report on progress,” said De la Espriella.

Organized crime and illegal armed groups have been involved in fuel theft for decades.
