World.title: From the archive: Learning Spanish? Don’t be shy or afraid of making mistakes
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article, for example — originally published in November 2019 — explores the leap of faith required when learning Mexican Spanish.

When I first arrived in Mexico, I had two years of college-level Spanish under my belt. While I was an enthusiastic learner, I was also a very self-conscious speaker, terrified of making embarrassing mistakes and generally sounding like a 2-year-old.

I did, in fact, sound like a 2-year-old at first, as there’s simply no way around being a “baby” when one is first learning. Happily, I survived that stage and now speak at least as well as a know-it-all 13-year-old.

Part of my apprehension with the language was the sense that Mexico’s love-hate relationship with the United States would lead to some situations in which I’d be mocked for my accent or mistakes that I would inevitably make.

After all, most people here know very well how Latinos are treated by certain segments of the U.S. population when they’re on the other side of the border, so I’d imagined that the temptation to dish some out to us collectively would be at least a little irresistible.

For the most part, that didn’t happen. It’s also possible that I simply didn’t realize it was happening, but I think most of us humans have a pretty good sense of when others are laughing at us.

Once in a while someone will have a longish conversation with me (in Spanish) and then say something like, “So, you don’t speak Spanish, eh?” or they’ll point out that they “could tell right away that I was American because of my accent” which always makes me bristle, as I’m pretty sure my accent is, while definitely existent, not obviously American.

(My Mexican friends may disagree with me on that one; I’d ask them, but the answer might be too painful for me to hear.)

There’s some sting in it, but I do my best to chalk up any unflattering comments about my Spanish to cosmic justice and not take it too personally.

In the part of Mexico where I live, English is not considered an essential skill the same way it is in the north or in tourist areas. Because of this, most foreigners in my area do their best with the language: they take classes, they practice, they work hard to get better.

Learning a language is sign of respect

They understand, above all, that learning the language of your hosts, if you are able, is a matter of respect.

When I traveled to Los Cabos recently to visit a friend, I saw how different things were in a town that depends on tourism from their English-speaking neighbors: I was addressed in English at all times, and if I answered in Spanish it almost seemed to startle people, as if they’d come into contact with a dog that had learned to produce human sounds.

For the most part, Mexicans are charmed when we non-native speakers at least try. They’re patient and encouraging, and try their best to be helpful. Mexico really is an ideal place to learn Spanish, as I can’t imagine another place in which more impromptu and consistent support among the general population would be given.

That said, I know many of my compatriots are shy about learning — and especially about using — the Spanish that they know already. I completely understand: there’s nothing that makes us feel quite as vulnerable as not being able to “prove” that we are smart, complex, discerning individuals.

There’s no way around sounding like a simpleton when we’re on that long uphill trajectory, and simply put, it can be a humiliating experience.

But again: at least attempting to learn the local language, if one is able, is a matter of respect. “Well then, what about all the people in the U.S. that haven’t bothered to learn English? I bet you don’t go around preaching to them about respect, do you?”

The short answer is that no, indeed I do not. Because here’s the difference: most people who go to the U.S. without already speaking English are in survival mode, just trying to make it from one day to the next, often working a dizzying number of hours both to both survive, and likely to send money back home.

Most Americans and Canadians, however, come to Mexico either in vacation or retirement mode. Some, sadly, come because their spouses or loved ones have been deported and they want to keep the family together.

If one is on vacation, of course, learning the language won’t be expected. But if you settle here, an effort must be made.

Find a school, or find a teacher. Find someone to sit and help you practice. Spend time just listening to people with no intention of adding to the conversation. One of the best pieces of advice I’ve ever received for learning a language is literally to pretend to be a baby: listen to the sounds, watch people, let whole social situations piece themselves together and come into focus slowly.

Babies, after all, spend at least a couple of years listening and observing before they try to string together a sentence with more than four words in it.

On my first plane ride into Mexico, my nervousness increased with each sentence given in Spanish by the flight attendants: the more they spoke, the more I realized I wasn’t catching anything at all that they were saying.

Since then, I’ve made about a million mistakes, linguistically embarrassed myself in every way imaginable, and surely sounded much less sophisticated than I imagine myself to be.

But I’ve gained the ability to talk to most people on this side of the world and have developed some of the closest relationships of my lifetime in this language.

Hands down, totally worth it.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: A governor takes a U-turn, CJNG loses more ground and business booms
World.content:
Listen to this article

The week of Aug. 24 in Mexico began on awkward footing following a Morena party faux pas in Sinaloa. Rubén Rocha Moya, currently under investigation in the United States for alleged collusion with the Sinaloa Cartel, briefly reclaimed the Sinaloa governorship after months on leave, only to retreat again two days later. Meanwhile, several storm systems dumped rain on most of the country, and an investigation into fuel theft in Tamaulipas turned up a startling menagerie of exotic animals.

Also this week, President Sheinbaum revealed new reforms and a US $6M windfall for Guerrero schools as she prepares to soon give her second annual report to the nation.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Sheinbaum weighs in on Rocha’s status in Sinaloa

President Claudia Sheinbaum spent the week fielding questions about the fallout from Rocha Moya’s brief return to the Sinaloa governorship from Aug. 21–23 and the future of Sinaloa’s leadership.

At Monday’s mañanera, as Sonora’s cattle trade with the U.S. reopened, she addressed the episode directly for the first time, saying she learned of Rocha’s Friday return through his social media post and had no prior knowledge of his plans. “I didn’t think it was appropriate, to say the least,” she said, later calling the decision “imprudent.” She credited Rocha’s renewed leave request — approved unanimously by Sinaloa’s Congress that Sunday — as “the best thing for Sinaloa,” and dismissed rumors that former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador had encouraged Rocha’s return as “political fiction.”

Sheinbaum extended the same standard to other Morena officials swept up in the same U.S. indictment. Asked on Tuesday about Senator Enrique Inzunza — one of 10 Sinaloa-linked officials accused by U.S. prosecutors of drug trafficking ties, who had signaled he might return to the Senate — she said the same principle applied. “Yesterday I gave my opinion on the case of the governor of Sinaloa, who is now on leave. I feel the same way about all 10 cases under investigation by the Attorney General’s Office,” she said. Inzunza subsequently separated from Morena’s Senate caucus on Wednesday, though he remains in office as senator.

Multiple CJNG busts across three states

Security forces delivered a string of blows against the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) this week. A coordinated operation across Hidalgo, Jalisco and Michoacán from Aug. 21–23 resulted in 20 arrests and the seizure of weapons, drugs and exotic animals tied to the cartel, with authorities raiding 36 properties and confiscating firearms, fentanyl, methamphetamine, 113 vehicles and a drone jammer.

That action followed a separate military-led operation in Michoacán targeting alleged CJNG leader Heraclio “El Tío Lako” Guerrero Martínez last week, which produced roughly a dozen more arrests, including relatives of the suspect. Combined, the two operations brought the week’s tally of alleged CJNG detentions to 32, part of what Security Minister Omar García Harfuch described as an effort to systematically dismantle the group’s operational and financial capacity rather than simply rack up arrests.

Confusion and concern in Mexicali

A U.S. security alert warning of a possible “August 25 threat” in Mexicali created a tense but ultimately murky standoff between caution and normalcy. The alert prompted the U.S. Mission to suspend official travel and activity in the border city, reportedly linked to fears that the crime gang Los Rusos might retaliate after a 120-kilogram fentanyl seizure — roughly 4 million doses — from a property connected to the group.

Mexican officials responded by increasing patrols around public buildings, but as Tuesday came and went without a major incident, the federal security cabinet said it had found no evidence of a specific or imminent threat to the public. Residents described a largely normal day, and the Mexicali-Calexico border crossing remained open throughout, leaving the alert’s basis and its practical necessity still unclear.

Economic data: Record highs alongside warning signs

Revised GDP figures showed the economy grew in the second quarter but contracted in June, with the primary sector contributing the steadiest growth. Foreign direct investment in Mexico yielded US $34.968 billion in FDI in the first half of 2026, its highest semester total ever recorded, up 2.1% year over year, even though the second quarter alone saw a 3.5% annual decline. Manufacturing captured 38.6% of that investment, and the United States remained the dominant source at $16.871 billion.

Trade data added to the good news: July exports hit a record US $81.4 billion, up 43.7% annually, driven by a 134% surge in electrical and electronic equipment shipments tied to U.S. demand for AI and data-center infrastructure inputs. At her Wednesday press conference, Sheinbaum cheered the numbers as proof of a “strong” economy, pointing to record FDI, 60 million people employed and a firm peso, and argued that years of minimum-wage increases had not triggered the inflation or capital flight critics once predicted.

That optimism gained further support when Mexico placed among the OECD’s fastest-growing economies, ranking sixth with 1.4% quarterly growth against an OECD average of 0.5%. But the jobs report complicated the picture: Mexico posted its best monthly job gain of 2026 in July, yet the increase was driven entirely by informal employment, with more than 1.08 million informal jobs added while over 412,000 formal positions vanished. Informality climbed to 56.2%, its highest level since December 2021 — a reminder that headline growth figures can mask deteriorating job quality.

This week’s investment announcements

Schneider Electric announced a major expansion of its operations in Querétaro, reinforcing the state’s role as an industrial and technology hub. Danish firms unveiled a US $510 million renewables project set to boost Campeche’s clean energy supply, adding to the country’s growing green energy portfolio. And Jalisco is set to host Mexico’s first solar panel recycling plant, a facility in Ciudad Guzmán capable of recovering up to 95% of materials from the roughly 1.6 million panels already installed statewide.

A fresh framework for environmental protection

Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena presented a bill to put environmental justice at the center of Mexican law, proposing reforms to the General Law of Ecological Balance and Environmental Protection. The initiative would require more forward-looking assessment of major projects, close loopholes that let developers split projects to dodge full environmental review, strengthen restoration and remediation requirements and add specific protections for environmental defenders and Indigenous, Afro-Mexican, rural and urban communities.

Foreign Minister strengthens ties in South Korea and Washington

Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco kept a packed international schedule this week. In Seoul, he met with South Korean officials and executives from Samsung, Hyundai, LG and Posco to promote investment in technology, semiconductors and education, part of groundwork for a 2026–30 bilateral action plan ahead of a planned visit by South Korea’s president. He then traveled to Washington, where he held his first face-to-face meeting with Secretary of State Marco Rubio. While both sides publicly stressed cooperation against drug and arms trafficking, Bloomberg reported that Washington privately pressed Mexico to do more to stop its own citizens from crossing into the U.S.

Aura farming battles debut in Mexico

A new social-media-driven trend reached Mexican public squares this week: aura farming battles, in which participants strike poses, dance and reference memes to project confidence and style while crowds judge who accumulates the most “aura.” Events popped up at Mexico City landmarks as well as in Xalapa and Torreón, though at least one Veracruz municipality banned the contests in public parks on administrative grounds.

Sheinbaum proposes dual-citizenship ban

Sheinbaum also unveiled a constitutional amendment that would bar dual nationals from running for president, governor or Mexico City mayor unless they renounce their other citizenship before registering as candidates. The government argues current constitutional language contains a loophole and that the country’s highest offices should be held only by people with unambiguous national allegiance — a proposal likely to draw scrutiny over its impact on Mexican-born citizens with binational ties.

Mexican athletes shine internationally

Cyclist Isaac del Toro won the Tour of Germany, becoming the first Latin American rider to capture the race, finishing 53 seconds ahead of France’s Louis Barré.

Mexico won two gold medals and a bronze at the World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam: Aylín Ibarra and Melissa Márquez took gold in women’s lightweight double sculls, Kenia Lechuga won gold in lightweight single sculls, and Alexis López earned bronze in men’s lightweight single sculls.

Looking ahead

The coming weeks will test whether this week’s political and security cracks widen further. In Sinaloa, the ongoing conflict between Los Mayos and Los Chapitos remains unresolved, complicating the search for a permanent successor. Pressure is also unlikely to ease on other Morena-aligned officials named in the same U.S. indictment, amid broader questions about the party’s exposure to organized crime in states beyond Sinaloa. With Sheinbaum’s second annual report to the nation approaching, how she navigates these overlapping crises could shape both her security narrative and her party’s credibility heading into the fall.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Activists rally to stop luxury project on Yucatán dunes
World.content:
A proposed luxury real estate development along a protected beach community in Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula has sparked protests and backlash online. It’s the latest in a string of projects that activists have sought to stop, saying the developments will have detrimental impacts on their communities.

Las Dunas tourist complex is a planned luxury real estate and tourism venture that aims to encompass 92,000 square meters (more than 22 acres) of virgin beach area less than an hour’s drive from Mérida, the state capital of Yucatán, including more than 70 apartments spread across six towers.

Given its size and scope, activists say the project will have a significant economic and environmental impact on the small beach town, and that it ignores pressing issues that need to be addressed.

“In Chuburná, there are real needs – problems stemming from a lack of basic infrastructure and systematic neglect by the authorities,” Salvemos las Dunas, a local environmental activist group, told Mexico News Daily. “They want to foster the false belief that megaprojects bring economic benefits, but the question is: benefits for whom?”

‘A crime against biodiversity’

It’s not just Salvemos las Dunas that’s sounding the alarm.

Mexico’s Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat) denied the project’s initial proposal in December 2023, as the site was deemed highly vulnerable. However, in April 2025, after adjustments were made to the proposal, the project was federally approved.

As the Las Dunas development began to take shape, the outcry from community members and activists was swift. Salvemos las Dunas launched a petition calling for a halt to the project and an official review of the proposed plan.

“[A]bove all, this area is not just a stretch of sand; it’s the history and identity of the people who already live there,” Salvemos las Dunas said.

Their concerns were supported by a three-day inspection led by the Federal Prosecutor’s Office for Environmental Protection (Profepa) in late July. That report detailed multiple violations of federal regulations, some of which could carry criminal charges.

“Omissions, non-compliance and subsequent damage to species of wild flora and fauna protected by Official Mexican Standards may transcend the administrative scope and constitute a crime against biodiversity,” Profepa wrote in a statement shared with Mexico News Daily.

Profepa and the government of Yucatán have since paused the project while they verify its compliance. During a press conference in early August, Gov. Joaquín Díaz Mena said that the “protection of Yucatán’s natural heritage will prevail over any particular project.”

Meanwhile, Salvemos las Dunas’ petition to protect the dunes has garnered more than 140,000 signatures. A protest was also held at the Monumento a La Patria in nearby Mérida in late July.

The public opposition to the project appears to be working.

“Given the concern of citizens, the State Government formally requested, since last July 25, Semarnat and the Federal Attorney General’s Office for Environmental Protection (Profepa) to verify the timely compliance with the project authorizations and delivered all the technical information it has,” Yucatán’s government wrote in a statement.

Designia Desarrollos, the development firm behind Las Dunas, declined to comment on the ongoing proceedings.

“This project is completely contrary to environmental protection laws, contravening the human rights that guarantee access to a healthy environment, especially for the residents of Chuburná Puerto,” Salvemos las Dunas said. “The lack of regulation and the ease with which permits are granted to real estate developers have hijacked the state.”

How important are the Chuburná Dunes?

The Chuburná Dunes are an integral part of the coastal ecosystem, recognized as one of the most well-preserved in Yucatán. Hosting various endangered wildlife species, including some that are endemic to Yucatán, as well as a nesting ground for a tortoise species on the brink of global extinction, the current ecosystem is both fragile and consequential.

Among the animals that call the dunes home are the Mexican sheartail hummingbird (doricha eliza) and the Yucateca wren (campylorhynchus yucatanicus), both of which have been granted a protective status, as well as the hawksbill sea turtle (eretmochelys imbricata) and the green sea turtle (chelonia mydas).

The dunes also serve as a natural protector against wind, tides, hurricanes, erosion and other storm systems that frequently batter the area, meaning any damage to them could prove irreversible.

“We believe that progress can be achieved consciously, hand in hand with environmental protection and citizen participation, but above all, by safeguarding the interests of the people, not just a few families in Mérida,” Salvemos las Dunas said.

A stalled Royal Caribbean project

The Las Dunas tourist complex is just the latest in a string of recent developments that didn’t sit well with local activists and conservationists.

Earlier this year, a Royal Caribbean megaproject in Quintana Roo came to a halt after citizens and activists expressed concerns.

The project, known as “Perfect Day,” is a proposed amusement park in the municipality of Othón P. Blanco, in the small fishing village of Mahahual. The famous cruise line had purchased the property, located close to the port of Costa Maya, which Royal Caribbean also owns, for $292 million.

An online petition against the development has garnered more than 5 million signatures to date.

Royal Caribbean officially withdrew its environmental assessment application in May, citing Semarnat’s intentions to deny the project. The company said it was “disappointed” in Semarnat’s decision and would “respect the role of Mexico’s environmental authorities,” but stopped short of saying “Perfect Day” would be scrapped entirely.

“We continue to believe in Mexico, and are optimistic in the potential to advance our investment responsibly,” the company wrote in a statement at the time. “Over the coming weeks, we will re-engage stakeholders to move forward in a way that delivers shared prosperity through the development of essential environmental infrastructure, the creation of thousands of local jobs, and community programs that support the people of Mexico.”

Tren Maya’s 900-mile development

The activism surrounding both Las Dunas and Perfect Day is set against the backdrop of the Tren Maya megaproject, which was completed in 2024 under then-President Andrés Manuel López Obrador.

So far, the 900-mile train route spread across five states in Mexico’s southeast has failed to realize its promised financial benefits for local communities, while also understating its overall environmental impact.

Tren Maya carried its first passengers in December 2023. Since then, 42 trains have been inaugurated, traveling more than 900 miles of track across Chiapas, Tabasco, Campeche, Yucatán and Quintana Roo.

According to an August 2023 report by CartoCrítica, Tren Maya’s construction spans more than 26,000 acres, requiring deforestation efforts in 61% of the surrounding jungle. The report alleges that 87% of the deforestation was done without the necessary permits.

This, despite López Obrador’s assertions in a 2018 interview that “Not a single tree” would be cut down. Semarnat similarly released a statement in January 2023, saying that “More than 64,000 plants have been rescued with 85% survival.”

However, Priscila Alaniz Uribe, the general director for the Sélvame nonprofit, has a different take.

“About 12 million trees have been cut down, and around 125 cenotes have been damaged,” Alaniz Uribe told Sierra Club in July. “There are 15,000 piles of concrete poisoning the water in underground rivers – water we humans, animals, and plants use to live here.”

Such concerns define the environmental activism that has taken place around the Yucatán Peninsula in recent years.

“This project is completely contrary to environmental protection laws, contravening the human rights that guarantee access to a healthy environment, especially for the residents of Chuburná Puerto,” Salvemos las Dunas said of the project they’re working to stop. “If this area is cleared, it will leave the residents who have cared for their city for years unprotected; not to mention that it is home to endemic species of the area that are in danger of extinction.”

Jesse Foley-Tapia is a writer and photographer living in the Yucatán Peninsula, where he has dedicated his time and energy to shedding light on issues affecting Indigenous communities. His biggest journalistic accomplishment is interviewing Kendrick Lamar in 2010. His work has appeared in The Sun Magazine and BreakThrough News.

World.title: A flavorful, vanilla-scented hideout awaits along Mexico’s Gulf Coast
World.content:
You may have seen it: a group of high-flying performers, dressed in a colorful array of traditional garments, climbing a 100-foot-tall pole in a group of four, before diving into the air, upside down, to spin as a human cyclone — held only by a rope tied to their feet — while a fifth member sits atop the pole, performing a ceremonial dance and song with a flute and small drum.

The UNESCO-recognized tradition can be traced back to Tajín, an archaeological site that once served as the capital of the Totonac Mesoamericans from A.D. 800. Today, it is one of Mexico’s most celebrated and active Indigenous rituals, known as the “Danza de los Voladores,” or “Dance of the Flyers.”

Interestingly, the Totonac did not invent the dance — that was likely the Nahua of Central Mexico — but they have preserved it, inextricably linking the practice to their history and culture in the process.

Ancient traditions in the modern world

These airborne avatars of the Totonac people are native to the northern region of Veracruz, where the modern Pueblo Mágico of Papantla can be found, roughly four hours northeast of Mexico City. They are famed throughout the country, with representatives performing their millennia-old routine in tourist centers such as Mexico City’s Bosque de Chapultepec and Xcaret Park in Playa del Carmen.

The voladores maintain their practices and Indigenous language through generations of flyers and community-supported programs, including the Escuela de Niños Voladores in Papantla. They are one of Veracruz’s greatest cultural exports and have inspired an inside joke among Mexicans, who sometimes shout “Papantla, tus hijos vuelan!” when something funny or unexpected happens in daily life.

And yet, as impressive and fun as the voladores are on a sweltering summer day, the region has also gifted Mexico, and the world, even more than its high-flying customs: Papantla is the global cradle and origin of vanilla.

I drove four hours north of Xalapa along the Gulf Coast to Papantla — admiring the decaying majesty of its tropical vastness and curving, mountainous shoreline — to visit the historical ruins and learn about its contemporary tastes.

‘The city that perfumed the world’

Papantla, a town of 55,452 inhabitants according to national census data, was once the global leader in vanilla exports. From 1870 to 1910, the modest pueblo in Veracruz state — located on steep, labyrinthine roads in the middle of a tropical forest — became the epicenter for vanilla, one of the most expensive spices in the global market. Much of it was exported to Europe and the United States, and the region was dubbed “the city that perfumed the world” for the sweet, refreshing scent that vanilla emits.

Sadly, naturally grown vanilla from Papantla — which a researcher at UNAM designated as one of Mexico’s greatest contributions to global cuisine, along with cacao, amaranth, chile peppers and tomatoes — is no longer what it used to be. Nowadays, artificial vanilla dominates, and the market value of small-batch vanilla bean production from Papantla is nowhere near what it once was — in many ways a metaphor for the greater significance of Veracruz as a state.

The rise and fall of the vanilla trade

Historical documents reveal that vanilla cultivation dates back to the Totonac peoples, who gathered the fruit of orchid plants in surrounding areas before any other known society. Writing in her journal article “The History and Ecology of Vanilla,” Dr. Mariana Hernández Apolinar, a biologist and faculty member in UNAM’s science department, notes that for more than 200 years, “Mexico was the world’s only supplier of vanilla, bringing the country considerable profit.”

That declined in the mid-19th century when Europeans intervened. According to Hernández Apolinar, “it was discovered that vanilla flowers could be fertilized manually. This made it possible to produce the fruit on plantations outside its natural area and led to intensive vanilla cultivation in different tropical regions, making its production intensely commercial.”

Fast-forward to today, and the vanilla economy has been at risk for more than a decade. As NPR reported in 2019, local farmers have found themselves the target of robberies and violence at the hands of organized criminal gangs. In addition, a group of Mexican professors and biologists have outlined how issues of deforestation, soil erosion, shifting weather patterns and the marginalization of rural communities have negatively impacted modern vanilla productivity in the region.

At the same time, efforts to restore vanilla’s potential within the Mexican agricultural sector have been underway, including Papantla’s growing tourism sector.

Exploring ‘The Vanilla Route’

Originally known as “xanat” or “xanath” in the local dialect, the region upholds a proud legacy of vanilla. Vanilla tours are widely available, allowing visitors to tour nearby plantations that grow the spice. Family-owned shops abound, selling everything under the sun with an added touch of vanilla: ground coffee mixed with vanilla extract, vanilla-flavored cigarillos, vanilla sodas, horchata with vanilla, bottled vanilla concentrate, vanilla-scented candles, vanilla perfumes, vanilla liqueurs and more. Each shop explains the benefits and uses of its products. For example, vanilla’s aroma is considered an effective aromatherapy treatment for stress, while eating it is believed to offer digestive and anti-aging properties.

For a deeper immersion, there are excursions like “The Vanilla Route,” which spans two days of history and includes guided visits to the Xanath ecological park, a 54-acre plot of land that is preserved for sustainable vanilla growing, as well as a visit to a family-owned vanilla farm, where guests can witness firsthand how vanilla is turned into artisanal products.

Savoring local gastronomy

I made it a point to find as much local gastronomy as I could during my visit. I stayed at a small hotel with classical architecture dating back to the 18th century, less than a block away from the town’s main plaza, which stays abuzz at all hours and where street vendors sell goods and regional treats, such as homemade vanilla ice cream and atole morado, an iced, purple corn beverage to stave off the jungle’s humidity.

For breakfast, a trek up the nearby hillsides led to Saberes Ancestrales de la Vainilla, a family-owned business with two locations, one of which offers a vanilla museum and sweeping vista of the town. “Saberes” is the Spanish word for “knowledge,” and embodies the spirit of the restaurant and museum, which was founded to preserve the culinary essence of vanilla in its multitudinous forms.

Here, I began my self-guided tour of Papantla with a café de olla, a traditional coffee brewed in a clay pot and doused with natural vanilla, giving it a rich, natural sweetness to balance the drink’s dark bitterness.

Indigenous flavors and regional dishes

To eat, we had bocoles, a Huastecan dish featuring girthy tortillas made from bean or chicharrón masa stuffed with a protein of choice, as well as espolvoreadas de pipián, a lard-rubbed heap of thick tortillas, served in a pancake-style stack, and topped with ground pumpkin seed powder. The dish is simple, but in its simplicity, the orchestra of corn, pumpkin and oily grease is a representation of Mexico’s indigenous flavors without any unnecessary pomp.

The meal was so good that my family and I returned to Saberes Ancestrales de la Vainilla’s original location near our hotel in the main zócalo, where I ordered a chicken breast simmered in a smoky vanilla-pepper sauce. It was tangy and piquant, reminiscent of an American Southern barbecue dish, but in a tropical context.

For dinner, we visited Nakú, a restaurant named in honor of the Totonac word for “heart.” Its outdoor eatery offers tours and artisanal products, while highlighting an indigenous diet specific to northern Veracruz.

Art, history and unforgettable flavors

There are hard-to-find dishes like zacahuil, served on Sundays only, and pulaklh, which are regional varieties of tamales with ingredients such as sesame seeds and acoyo, popularly known as hoja santa. Other unique offerings include tachula xa talhtsi, a bowl of buttery beans coated with crumbled pumpkin seeds; liwa xalak kakwin, rabbit in a spicy al chiltepín salsa; and pollo en salsa de vainilla y pulque, chicken bathed in a chilpaya, pulque and vanilla sauce, served with steamed vegetables and a stack of espolvoreadas de pipián.

Any visit to Papantla and nearby Tajín should include more than vanilla. One highlight that may surprise tourists is the murals and work of Teodoro Cano García, a Papanteco sculptor, painter and muralist who was mentored by Diego Rivera and who gifted the town a massive mural depicting the historical evolution of the Totonac people in the town square, to go along with a monument of the voladores de Papantla.

An overlooked attraction

In addition, the small but impressive Teodoro Cano Museum offers a rare contemporary art space in the pueblo, housing his paintings alongside Totonac artifacts, and is open to the public for free. Regardless of interests, Papantla is a historically significant, if not overlooked, part of Veracruz’s — and Mexico’s — rich past, and remains a culturally informative, intensely flavorful visit that will not break your bank.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: What I learned from our two summer interns: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Part of our team’s passion for journalism extends to making sure that we do our part to help inspire the next generation of journalists. This summer, the MND team had two students working with us in our San Miguel office — Jared and Zella. The two have completely different life experiences, different personalities and different passions, so it was fun to have them both on the team.

Jared grew up in the Chicago area and is about to start his senior year at the University of Washington in Seattle. He is a journalism major and is passionate about sports journalism. Although he had been to Europe several times with his family, he had never been to Mexico. Despite having taken five years of Spanish in school, his speaking skills were quite “rusty” (to put it mildly). Jared is very much a self-proclaimed introvert.

Zella was born in Manhattan and moved to San Miguel with her family when she was six months old. She then lived in SMA until she was 15 years old, though her freshman year in high school. For the final three years of high school, she is going to a boarding school in California (her parents still live in SMA). For her upcoming senior year, Zella will be the editor-in-chief of her high school paper. She is completely bilingual and very extroverted.

As many people on our team do not have children, it presented an interesting opportunity for us to work with two kids at different phases of their “journalism journey.” At some points this summer, our office in San Miguel had team members aged 17, 21, 27, 28 and 32 (my wife’s and my ages are confidential!). The following is a list of what I learned from our two interns this summer, offered less as a verdict on them and more as a snapshot of the moment their generation is navigating.

1. Artificial intelligence presents a real dilemma for them. On one hand, they see how easy it can make their life, yet on the other hand, they also realize that it can make them overly dependent on it and lazy. It’s like the ultimate superpower, but at the same time you know it carries real risks. We made it clear to them that at MND we would allow zero AI in their writing, but that it is perfectly fine to use for research purposes.

2. Neither one of them wanted to think too much about what AI could do to the journalism profession, the news industry or their career prospects in general. It was refreshing, albeit somewhat concerning, to see them so … naive? In denial? Innocent? … about what AI could mean for them in the future. They didn’t really want to talk about it, so I didn’t push it much.

3. It’s troubling to see how few actual books they read. TikTok or Instagram videos are the new version of reading. Which, of course, is concerning. This isn’t unique to Jared and Zella — it reflects a broader shift in how information is consumed across most of their peer group.

I asked Jared when he last read a non-fiction book, to which he replied, “I don’t think I ever have read one.” So I promptly gave him two books to read: The first was “The Last Emperor of Mexico” by Edward Shawcross, a great book about Maximilian and a fascinating part of Mexican history. He loved it. The second was “Comfort Crisis” by Michael Easter, which is about the mental and physical health benefits of embracing discomfort. I have written previously about how important I think embracing discomfort is, and how important it was to me as I studied abroad years ago. I also see the benefits in it from my wife’s journey to the U.S. from India, as well as from many other immigrants. I don’t think he appreciated the book yet — these things sometimes take time to land — but I find it very unfortunate that many in society seem to be somewhat giving up on expecting kids to read books, especially non-fiction. That is not a good trend.

4. It was fascinating to see how both interns’ faces literally lit up when they were writing. For both of them, writing is clearly a “happy place.” I loved seeing that. I truly believe that writing is a wonderful demonstration of comprehension, communication and logic. If someone is unable to put something in writing, they likely will not be able to communicate it well. And if someone relies too much on AI to do the writing, they likely haven’t comprehended much. Both interns loved writing, loved putting their thoughts into the written word. Seeing this made me equally happy and saddened. Happy to see the passion stirred up in them. Sad to think about how quickly our society is seemingly deprioritizing the importance of reading and writing — crucial tools to create a generation of young people who are well-informed and can intelligently communicate their thoughts and ideas. It left me wondering: Who will read the great writings of this new generation of journalists?

5. American parents and administrators: Relax!! I was shocked at the monitoring, tracking, guiding and checking in that Jared seemed to be subject to. Zella’s parents, having lived in Mexico for years, were much more chill. Just a generation ago, a study abroad experience was a true adventure — a chance to get uncomfortable and disconnect from family, friends and authority. Every family navigates this differently, and there are good reasons parents stay closely connected today that didn’t exist a generation ago. Still, it’s worth asking whether some of today’s students are being given less room than earlier generations had to grow through that kind of independence.

We look forward to welcoming interns again next summer, giving them a chance to learn from our team — and giving us a chance to learn from them.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: ‘Confidently Wrong’ podcast: What one man’s heart surgery story reveals about healthcare in Mexico
World.content:
“Confidently Wrong” is back with a new episode from Mexico News Daily, and this time we are doing a deep dive into the realities of receiving urgent healthcare in Mexico. In an earlier episode, we tackled one of the most asked — and most misunderstood — topics: healthcare in Mexico. We reviewed the Expat Healthcare Survey results, digging into the responses of over 700 foreigners actively using healthcare in the country.

You can see the results of the survey here: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/mnd-intelligence/mnd-mexico-healthcare-experience-survey-1/

And you can see the episode of the podcast here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=drRwz5bIuOE&list=PLejJ221QSkEk&index=4

After the usual questions about safety and life in Mexico, the conversation almost always turns to healthcare. Do you have a doctor? Is it affordable? Can you trust the system? In that episode, we broke down those questions using real data and real experiences.

The MND team surveyed foreigners living across Mexico to better understand what healthcare here is actually like. From routine dental cleanings to major procedures like heart surgery, respondents shared insights on cost, accessibility and quality of care. While no single survey can cover everything, the results offer a grounded, firsthand look at the system.

In this episode, we do a much deeper dive into the nitty-gritty of the healthcare system. We review the real-life example of George Reavis, my co-host, and his recent heart surgery in Mexico. We discuss the entire process including interactions with doctors, the procedure and health insurance. We also review what went well and what he thinks he should have done better.

I’m sure you will find, as I did, his story extremely insightful and helpful to better understand how to navigate the healthcare system in Mexico. It’s filled with unbiased, real-life anecdotes relevant to anyone wanting to learn more about the realities of receiving urgent healthcare in Mexico.

Check it out below.

World.title: Mexico nets 2 Gold Medals at World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam
World.content:
Mexico made history at the 2026 World Rowing Championships, winning two Gold Medals and a Bronze at the event in Amsterdam.

Aylín Ibarra and Melissa Márquez started things off Thursday with a victory in the women’s lightweight double sculls to become the first Mexican rowers to win a Gold Medal at a senior World Championships.

ESPN reported that the duo — which won gold last month at the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games — dominated from the outset and resisted attacks from Greece, the reigning under-23 world champion, to claim victory with a time of 7:10 minutes.

Mexico had never before won a Gold Medal at this event and its rowers had never won more than one medal at a single World Championships.

Kenia Lechuga helped turn that history around by winning the lightweight race, capturing the world title that had eluded her until now. Lechuga — Mexico’s most decorated rower — won silver in this event in 2023 and came home with a Bronze in 2025. She won gold in this event at the 2019 Pan American Games.

On Thursday, the 32-year-old Nuevo León native took the lead from the start aboard her signature pink boat and maintained control to the finish line. She completed the standard 2,000-meter course in 7:29 minutes

“We are competing fearlessly against the European monarchs,” Lechuga said afterward.

It is believed that this year’s World Championships was the last time Lechuga will compete in the lightweight category as she is expected to focus on the individual sculls leading up to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

Lechuga competed in the 2016 Rio Games (finishing 12th), the 2020 Tokyo Games (finishing 16th) and participated in the open weight category at the 2024 Paris Games.

Finally, Alexis López earned a bronze medal in the men’s lightweight individual sculls, completing the 2,000-meter race in 6:52 minutes, placing him third behind Greece’s Petros Gkaidatzis and Uruguay’s Felipe Kluver. Gkaidatzis, is the reigning European champion and Kluver was world champion in 2025.

López, a native of San Felipe, Baja California, won four medals at the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games — two gold (individual and mixed double) and two silver (men’s double and men’s quadruple).

With reports from ESPN, Aristegui Noticias, El Universal, La Jornada and Zeta

World.title: Bahia Rare Earths Project Has a Plan but No Funding Yet
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Brazil · MINING

Key Facts — Company Brazilian Rare Earths, listed in Australia, operating through Borborema Recursos Estratégicos.

— Sites Mining at Jiquiriçá and Ubaíra, chemical separation planned at Camaçari.

— Money About R$5 billion (US$961 million), none of it committed so far.

— Reserves Brazil holds 21 million tonnes, second to China, says the USGS.

— Exchange rate PTAX venda closed at 5.2005 reais per dollar on August 28.

The Bahia rare earths project has a number, a map and a slide deck, but no financing and no environmental licence.

Brazilian Rare Earths presented a five billion real plan to Bahia industry leaders on August 27, 2026. The Bahia rare earths project would dig ore inland and refine it near Salvador, if the money ever arrives.

Rare-earth ore. Brazil holds the world’s second-largest reserves but mines almost none. Photo: subarcticmike, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr.

What was actually presented in Salvador

Brazilian Rare Earths took its plan to the Federação das Indústrias do Estado da Bahia on August 27. That body, the Bahia state industry federation, is known by the short form Fieb.

The company put the cost at approximately R$5 billion (US$961 million). It named no financing source, no lender and no signed construction contract.

Company president Renato Gonzaga called it a project with mineralisation unique in the world. Fieb president Carlos Henrique Passos said the federation would help overcome obstacles.

That is the language of a pitch, not of a decision. Nothing presented in Salvador binds anyone to spend a single real.

Edvaldo Amaral, who heads the Bahia mining employers group Sindimiba, called the moment important for the state. He did not announce any commitment either.

The company and the ground it holds

Brazilian Rare Earths is listed on the Australian Securities Exchange and works in Brazil through Borborema Recursos Estratégicos. The Bahia rare earths project sits inside what the company calls the Rocha da Rocha province.

That province covers more than 200 mineral rights across roughly 300,000 hectares. The ground runs about 160 kilometres, from Jiquiriçá and Ubaíra towards Jequié.

The flagship deposit is Monte Alto, and it is hard rock rather than ionic clay. That distinction matters, because hard rock is costlier to crush and treat.

The company reports neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium and terbium in the ore. Uranium, tantalum, scandium and niobium appear as possible by-products.

Drilling results released on August 26 included 25.6 metres grading 17.4% total rare earth oxides. The company stressed those holes are not yet a declared resource update.

Two phases, and a start date that keeps sliding

Phase one would mine and concentrate ore in the Jiquiriçá valley. Phase two would build hydrometallurgy and separation units at the Camaçari petrochemical complex.

The company now expects concentrate output around 2031 and Camaçari operations around 2034. Senai Cimatec, a Bahia research institute, is helping design the pilot plants.

In July 2024 the same company signed a protocol of intentions with the Bahia government. That document put the bill at R$3.5 billion (US$673 million) and promised first output in 2028.

By April 2026 the figure had become R$3.6 billion (US$692 million), split into R$600 million (US$115 million) for phase one. Four months later the headline number is R$5 billion (US$961 million) and first output moved to 2031.

So the Bahia rare earths project has grown by about 43% in cost since 2024. Its first production date has slipped by three years over the same period.

The valuation the company itself withdrew

On August 13 the miner published a scoping study valuing the asset at US$7.9 billion. It cited an 89% internal rate of return and a payback of 1.1 years.

Six days later that valuation fell to US$6.0 billion. The company also withdrew and cancelled its Rocha da Rocha production target and every financial projection attached to it.

The stated reason was the share of inferred mineral resources scheduled for mine plan years nine to fourteen. That share left no reasonable basis for the forward looking statements.

The withdrawal happened eight days before the Fieb presentation. Investors reading the R$5 billion (US$961 million) figure should know that forecast no longer stands.

A scoping study is the earliest and least binding stage of mine planning. It carries wide error margins and no commitment of capital.

No money has been committed

What exists with the Bahia state government is a memorandum of understanding, preceded by a 2024 protocol of intentions. Neither instrument obliges the company to build anything.

The company has said it still needs to raise the roughly US$969 million the scoping study requires. It has also said there is no guarantee the sum can be raised on the intended terms.

A pre-feasibility study began in 2026 and is due to finish in 2027. Process definition, engineering and environmental licensing all sit ahead of any construction decision.

No job figure was given at the Fieb event. The 2024 protocol had promised 200 permanent posts in phase one and up to 1,250 construction jobs in phase two.

Rare earth announcements in Brazil have a long record of stopping at this stage. This plan has now been announced three times without a shovel moving.

Where Brazil really stands on rare earths

The United States Geological Survey, or USGS, puts Brazilian reserves at 21 million tonnes. That is second in the world, behind China’s 44 million tonnes.

Output tells a different story. Brazil mined about 2,000 tonnes in 2025, against a world total near 390,000 tonnes and 270,000 tonnes in China.

Serra Verde, at Minaçu in Goiás, is the only Brazilian mine whose main product is rare earths. Araxá and Angico dos Dias yield rare earths as an unseparated phosphate by-product.

Serra Verde is being bought by a United States company with backing from Washington. Its output, not any Bahia plan, is what lifted Brazil’s numbers.

Brazil still has no industrial solvent extraction plant separating rare earths. That gap, not the reserves, is what the Bahia rare earths project claims it would close.

The policy backdrop in Brasília

The critical minerals bill, PL 2780/2024, reached the Senate on May 7, 2026 and has waited since. On August 28 it was placed on the order of business for September 2.

Senator Eduardo Braga was named floor rapporteur that same day. An urgency request filed in July, numbered RQS 506/2026, is still awaiting a vote.

The bill’s own text offers tax credits of R$1 billion (US$192 million) a year from 2030 to 2034. That is R$5 billion (US$961 million) in total, the same figure as this one project’s cost.

The Rio Times has covered the bill’s slow passage and Vale’s description of critical minerals as the new oil. The Bahia rare earths project shows how far the talk still sits from a working mine.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has any money been committed to the Bahia rare earths project? No. There is a memorandum of understanding with the state government and a 2024 protocol of intentions. Neither carries financing or a construction contract. Why did the company cut its own valuation in August 2026? Too much of the mine plan for years nine to fourteen rested on inferred resources. The company withdrew its production target and all attached financial forecasts. Does Brazil already refine rare earths? Not at industrial scale. Serra Verde in Goiás produces concentrate, and no solvent extraction separation plant is operating anywhere in the country.

World.title: Jamaica Signs Three-Year Public Sector Wage Deal With Unions
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Jamaica · PUBLIC FINANCE

Key Facts — Signing The public sector wage agreement was signed in Kingston on 27 August 2026.

— Period The contract runs from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2028.

— Money A one-off grant of J$80,000 (US$502) precedes two five per cent increases.

— Wage bill Compensation of employees stands near 13.5 per cent of gross domestic product.

— Open items The Jamaica Police Federation is still negotiating separately with the finance ministry.

The 2025-2028 public sector wage agreement lands with the fiscal rules suspended and the debt target out of reach.

Jamaica has signed a three-year public sector wage agreement with its main trade union grouping, covering April 2025 to March 2028. The deal pairs a one-off grant with two five per cent increases, in a very hard fiscal year.

Orange Street in downtown Kingston. The public wage bill is running near 13.5 per cent of GDP. Photo: Ralf Steinberger, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

What was signed, and by whom

Minister of Finance and the Public Service Fayval Williams signed the deal at her ministry in Kingston on 27 August 2026. The Jamaica Information Service, the government’s news agency, reported the ceremony the following day.

Across the table sat St Patrice Ennis, president of the Jamaica Confederation of Trade Unions, known as the JCTU. He was joined by Techa Clarke-Griffiths of the Jamaica Civil Service Association.

Kavan Gayle, president-general of the Bustamante Industrial Trade Union, also signed. So did Senator Lambert Brown of the University and Allied Workers’ Union.

State Minister Zavia Mayne took an active part in the negotiations. The confederation had served its claim on the government back in November 2024.

The public sector wage agreement covers the contract period from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2028. That spans three financial years: 2025/26, 2026/27 and 2027/28.

How the package is phased

Year one carries no salary scale change. Instead it brings a one-time tax-free grant of J$80,000 (US$502) for each covered worker.

The 2026/27 financial year brings a five per cent salary increase. A further five per cent follows in 2027/28.

On top of that, most workers draw a normal annual increment of 2.5 per cent. Williams said that gives most of them about 7.5 per cent this year.

All Jamaican dollar sums here are converted at 159.2314 per United States dollar. That is the Bank of Jamaica weighted average selling rate for trade date 28 August 2026.

Williams stressed what the package does not contain. There is no wage freeze, no layoffs and no deferral of sums already owed.

Set against Jamaican inflation

The Statistical Institute of Jamaica put point-to-point inflation at 7.5 per cent in July 2026. That is above the Bank of Jamaica target band of four to six per cent.

So the combined 7.5 per cent for this year roughly matches the current rate. Williams described the outcome as “roughly holding your ground” against prices.

She argued that the picture improves if inflation eases over the life of the deal. On that path the public sector wage agreement would deliver a modest real gain.

She also conceded the increase does not fully offset the pressure workers face. Her words were that it is “a real increase, honestly funded in a very tough year”.

The 2022 restructuring behind the numbers

The current pay structure dates from a reform announced in the 2022/23 budget debate. Then finance minister Nigel Clarke put its cost above J$100 billion over three years.

At the 28 August 2026 rate that is roughly US$628 million. The old system it replaced held 325 separate salary scales and 185 allowances.

Implementation started on 1 April 2022 and ran in three annual steps. About J$79.4 billion (US$499 million) was provided in 2022/23 alone for the first year.

That exercise changed what counted as wages in the public accounts. It is the direct reason the old statutory wage cap was scrapped.

Several groups held out for months before signing under the restructured scheme. Clarke warned in March 2023 that unpaid balances would be spread over later years.

A wage bill without a legal ceiling

Until 2023, Jamaican law said the public sector wage bill must not exceed nine per cent of gross domestic product. Parliament removed that rule in April 2023 by amending the Financial Administration and Audit Act.

Nothing replaced it. Williams told the signing ceremony that three years on there is still “no number and no date”.

Compensation of employees now sits close to 13.5 per cent of gross domestic product. By the end of 2026/27 wages should absorb 54.4 per cent of tax collection, against 44.9 per cent four years earlier.

Williams invited the unions to help negotiate a new anchor before the next round. She noted the Independent Fiscal Commission has twice formally recommended restoring such a rule.

Two hurricanes and a suspended rule book

Williams framed the deal against damage from Hurricanes Beryl and Melissa. She cited an estimate of US$8.8 billion in physical damage, close to 57 per cent of gross domestic product.

That assessment came from the Planning Institute of Jamaica and the United Nations Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean. Tax revenue fell below projection last year.

In December 2025 the House approved an order suspending the fiscal rules for an initial year. The Independent Fiscal Commission had valued the hurricane hit at 5.3 per cent of gross domestic product.

The statutory debt target is 60 per cent of gross domestic product by 31 March 2028. Debt was 62.4 per cent in 2024/25 and is projected near 68.2 per cent for 2025/26.

That deadline was itself pushed back by two years in May 2020. Ministry projections now show the ratio still above 63 per cent in 2028/29.

What the unions said, and what is left

Ennis praised the minister for a calm and unhurried process, free of rancour. He said the two sides took the negotiation as far as they could.

He also called this the first of several settlements still to come with individual bargaining units. Williams confirmed that elements outside the wage component remain under discussion.

The Jamaica Police Federation, which represents rank-and-file officers, is bargaining on a separate track. A ministry statement in June 2026 said those talks had not concluded.

Neither the ministry nor the union confederation published a headcount or a costing for the public sector wage agreement. Both figures remain unconfirmed at the time of writing.

Economist Keenan Falconer told The Gleaner the raises could lift consumer spending in the short run. He warned that cuts to infrastructure spending could still hold back longer-term growth.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which financial years does the deal cover? It runs from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2028. That covers the 2025/26, 2026/27 and 2027/28 financial years. How much do public sector workers actually get? Year one brings a tax-free grant of J$80,000 (US$502). Five per cent increases follow in 2026/27 and again in 2027/28. Does the deal endanger Jamaica’s debt target? Williams said the debt anchor moves further out because of this public sector wage agreement. The fiscal rules are in any case suspended after Hurricane Melissa.

World.title: Chile Clears Cruz Verde for Digital Medicine Sales on Mercado Libre
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Chile · RETAIL

Key Facts — Date The alliance was announced on August 28, 2026, after the health institute’s authorisation.

— Scope Digital medicine sales cover non-prescription products only, at 13 of nearly 900 stores.

— Licence The pharmacies hold the sanitary permit, while Mercado Libre supplies only the technology platform.

— Catalogue Seven smaller pharmacies already list more than 550 non-prescription products on the platform.

— Objection The pharmacists’ association warns the model needs permanent and adequate sanitary inspection.

The permit covers over-the-counter products at 13 of nearly 900 stores, not a licence for online-only pharmacies.

Chile has taken its biggest step yet toward digital medicine sales, and it is a smaller step than it looks. The Instituto de Salud Pública authorised 13 Cruz Verde stores to sell non-prescription medicines on Mercado Libre.

A Cruz Verde store in Vitacura, Santiago. The pharmacy, not the platform, holds the sanitary licence. Photo: Carlos Figueroa Rojas, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

What the health institute actually authorised

The Instituto de Salud Pública (ISP), Chile’s medicines regulator, cleared Farmacias Cruz Verde to offer direct-sale medicines through Mercado Libre. Direct sale is the Chilean term for products that need no prescription.

The permit covers 13 stores out of a network the company puts at more than 890. Six sit in the Santiago region and seven in other cities.

The regional stores are Puerto Montt, Chillán, Talca, Temuco, Rancagua, Concepción and Viña del Mar. In Santiago they are Bulnes, Las Condes, Puente Alto, Maipú, San Miguel and Providencia.

Neither company published a resolution number when it announced the deal. That gap matters, because the scope of digital medicine sales in Chile turns on the wording.

Prices on the platform are quoted in Chilean pesos, not dollars. The Banco Central de Chile set its dólar observado at 925.25 pesos on August 28, 2026.

How the delivery model works

The 13 stores hold the offer and make the sale, and Mercado Libre connects buyers and sellers. The platform supplies the website, the payment system and the logistics.

Each store keeps operating under its own technical director, a licensed pharmacist required by Chilean law. Both companies say every sanitary rule stays in force.

Dispatch follows the coverage area each establishment is authorised to serve. Third-party carriers approved to move medicines handle the delivery itself.

That last point is the practical brake on digital medicine sales across the country. Transport rules, rather than the sales permit, decide how far a parcel can travel.

What MercadoLibre does. MercadoLibre, Inc. operates online commerce platforms in Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, and internationally. The company operates Mercado Libre Marketplace, an online commerce platform that can be accessed through mobile app or website; and Mercado Pago, a financial technology solution platform, which offers comprehensive set of financial technology services to users and other users…

Who holds the pharmacy licence

Mercado Libre is not a pharmacy in Chile and holds no sanitary permit of its own. The licence sits with each authorised Cruz Verde establishment.

Gonzalo Durán, general manager of FEMSA Salud Chile, said the deal widens access to health products. FEMSA Salud Chile is the parent company of Farmacias Cruz Verde.

Rafael Lira, interim marketplace head for Chile, Peru and Ecuador, described his company’s role narrowly. He said the task is to lend third parties the site, the payments and the logistics.

Seven smaller pharmacies joined the platform before Cruz Verde did, starting in 2025. They are Meddica, Farmex, RedFarma, Meki, Farmaloop, Zupharma and Eco.

The rules on selling medicines outside a pharmacy

Chilean law does not recognise a pharmacy that exists only online. A store must be physically installed, authorised and run by a pharmacist technical director.

Jorge Canales heads the ISP’s Agencia Nacional de Medicamentos, the national medicines agency known as Anamed. He said electronic dispensing is an accessory channel to that authorisation, not a substitute regime.

Canales pointed to Title VI Bis of Supreme Decree 466, the regulation covering pharmacies. Its first requirement is prior authorisation of the physical establishment.

Anamed says any mass internet project must rest on one or more licensed physical pharmacies. It must also meet rules on prescriptions, stock lists, dispatch, returns, advertising and data protection.

Ley de Fármacos II is still unfinished

Congress approved the first Ley de Fármacos, Chile’s drugs law, in January 2014. It pushed bioequivalent generics, prescribing by active ingredient and unit-dose sales.

A second version, called Ley de Fármacos II, has sat in Congress for more than a decade. Filed as Boletín 9914-11, it has never been enacted, yet it still frames the price debate.

Health Minister May Chomali told senators in April 2026 she wanted to rescue parts of that bill. Asked about a Ley de Fármacos III, she said the matter was under study.

The ministry’s stated priority is a different bill, Boletín 15850-11, on illegal medicine sales. It remains in its first committee stage.

A market still shaped by a collusion case

Three chains have long dominated Chilean retail pharmacy: Cruz Verde, Salcobrand and Farmacias Ahumada. Reporting in 2009 put their combined share at about 90 percent of the market.

In January 2012 the competition tribunal fined Cruz Verde and Salcobrand 20,000 annual tax units each. Chilean coverage valued each penalty at roughly US$19 million at the time.

The Supreme Court confirmed the fines in September 2012. Farmacias Ahumada had admitted the conduct and handed documents to the antitrust prosecutor.

The scheme ran from November 2007 to April 2008, with the chains raising prices in sequence. That case still colours how Chile reads any pharmacy alliance.

Farmacias populares and the price benchmark

Recoleta opened Chile’s first municipal pharmacy, the Farmacia Popular Ricardo Silva Soto, in October 2015. Mayor Daniel Jadue ran it as a social programme rather than a shop.

It bought straight from Cenabast, the state medicines purchasing agency, skipping the usual distribution markups. Reported prices ran about 70 percent below the big chains.

More than 30 municipalities were studying the model within weeks of the opening. Fifty-two communes had no pharmacy at all at that time.

The association behind the network later collapsed financially, and Jadue was charged in a case over it. The model nonetheless set the benchmark against which digital medicine sales are now judged.

What the pharmacists and the independents say

Héctor Torres, president of the Colegio de Químicos Farmacéuticos, called the alliance potentially very dangerous. He tied that judgement to the absence of adequate and permanent sanitary inspection.

Torres argued that medicines are not ordinary products and that their distribution is a health act. He said it must follow every procedure that guarantees quality, efficacy and safety.

María Adriana Calvo leads the Asociación de Farmacias Independientes de Chile, the independent pharmacies’ body. She said new models favour large players while independents face rising costs and restrictions.

Calvo said she does not question innovation, but she does question unequal conditions. Firms with dominant positions and advantages others lack raise competition concerns, she argued.

Critics also say Mercado Libre’s real goal is a pharmacy that is purely digital. Public lobby filings record 15 meetings with sector authorities since 2025, eight with the ISP.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can Chileans now buy prescription drugs on Mercado Libre? No. The authorisation covers direct-sale products only, so digital medicine sales in Chile still exclude prescription medicines. Who is legally responsible for the medicines sold? Each authorised Cruz Verde store holds the sanitary permit and makes the sale. Mercado Libre supplies the platform, the payments and the logistics for digital medicine sales. Does this let Mercado Libre open its own online pharmacy in Chile? Not under current rules. Anamed says an online-only pharmacy is not recognised, so digital medicine sales must run through a licensed physical store.

World.title: Uruguay Green Hydrogen Project Advances as UTE Price Gap Narrows
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Uruguay · ENERGY

Key Facts — Date Orsi said the green hydrogen plant numbers had moved closer on August 28, 2026.

— Price HIF Global has asked for US$40 per megawatt-hour since 2023, unchanged.

— Size The green hydrogen plant would run a 1.1 gigawatt electrolyser in Paysandú.

— Investment The December 2025 memorandum values the project at US$5.385 billion.

— Status No contract exists, and the final investment decision is expected next year.

The state utility and HIF Global are closer on the power tariff for the green hydrogen plant, yet no contract and no investment decision exist.

Uruguay’s president said the price gap holding up a green hydrogen plant in Paysandú has narrowed. Yamandú Orsi spoke in Guichón on August 28, and urged caution about what comes next.

Wind power in northern Uruguay. The electricity price is the last open item between HIF Global and UTE. Photo: Mx. Granger, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

What Orsi said in Guichón

President Yamandú Orsi was asked on August 28 about the state of the talks. He answered that the project keeps moving, and that the numbers had come closer.

The remark referred to the power tariff under negotiation with UTE, the state electricity company. Its full name is Administración Nacional de Usinas y Trasmisiones Eléctricas, and it buys and sells almost all Uruguayan power.

Orsi spoke after inaugurating the first stage of a rehabilitation of Ruta 4 near Guichón. He asked to be very prudent about the tariff, and gave no figure.

He linked the timing to the international hydrogen market, which he said would shape the final schedule. He also said moving the plant to a new site means fresh environmental impact studies.

The number that decides the project

HIF Global has asked for electricity at US$40 per megawatt-hour, and says it has not moved since 2023. Martín Bremermann, chief executive of HIF Uruguay, repeated that figure to reporters in March 2026.

Large industrial users in Uruguay pay between US$60 and US$80 per megawatt-hour, the Paysandú daily El Telégrafo reported. The distance between those numbers is what the green hydrogen plant talks are about.

In July the same paper reported a landing zone near US$45 per megawatt-hour, citing the agency Uypress. Neither UTE nor the executive has published a tariff formula, so that figure remains unconfirmed.

Alejandro Sánchez, secretary of the presidency, said on July 10 that UTE and the company had agreed a formula. HIF Uruguay declined to comment, and Industry Minister Fernanda Cardona said days later that no contract existed.

Why the power bill dominates the maths

Electricity accounts for about 70% of the plant’s operating cost, Bremermann told reporters. Roughly 70% of that power would come from the company’s own solar and wind parks.

The remaining share would come from the grid, to fill the gaps when wind and sun fade. That firming role is precisely what UTE has to put a price on.

The company plans a wind farm called Elena rated at 1,137.6 megawatts and a solar park called Lucía at 1,162 megawatts-peak. Both are dedicated to the green hydrogen plant rather than to the national grid.

Bremermann said rivals quote lower power prices, naming Paraguay at US$25 and Chile at US$32 per megawatt-hour. He put Brazil at US$36, and said Uruguay had not reached US$40.

What the complex would build and make

The December 2025 memorandum values the investment at US$5.385 billion, the largest ever announced in Uruguay. Industrial plants account for US$2.881 billion of that total.

Renewable parks take US$1.277 billion, and infrastructure, effluent treatment, water supply and power transmission take US$1.226 billion. The complex is designed in four modules rather than one build.

HIF Global’s own project page lists a 1.1 gigawatt electrolyser and about 876,000 tonnes of e-methanol a year. Part of that methanol would then be converted into synthetic gasoline and liquefied gas.

Carbon dioxide would come from bioethanol production at ALUR, the state ethanol arm Alcoholes del Uruguay. The company says 150,000 tonnes a year are secured, with other biogenic sources to follow.

Water for electrolysis and cooling would come from the Río Uruguay, which forms the western border. A researcher at the Laboratorio Tecnológico del Uruguay put the intake near one thousandth of the river’s low flow.

The move that reset the environmental file

HIF Global filed its prior environmental authorisation application on March 13, 2026, for a site at Constancia. That location sits about 15 kilometres from Paysandú city, close to the river.

Since then the government and the company have discussed moving the works closer to town. Reports place the new site beside the Portland cement plant of ANCAP in Nuevo Paysandú.

ANCAP is the state fuels company, formally Administración Nacional de Combustibles, Alcohol y Portland. Its land sits near ALUR, which would shorten the carbon dioxide link and remove three planned pipelines.

Orsi confirmed on August 28 that the move requires new environmental impact studies. The area and legal terms of the new site have not been officially published.

Argentina drops its court challenge

Three legislators from Entre Ríos had gone to court in Argentina over the project. They are Guillermo Michel, Marianela Marclay and Adán Bahl, and their action has now been withdrawn.

Orsi called it a criminal complaint, but it was filed in March as a civil damage prevention claim. It questioned the procedure followed under the Estatuto del Río Uruguay, the shared river treaty.

The case had advanced a week earlier with a judicial inspection on the shoreline at Colón. Its withdrawal removes one cross-border obstacle in front of the green hydrogen plant.

Colón lies across the water from the original Constancia site, and its tourism sector objected loudly. Uruguay’s electoral court separately rejected a departmental plebiscite against the project in July.

What is still missing

There is no signed investment contract, and no final investment decision has been taken. Cardona said in July that the company would decide next year.

The Rio Times reported on August 10 that a decision was expected in late 2027 or 2028. Bremermann had earlier aimed to close the financing by the end of 2026.

Rail access charges, freight to the port of Montevideo and who pays for the grid connection all remain open. First exports have been projected for 2029, mainly to Germany.

HIF Global says the first module’s output is fully sold, and construction would average 1,400 workers. Operations would employ about 300 people directly, plus roughly 100 at the renewable parks.

The domestic argument about the tariff

The staff association at UTE rejects the negotiation as opaque and says it would decapitalise the public company. It puts the proposed price at about half the market value.

The union warns of knock-on effects on household tariffs, network investment and social programmes. The government has published no figures that would settle the argument either way.

Opposition leader Álvaro Delgado warned in August that Uruguay risked losing the investment altogether. Frente Amplio chair Fernando Pereira replied by asking whether the country should give the energy away.

Orsi framed the wider problem as the absence of a stable energy framework for large projects. He said Uruguay bargains case by case with pulp mills, data centres and now the green hydrogen plant.

Frequently Asked Questions

What exactly are UTE and HIF Global negotiating? The price of the electricity UTE would supply to the green hydrogen plant, and who funds the grid connection. No tariff formula has been published. Has Uruguay approved the project? No approval exists yet. A prior environmental authorisation application was filed in March 2026, and the proposed relocation now requires new studies. When would the plant start exporting? First exports have been projected for 2029, mainly to Germany. That date depends on a final investment decision that has not been taken.

World.title: Ecuador Colombia Border: Quito Prepares Joint Military Operations With Bogotá and the US
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

ECUADOR · SECURITY

Key Facts —What happened: Ecuador is preparing joint military operations with Colombia and the United States along the Ecuador Colombia border. —How it would work: Field teams on the Ecuador Colombia border would get autonomy to act on “targets of opportunity” spotted by patrols, flyovers or drones. —The command plan: Quito and Bogotá discussed unified command posts for surveillance operations in the shared strip. —Why now: A new Colombian president and a shared US-backed security initiative created what Ecuador calls a “golden opportunity”. —The catch: The plan is still in preparation, with no start date, troop numbers or rules of engagement made public. —What comes next: Talks with the US Southern Command will decide Washington’s exact role in the joint strategy.

Ecuador, Colombia and the United States are preparing joint military operations along the Ecuador Colombia border, with field teams that would have the autonomy to strike targets of opportunity, Defence Minister Gian Carlo Loffredo said on 27 August.
