World.title: Breaking: 'There's only one Tony Mundine': Legendary boxer dies aged 75
World.content:
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the name of a person who has died.

Australian boxer Tony Mundine has died aged 75.

One of the country's most accomplished Indigenous fighters, Mundine was the only Australian boxer to compete professionally in four weight divisions.

He held the Australian titles at middleweight, light-heavyweight, cruiserweight and heavyweight.

His death was confirmed by his son, boxer Anthony Mundine.

"I don't know what to say, I'm broken," Anthony Mundine wrote on his Instagram.

"Dad I love you man, may Allah bless your soul," he wrote.

"I'm on my way home to say goodbye one last time till we meet again.

"Thanks for doing all you did for me and supporting me in every moment, showing love and strength, gonna miss you Tonza, there's only one Tony Mundine."

Tony Mundine was born in Baryulgil , New South Wales, where he took part in a number of tent boxing shows as a teenager.

His career peaked with a world title challenge in October 1974 against Argentina's Carlos Monzon.

Despite losing via a seventh-round knockout, Mundine said he had fulfilled a childhood dream.

"I was just a little chocolate boy from Baryulgil, and here I was travelling the world, you know," he said.

World.title: Iceland rejects EU-accession talks in close-fought referendum
World.content:
Iceland has voted to stay out of the European Union, referendum results show, as Icelanders reject a government push to reopen membership talks and side with those who said Iceland's fishing waters were too important to risk.

The Arctic island of 400,000 people has debated whether to join the EU for well over a decade and had initially been narrowly expected to back holding membership talks, but opinion polls this month showed views had changed.

Iceland referendum on EU Iceland is a nation divided as its people decide whether it should restart negotiations on joining the European Union.

In Saturday's referendum, 52.8 per cent of ballots cast were against the government's proposal to hold negotiations with Brussels, 47.2 per cent were in favour, and 82.5 per cent of eligible voters took part, public broadcaster RUV and other Icelandic media reported.

The vote count through the night had the nation on edge as the “Yes” vote took an early lead before eventually swinging in favour of the opposition.

By dawn, a margin of only a few hundred votes separated the two camps before the gap grew as more ballots were tallied in areas of the country where opposition was greater.

Supporters of the Yes campaign celebrate after Reykjavik results put their side into a narrow lead early into the election-night. (AP Photo: Marco Di Marco)

The government framed membership as a shield against trade wars and Arctic rivalry and presented the referendum as a "now or never" moment. Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir said a "no" would end the debate for as long as her centre-left coalition was in power.

The government is set to hold a press conference at 1pm local time on Sunday.

Decades of membership debate

In Brussels, some officials had voiced hopes a vote to join from Iceland could ease scepticism toward EU enlargement and strategically strengthen the bloc when Arctic security is in focus.

Europe weighs how to deal with Trump's Greenland threats America's rattled European allies are debating how to stand up to Donald Trump after he escalated his threats to take over Greenland and pledged to punish its supporters with tariffs.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly said he wants to do a deal to acquire another Arctic island, Greenland.

More broadly, geopolitical turmoil, including war in the Middle East, has stoked inflation and increased the vulnerability of smaller economies.

Iceland first applied to join the EU in 2009 when a financial crisis hit the country's small, exposed economy.

A Eurosceptic government ended talks in 2013.

Interest rates and cost of living

Debates inside Iceland have focused on interest rates, fishing rights and the cost of living rather than on security.

Iceland has grappled with high inflation and interest rates that have made mortgages expensive.

Supporters of a "yes" vote have said EU membership, and possibly adopting the euro, could bring relief.

Iceland's central bank interest rate is 8 per cent, compared with 2.25 per cent at the European Central Bank.

"It would not solve Iceland's structural faults, but it could become a catalyst to a more healthy economy," said chief economist Vilhjalmur Hilmarsson at Viska, one of Iceland's largest labour unions.

Opposition leader Gudrun Hafsteinsdottir, who led the "no" campaign, said the economic case is overstated.

Leaders of the No campaign react as early results from rural Iceland put the No side ahead. (AP Photo: Marco Di Marco)

"These are not problems that Brussels will solve for us. These are problems that Icelandic politicians must solve," she said.

Voter Ragnhildur Skarphedinsdottir, 70, said Iceland was managing well on its own and that she was voting "no".

"By staying independent as we are, we look brightly to the future," she said before casting her ballot in Reykjavik.

Under EU rules, fishing quotas are based on historical fishing patterns, among other factors.

Some Icelandic officials have said Iceland would therefore retain control of its waters, since no EU country has fished there for decades.

Ms Hafsteinsdottir disputes that.

"I know that the European Union will come up with some promises of some flexibility, especially in the beginning, but we know that it will not be for good," she said.

Reuters/AP

World.title: One Nation could revive NSW trade posts scrapped in 'jobs for the boys' saga
World.content:
One Nation NSW leader Mike Newman has said he would consider bringing back overseas trade commissioners if elected next year.

Mr Newman, 54, the party's candidate for Cessnock, was the state's senior trade and investment commissioner in Tokyo from 2022 to 2024.

The Minns government scrapped the roles when it came to power following a "jobs for the boys" scandal involving former deputy premier John Barilaro's appointment to the New York position.

Mr Newman (left) was NSW's senior trade and investment commissioner in Tokyo from 2022 to 2024. (ABC News)

The veteran investment banker, a critic of the state's "bloated" bureaucracy, told the ABC it was a mistake to get rid of the trade posts.

"I commend the Minns government, to be honest, for living up to an election promise. I'll give them that," Mr Newman said.

"But I think what they did was capture what was a scandal and turn it into perhaps a poorer decision.

"If I'd still been the senior trade and investment commissioner during Minns's term to date, he would have been harangued by me constantly to have gone into Japan, Korea, India.

"You can't be the hermit kingdom."

'Too many public servants'

During his announcement as leader on Friday, Mr Newman pledged cuts to the state's public service, which he said was the largest in the southern hemisphere.

"There is so much money and waste that is inside the public service," he said on Friday.

"Having worked inside, I saw firsthand how your money is being misallocated and misspent."

'Like Florida and Texas': One Nation's plans for NSW Former NSW investment commissioner Mike Newman will lead the party to the 2027 state election.

But in an interview with the ABC on Saturday, Mr Newman said the trade commissioners were valuable, and he would seek to reinstate the roles.

"If One Nation has the opportunity to lead, I would definitely look at doing something similar to that, but as I said I want to bring experienced people from the private sector," Mr Newman said.

The trade commissioners were paid a salary of about $487,000 plus allowances, according to a parliamentary committee report in 2023.

The committee reported that the six posts cost taxpayers $12.7 million in 2021-22.

Asked whether bringing back the jobs would increase the size of the bureaucracy, Mr Newman said he wanted to hire people that want to serve their state.

"When I talk about the bloated bureaucracy, I'm saying there are too many public servants, especially amongst those in the senior executive class, who basically see this as a self-serving situation.

" Put it this way, I could have done five times as much business [as trade commissioner] on one-fifth the number of staff. "

Mr Newman says he has seen firsthand how "money is being misallocated and misspent" in the public sector. (ABC News: Bridget Murphy)

Tomorrow, Premier Chris Minns begins a four-day visit to India to "attract investment", his first overseas trip as the state's leader, and one Mr Newman said he should have made much earlier.

On Saturday, Mr Minns said he was "pretty impressed" by Mr Newman's candour.

"He seems like he's going to say what's at the top of his head. I think it's going to be very difficult for Pauline [Hanson] to muzzle him," Mr Minns said.

"I think he's going to say whatever he wants to say. I think that's a good part of politics, I welcome him to the debate."

World.title: Rider dies after 'critical incident' during motorcycle racing event
World.content:
A rider has died after a "critical incident" at a motorcycling racing event south-east of Adelaide.

SA Police said emergency services were called to a private racetrack at a motorsport event at Elwomple following reports of a crash just before 11AM on Sunday.

"Sadly one person has died and a report will be prepared for the coroner," a police spokesperson said.

In a statement, Motorcycling South Australia and The Bend said a "critical incident occurred" during a motorcycle racing event.

The Bend is a motorsport park about 100 kilometres south-east of Adelaide.

"The rider was treated by paramedics and died at the scene," the statement said.

The statement also thanked officials, paramedics and first responders.

"We extend our deepest condolences to the rider's family, friends and the wider motorsport community.

"We ask that the privacy of the rider's family, friends and all those affected be respected at this difficult time."

Motorcycling Australia said it was working with the "relevant authorities" following the incident.

World.title: 'I was a wreck': Popyrin bares his soul before US Open bid
World.content:
Alexei Popyrin hit rock bottom when he feared he wouldn't enjoy even his own wedding next month.

From the giddy high of taking down Novak Djokovic at the 2024 US Open, Popyrin needed a wildcard into this year's New York grand slam after slumping to as low as number 139 in the rankings last month.

He knew then he needed professional help.

The fallen Australian tennis star turned to Oscar Piastri's esteemed mindset coach and credits Emma Murray for helping him find contentment again. To a point.

"It's not easy," Popyrin said in a raw interview ahead of his first-round Open date with former semi-finalist turned 2026 qualifier Grigor Dimitrov.

"A lot of that is what was eating at me, thinking about things, searching for that feeling of being at the career-high rankings, of playing at that level, and it becomes a kind of an unhealthy obsession.

"It becomes a really negative and bad balance between you and tennis and it's what was really not helping me and it was the main culprit in what has been happening over the last few months.

Emma Murray is now working with Alexei Popyrin as he tries to rise in the rankings. (Getty Images: Kym Illman)

"I needed to change that and I needed to change just the whole way I look at tennis as a whole, and it's still a work in progress and it's not going to be a quick fix over one or two weeks."

Popyrin took his first mental-health break after Wimbledon last year before needing another reset following a straight-sets first-round loss at the All England Club six weeks ago to Jiri Lehecka.

"After Wimbledon, I was a wreck," said the former French Open junior champion.

"I used to — well, I still do — every time I lose, I think I don't deserve to have fun. After, I think I don't deserve to be happy.

Popyrin's birthday win Alexei Popyrin has won for the 12th time in 13 matches at the Canadian Masters, giving himself a 27th birthday present by reached the last 32 for the third year in a row.

"I was worried that I wouldn't enjoy my wedding because of my tennis, and when I had that thought for the first time I was like, 'OK, something is really, really wrong and I've really got to take some time and figure things out.'"

The 27-year-old one-time world number 19 has been working with Murray for only a short time, but already the high-performance emotional regulator is making progress.

"I'm trying to not associate my results with how I feel as a person," Popyrin said.

"I'm trying to look at it in a way that it's just a journey that I'm on. Where I am is where I am and what I have to do is just continue trusting the process that I'm on.

"I've stuck with the same team and I haven't changed anything. I believe in the guys. I believe in myself. I believe that everything is just mental for me.

"And if I'm able to make those changes up in my head, then I'm able to not only get to where I am, but I believe I can go further.

"I've got to kind of start from scratch, which is never easy. It's something I have done before, but it's even harder for me to do that because of where I have been and what I have done and what I have achieved.

"But it's important for me if I want to continue playing tennis that I get through this, and the way I get through this is continuing on the trajectory that I have been the last month."

AAP

World.title: Dees deliver Lions' greatest AFLW defeat, Port star's cruel injury blow
World.content:
Melbourne has steamed past an injury-ravaged Brisbane by 56 points to claim a perfect 3-0 start to the AFLW season.

Elsewhere, Port Adelaide lost star forward Indy Tahau to a suspected serious knee injury, overshadowing a thrilling four-point win over GWS in Canberra, while Richmond, Carlton, Hawthorn and Geelong all claimed victories on a busy day across the league.

Carlton's subtle transition from AFLW darling to contender After a breakout AFLW season last year, Carlton is using some subtle tweaks to take the difficult next step of challenging for the premiership.

Brisbane grabbed the first goal but the Demons were unstoppable from there, kicking the next 12 and going on to hand the Lions their heaviest AFLW defeat, a 14.5 (89) to 4.9 (33) shellacking at Casey Fields.

Liv Purcell (31 disposals) continued her magnificent form along with Tyla Hanks (24 disposals, eight tackles and a goal), while Kate Hore (24) was prolific, and Tahlia Gillard (11 intercepts) led an impressive defence.

Ryleigh Wotherspoon (three goals, eight tackles), Georgia Gall (two), Mia Austin (two) and Megan Fitzsimon (two) hit the scoreboard.

Lions Marlow Graham (concussion) and Neesa Dooley (collarbone) were both hurt in the first quarter.

Then Belle Dawes (right shoulder) and Ruby Svarc (concussion) were worse for wear after colliding with each other.

Dawes played through pain and finished with 24 disposals and a goal, while Orla O'Dwyer (21) was strong.

Sophie Conway (left knee) and Eleanor Hartill (foot) also played through issues.

Tahau, who previously tore her left ACL, was helped off with a right knee injury late in the third quarter of Port Adelaide's 7.10 (52) to 8.0 (48) victory at Manuka Oval.

It was a tight contest all day and Port led by nine at three-quarter time before Brodee Mowbray goaled twice to put GWS in front.

GWS led until the death, when Port's Matilda Scholz took a terrific intercept mark to create a late attack that ended with Lauren Young marking and kicking the winner with seconds left.

Scholz (30 hit-outs, 24 disposals) was dominant, while Piper Window kicked three goals.

Alyce Parker (21 disposals) was busy for GWS (1-2), who shared the goals around.

Aine McDonagh (left) kicked another three goals in a strong start to the Irishwoman's season, in Hawthorn's win over the Pies. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

At Victoria Park, Hawthorn won their second game of the season, with a 28-point victory over Collingwood.

It was a close game in the opening quarter, with the Hawks leading by eight points at the first change.

They then went on with it, however, kicking 6.3 to 2.7 in the final three terms.

A four-goal-to-one third quarter made the difference, with Jasmine Fleming kicking one of the goals of the day with a brilliant right-foot finish from deep in the pocket.

Aine McDonagh, who last week surpassed Cora Staunton as the most prolific AFLW goal-kicker from Ireland with three goals against Port Adelaide, repeated the dose with another three majors against the Pies to take her career haul to 59.

Ruck Lucy Wales had another big game for Hawthorn, with 23 disposals, 22 hit-outs, nine marks, five tackles and four score involvements.

For the Pies, there were no multiple goal-kickers, with majors to Ruby Schleicher, Ash Centra and Dominique Carbone.

A five-goal final quarter from the Suns was not enough, as Gold Coast fell seven points short against Geelong at Carrara.

The Suns led by two points at quarter time, and four at the long break before a three-goal-to-one third term gave Geelong the break.

Gold Coast came home with 5.1, but the Cats kicked 4.1 to hold on to win 10.4 (64) to 8.9 (57).

Charlie Rowbottom had 39 disposals in a losing cause, while Havana Harris kicked three for the Suns - including the final goal of the game on the siren.

Ava Usher and Alannah Welsh both booted two for the home side.

Geelong's Georgie Prespakis had 33 disposals and eight clearances, while Chloe Scheer kicked three and Ava Murray two for the visitors, who lost Emma Kilpatrick with a dislocated shoulder and Piper Dunlop with a knee injury.

At Cockburn ARC Oval in Perth, it was a tale of the breeze and who dealt with it better, as Carlton beat Fremantle by six points to remain undefeated.

The Blues had the advantage of the wind in the first quarter, kicking 3.2 to no score.

Then, in the second term, Fremantle turned it right around, booting 4.3 to no score kicking to the Remembrance Avenue end.

The home side had an injury blow in the first half as Irish player Aisling McCarthy went off with a knee injury. She spent a long time on the sidelines being assessed before coming back on the field in the third quarter.

The third term was tighter, with Fremantle keeping the Blues to just 2.2 while unable to score themselves, leaving the visitors with a seven-point lead.

Erone Fitzpatrick and Sophie McKay combined down the left for Carlton in the final term with Fitzpatrick's kick from 50 trickling through for the first point of the day at the open end.

Hayley Miller drilled a great set shot from the right forward pocket for Fremantle, but Mimi Hill's checkside kick on the run with seven minutes on the clock gave Carlton the edge and Fitzpatrick was on the end of a counter move to seal the win near the end.

Gabby O'Sullivan managed a late goal for the Dockers, and then the Wharfie Time bells sounded at the oval, but the Blues hung on, 7.6 (48) to 6.6 (42).

Carlton's win means there are still four unbeaten teams remaining in the AFLW: North Melbourne, Melbourne, the Blues and Sydney.

The Tigers left it late to claim victory in the final game of the day. (Getty Images: Celina Whan)

In the final fixture of Indigenous Round, the Dreamtime game in Darwin, Richmond left it late to compete an enthralling five-point win over Essendon.

Caitlin Greiser kicked the game's decisive goal in the dying embers of the final quarter, securing a 5.8 (38) to 4.9 (33) for the Tigers and condemning the Bombers to a third consecutive loss to start the season.

That came after Essendon had surged to a 14-point lead at half-time.

Midfielder Monique Conti was amongst the best for the Tigers, finishing with 29 disposals and a goal, while Greiser booted three majors in Richmond's first AFLW win in the Top End.

AAP/ABC

World.title: 'Hit by a bus': What 'biohacker' Bryan Johnson thinks will kill him
World.content:
Bryan Johnson just marked another birthday, a potential inconvenience for the man who says he wants to live forever.

Last week, the controversial Silicon Valley mogul turned 49.

But according to his Australian girlfriend, Kate Tolo, that number does not fit with Johnson's physical and mental state.

Loading...

"He annoyingly feels younger than me!" the 30-year-old tells triple j hack.

" I get off the couch and my knees hurt but he is springing up and trying to dunk [a basketball] at the moment. "

Mackay-born Tolo, who has recently joined her boyfriend on his biohacking mission, seeking to become "the world's most measured woman", says she is excited by what is to come.

"In the back of both our minds, female health was always next, and it's such an important and deeply personal issue to me.

"I feel so fortunate."

"Biohacking" refers to the practices of those committed to extreme anti-aging and longevity regimes.

Bryan Johnson recently visited Australia to meet Kate Tolo's family. (X: Bryan Johnson)

American millionaire Bryan Johnson is the movement's poster boy.

Some of his most notable headline-grabbing endeavours include the multi-generational blood plasma swap he engaged in with his teenage son and father, sharing night-time erection tracking data, and more recently claiming that he had cloned himself.

"We are ridiculous people. We are absurd," he tells hack.

"I am a very weird person, and that's OK.

"We love the haters."

Rage baiting vs communication

Johnson's announcement last month that he had cloned himself as a newborn to become his own "blood boy", as well as to "test therapies" and "grow organs for transplantation" was immediately challenged by the internet, scientists and the medical establishment.

"Human cloning is not possible," read the community note underneath Johnson's post on the social media platform X.

What Johnson had actually done was create induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), a method to reprogram adult cells back into a versatile stem cell state — a technology scientists admit is exciting, but does not equate to human cloning.

"I actually listed out in great detail exactly what steps we followed," Johnson tells hack.

Asked whether he "rage baits" — intentionally posting provocative material to boost engagement — Johnson pauses for a second.

"Kate and I have moved the conversation of eight billion humans on planet Earth to discuss the idea of Don't Die," he says.

"So we have a way of communicating things to people that they understand … gets them talking.

"Sometimes we're like, 'are we just over the edge?'

"We're always trying to find that sweet spot because trust and credibility is the number one thing we care about."

'We are artists'

"Don't Die" is the name of the movement started by Johnson, who is still committed to his goal of achieving immortality by 2039.

Earlier this year, he revealed that he had been diagnosed with autoimmune gastritis, a chronic inflammatory condition of the stomach with no cure.

"Points for irony and points for the haters!" he laughs.

" There's a substantial portion of the world that wants me to die. "

While Johnson says it is highly likely he developed the condition long before he started his longevity journey, doctors say that cannot be confirmed conclusively.

Bryan Johnson working out while wearing a VR headset. (Twitter: Bryan Johnson)

Now his focus is on finding a cure.

"The only way we prove ourselves worthy of this mission is if we both get diagnosed with an incurable disease and we have to solve it.

"We're trying to broker a peace between all humans, all countries, AI, and the planet and say, 'can we just be sober for this moment and say none of us want to die, right now?'

"At heart, we are artists … and [Kate and I] just want to play.

"We think it's really a spectacular time to be alive and we're grateful to exist."

The female Bryan Johnson

Kate Tolo's long journey from north Queensland to the centre of Bryan Johnson's biohacking empire in the United States might surprise many, including herself.

She is now listed as the co-founder of Johnson's brands Blueprint, Don't Die, and Immortals, and featured in the Netflix documentary Don't Die: The Man Who Wants to Live Forever.

Australian Kate Tolo is aiming to become the "world's most measured woman" (X: Kate Tolo)

Tolo has now signed up to collect "14 million data points on her menstrual cycle", as part of a protocol that she says involves more than 100 tasks a day and dozens of devices.

"I didn't know how bad the literature was around female health," she tells hack.

"We're measuring my skin, my brain, my microbiome and my gut, my mouth, my stool, my vaginal microbiome, literally everything.

"We're measuring every single day … to translate the lived female experience into numbers so that we can all appreciate and respect it and understand it.

"Let's talk about it. Let's get it out there."

Medical experts weigh in on biohacking

Brooke Nickel, a senior research fellow at the University of Sydney's School of Public Health, is cautious when commenting on the methods used by Johnson and Tolo to boost longevity.

Is Bryan Johnson’s quest to live forever killing us? Scientific discoveries that improve longevity are cause for celebration, but in promoting a rigid lifestyle that is incompatible with socialising, optimisation culture undermines the communal bonds that are central to human flourishing.

"I think there are some genuinely positive things related to the 'biohacking' trends being promoted in terms of prevention and taking an active interest in your health," Dr Nickel says.

"However, much of what is being discussed in these spaces seems to lack robust evidence of benefit and is often accompanied by commercial marketing, particularly when it becomes about 'optimising' or 'hacking' aging.

"So I am sceptical and think we should be careful not to confuse good public health practices with vested interests."

Johnson and Tolo dismiss suggestions that they are trying to make money by capitalising on society's fears around aging and dying, by selling supplements and serums under their brands.

"I think if the goal was for Kate and I to make money, we would not start this business," Johnson says.

"We are genuinely trying to do this to help.

"We don't expect people to believe that."

'I love Australia'

Away from all the headlines, marketing and controversy are ordinary facets of Bryan and Kate's relationship.

He recently visited Australia to meet Kate's family and attend her brother's wedding, which Kate says was one of her favourite moments in life.

"They loved him!" she says.

"He really just, like, integrated with the family."

Loading Instagram content

While Johnson admits the jet lag took its toll (he claimed it increased his biological age by 13 years), he says the long trip was worth it.

"Kate's family is lovely, and I love Australia.

"I did the math, trying to calculate what it would cost to move Australia closer to Los Angeles!"

Asked whether after all of his longevity and biohacking efforts he is worried he will die in a freak accident, Johnson laughs.

"I think I'll probably be taken out by a bus or similar," he says.

" I give everyone full permission to laugh and celebrate it and share with all their friends and family and tell everybody they told them so. "

Tolo's response is more serious.

"If the chances are that we fail, it doesn't stop us from trying anyway.

"We're enjoying our lives, we love this mission, and it's exciting for us to wake up every day and do it."

World.title: More than 30 years on from Lockerbie bombing, first US trial faces delay
World.content:
As the wreckage from Pan Am Flight 103 was being collected from across a small Scottish town, one phrase kept being repeated: "We do not know what happened."

Timeline of the Lockerbie bombing View a chronology of key events in the Lockerbie bombing case.

The plane fell from more than 9 kilometres in the air, crashing into the town of Lockerbie and leaving lives, homes and communities in ruins.

The plane, flying from London to New York on December 21, 1988, simply vanished from radar screens. One moment there, gone the next.

As it was falling, the sky lit up, according to local John Glasgow.

"We tried to get near the plane but it was completely on fire," Mr Glasgow told the Daily News in 1988.

"There were no bodies about. I don't think there would be any chance … It went up in a fireball."

After the Lockerbie bombing, families of victims received $US2.7 billion ($3.7 billion) in compensation from the Libyan government. (Reuters: Greg Bos)

Fragments of a circuit board and timer were later found by investigators, and they established a bomb was placed inside a radio in a piece of luggage on the plane.

Authorities confirmed all 259 people on board were killed, along with 11 people on the ground in Lockerbie.

Before the September 11 attacks of 2001, it was the deadliest terror attack in US history, with 190 Americans killed, and remains the deadliest in the United Kingdom.

The Lockerbie victims also included people from 21 different countries.

The Scottish town of Lockerbie in the aftermath of the bombing of Pan Am flight 103 in December 1988. (File)

US and Scottish investigators have accused a total of three Libyan intelligence operatives since 1991.

One has been acquitted, another convicted, and the third now faces trial in the US, which comes more than two decades since the ruling in the first Lockerbie case.

The trial was scheduled to begin in late August but has been delayed after new evidence emerged.

A hearing has now been set for September.

Interview led to clandestine extradition

In 2020, Abu Agila Mohammad Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi, a former explosives expert for Libya's intelligence service, became the latest person charged with the Lockerbie bombing.

A 2012 interview Al-Marimi gave to Libyan law enforcement became a crucial piece of evidence for US and Scottish authorities when they obtained a copy in 2017.

"At long last, this man responsible for killing Americans and many others will be subject to justice for his crimes," former US attorney general William Barr said in 2020.

A moment of hope for Lockerbie victims' families Before September 11, it was America's worst terrorist attack — now the alleged bombmaker faces trial

According to US officials, Al-Marimi admitted to building the bomb, working with others to carry out the attack and that it was ordered by Libyan intelligence.

Two years following the charges, Al-Marimi was taken into US custody.

"The families of those killed in the Lockerbie bombing have been told that the suspect Abu Agila Mohammad Masud Kheir Al-Marimi is in US custody," a spokesperson for Scotland's Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service said.

Al-Marimi admitted to building the bomb that took down Pan Am 103 in an 2012 interview, according to US official (AP: Alexandria Sheriff's Office)

US officials did not say how he was detained, but in late 2022 local Libyan media reported he had been kidnapped by armed men from his residence in the country's capital Tripoli.

Who were the other accused terrorists?

Before Al-Marimi, two other Libyan intelligence operatives were charged with conspiracy, murder and the destruction of Pan Am 103 in 1991.

Abdel Baset Ali al-Megrahi was also the head of security for Libyan Arab Airlines, and Lamen Khalifa Fhimah was the LAA station manager at Luqa Airport in Malta.

The evidence that linked them to the attack came from a small fragment inside a piece of a shirt, according to the FBI.

Abdel Baset Ali al-Megrahi remains the only person convicted of the Lockerbie bombing after he was sentenced to life in prison in 2001. (Manoocher Deghati: AFP)

The pair faced trial in 2000 by a panel of Scottish judges, in a purpose-built courtroom on a former US military base in the Netherlands called Camp Ziest.

In 2001, Fhimah was acquitted of the charges, while al-Megrahi was sentenced to life in prison.

He was later released on compassionate grounds in 2009, and died three years later.

In 2002 the Libyan Government offered to pay $US2.7 billion in compensation to victims of the Lockerbie bombing, but tied the payments to lifting US and UN sanctions on the country.

First US Lockerbie trial faces delay

Al-Marimi is set to become the first person accused of the Lockerbie bombing to be tried in a US courtroom.

Loading...

Jury selection for the trial was scheduled for August 25, but it has now been postponed following a judge's ruling after the emergence of new evidence.

But the nature of the evidence was not specified.

US District Judge Dabney Friedrich said the delay was because the defence needed time to "determine how best to defend" this case.

The judge had previously ruled to allow evidence of Al-Marimi's confession, which the defence said was disputed and given under duress.

The prosecution allege the Lockerbie bombing was carried out by Al-Marimi and others under the orders of former Libyan leader Moammar Gaddafi.

They also allege he brought a suitcase containing a bomb which was transported from an airport in Malta, and given to his co-conspirators for a flight to Frankfurt in Germany.

According to authorities, the suitcase then travelled from Frankfurt to London, and then it was loaded inside Pan Am flight 103.

Al-Marimi worked within the Libyan intelligence service between 1973 and 2011, according to the prosecution.

The man now in his mid-70s is facing two counts of destruction of an aircraft resulting in death, and if convicted, faces a maximum penalty of life in prison.

Former FBI special agent Dick Marquise, who led the Lockerbie case, said Al-Marimi was known at the time of the initial investigation.

"It went dormant because the Libyan government disavowed any knowledge of who he might be," Mr Marquise told ABC Radio National.

The judge has scheduled a hearing to discuss the status of the case on September 1.

ABC/AP

World.title: Privacy laws target AI, smart glasses right to erase Australians’ data
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPrivacy Privacy laws target AI, smart glasses right to erase Australians’ data James Massola August 30, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The federal government will unveil a raft of changes to Australia’s privacy laws designed to keep pace with new technologies including smart glasses and artificial intelligence. Attorney-General Michelle Rowland will on Monday release the draft legislation, which will also include new online safeguards for identity documents, called IDLock, and a right to have personal information destroyed by social media and search companies. Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses in a Ray-Ban eyewear store in Rome. Bloomberg Smart glasses look like normal glasses but can also photograph or film what the user sees, potentially without the consent or knowledge of other people. The Greens are already proposing new laws that would ban the import of the glasses for the next 12 months because of privacy concerns. The rise of AI, meanwhile, has seen tech companies shovel huge volumes of data into their systems to help “train” their AI models, with little regard for people’s privacy or copyright.



The law changes will include a right to erasure, so people can ask social media and search companies to have their personal information destroyed, rather than it being retained. The right to erasure will not apply to media organisations publishing news articles. Rowland said Australians deserved to have control over how their personal identity information, such as their driver’s licence or passport, is used to verify their identity online. “As data breaches, scams and cyber-enabled crime continue to evolve, Australia’s approach must evolve with them. With the launch of IDLock, our government is taking the next step towards a stronger, more robust identity verification framework that expands the focus from responding after identity credentials have been compromised, to enabling Australians to protect themselves before identity crime occurs,” she said. Attorney-General Michelle Rowland during question time at Parliament House in Canberra on Wednesday. Alex Ellinghausen “Whether their driver licence details have been exposed in a data breach or they are concerned about scams and identity theft, IDLock will give Australians an accessible and simple way to have greater visibility, control and confidence in how their identity documents are used.”



After an initial trial, IDLock will be added to Australians’ myGov accounts in 2027 and will allow people to block, unblock and monitor the use of their ID documents. It will help people ensure they do not have their ID stolen or misused in scams and other identity crimes, while also allowing them to see whether their data has been subject to a data breach or hacking incident. IDLock builds on the Credential Protection Register, created in 2022 by the government, which is supposed to stop compromised identity documents from being used to falsely establish an individual’s identity. The register has blocked over 830,000 fraudulent identity verification attempts since it was established. After the release of the proposed new laws, the government will consult industry and look to introduce the laws into parliament by the end of 2026. World.title: ‘Broken’: Anthony Mundine reacts to father and boxing great Tony Mundine’s death
World.content:
Breaking SportVale ‘Broken’: Anthony Mundine reacts to father and boxing great Tony Mundine’s death Sally Rawsthorne Updated August 30, 2026 — 9:56pm ,first published 9:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains images and the name of a deceased Indigenous person. Australian boxing great Tony Mundine has died, age 75. The boxer, who is also the father of professional boxer and rugby league player Anthony Mundine, died at the weekend, sources close to the family have confirmed to this masthead. Three generations of the Mundine family, Anthony, Rahim and Tony in 2022. Jessica Hromas Mundine was the only Australian boxer to compete professionally across four weight divisions and held four different Australian titles.



On Sunday night, Anthony Mundine said he was “broken” in an Instagram post. Anthony Mundine gets his hands taped by his father. Tony Mundine pictured at home in 1972. Antony Matheus Linsen/Fairfax Media “Dad I love you man my Allah bless your soul. I’m on my way home to say goodbye one last time til we meet again... there’s only one Tony Mundine.” In 2024, Anthony Mundine described his father as his “biggest inspiration” in and out of the ring.



“You’ve shown me what it means to be a man of strength and integrity, and for that, I’m forever grateful. I wouldn’t be who I am without your sacrifices, your wisdom, and your unwavering support,” he wrote at the time. Tony Mundine retired from professional boxing in 1984 and became a member of the Order of Australia in 1986 for services to sport, particularly boxing and Aboriginal youth. Anthony Mundine speaking at a press conference promoting his next fight with his father Tony Mundine next to him. A Bundjalung man from Baryulgil, just north of the NSW town of Grafton, Mundine moved to Sydney in the mid-1960s with the hope of becoming a first grade footballer. He played with the Redfern All Blacks and it was while doing some off-season training at a local boxing gym his talent was discovered.



Mundine had his first fight in Sydney in 1969 - competing in 96 bouts in a career that spanned till 1984 that also saw him travel the world and challenge unsuccessfully once for the World Middleweight belt in 1974. Upon his retirement from boxing, Mundine was heavily involved in a gym in the neighbourhood known as The Block in Redfern, on the corner of Eveleigh and Vine Streets. Mundine, the middleweight champion, did not raise a sweat as he disposed of Filipino Rapalo in two rounds in 1970. The gym had been set up inside an old shoe factory that had been acquired by the Aboriginal Housing Company and Mundine’s work had a positive impact on young Aboriginal people as the venue became a popular place for the community to spend time. World.title: The plastic pushing people
World.content:
Helen Kershaw of Killara is over the plastic hassle: “I was appalled to read ‘The Ooshies campaign has been a big winner for Woolworths’. Not a big winner for the environment, unfortunately – more plastic in landfills and more plastic in our oceans. Shame on you, Woolworths.”

“As a regular visitor to Parkes, we inevitably end up at one of the Chinese restaurants for dinner,” says Robert McElhone of Roseville. “This year, we knew it was the same restaurant as last year. When we sat down with our BYO bottle of wine, the waitress said the same thing as last year: ‘Would you like some glasses?’”

The licensing law-friendly culinary delights at the Chatswood Charles (C8) compares with that at the Decline Wine Bar (appropriately named The Decline Of Human Civilisation As We Know It) in Kingsford, usually full of UNSW students,” recalls Frans Boot of Gregory Hills. “At 8pm, staff brought out paper plates with tinned spag bol, sometimes even warmed up. You got a plate whether you wanted one or not. That must have added to the job of cleaning-up.”

“I’m chuffed to see the well-deserved accolades coming Boyd Exell’s (C8) way,” declares Keith Mayoh of Tathra. “He’s a graduate of Bega Public School where he learnt little about Four-In-Hand carriage driving but did very well in the more traditional subjects. His introduction to the sport came from the late, great Max Pearce, who was well known in the horsey world. As far as I know, the duke did not contribute to his success. Onya, Boydie!”

“My cousin, Mary Willsallen, was judging a Four-In-Hand driving competition in Britain where Prince Philip’s team suffered an equipment malfunction,” writes Katrina Watts of Murwillumbah. “The British judges also marked him down for, as a royal, swearing in public while encouraging the horses. Mary was insistent that he be judged on skill, not social status, and won the day.”

World.title: ‘You are not taking me from my daughter’: Coogee shark attack survivor tells of desperate fight for life
World.content:
NationalNSWSharks ‘You are not taking me from my daughter’: Coogee shark attack survivor tells of desperate fight for life Jack Gramenz August 30, 2026 — 8:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Shark attack survivor Leah Stewart has told of her terrifying battle with a great white shark at a Sydney beach, and how thoughts of her daughter growing up without her spurred her on as she “fought like hell” to stay alive. A little over two months after losing part of her left arm and a “catastrophic” amount of blood, Stewart told Nine’s 60 Minutes program on Sunday she could feel her life slipping away as she lay on the sand of Coogee Beach on a weekend morning in June. Leah Stewart can recall coming face to face with the great white shark. 60 Minutes “It just felt like everything was leaving my body and I was going somewhere,” Stewart said. But then she thought of her baby daughter, August, growing up without her mum.



“I just knew I couldn’t leave her … I know it sounds strange but I sort of willed myself back,” Stewart told the Nine program. It was the middle of a winter’s day and Stewart had been swimming between the flags in clear waters under blue skies at a beach that had not reported a shark attack in more than a hundred years. A beach closure sign at Coogee Beach in the hours after Leah Stewart was attacked on June 13. Sitthixay Ditthavong She was just about to head in to shore to play with August on the beach. “I heard a girl behind me … a shrill shriek. I turned and there was a huge, huge fin behind her. It was massive,” she said.



“I looked at the size of it and I realised that’s not a dolphin.” She began to swim to shore but felt movement in the water nearby. “I turned around, and it was right there … and it just was getting closer and closer and closer.” Stewart said she thought briefly about which limb she was willing to lose as she looked into the looming shark’s beady black eyes. “I’m right-handed, so I thought ‘let’s do a left hook’,” she said.



“I just kind of throw my left arm and it just grabs onto my forearm and rips, rips away my skin, my muscle, everything … there’s a big gap between my forearm and the hand.” But the shark wasn’t done. Leah Stewart has recounted how she fought off a shark at Coogee Beach in June. 60 Minutes Stewart took a deep breath as the four-metre great white grabbed onto her leg and pulled her under the water. She thought this was how she would die. But then she thought of daughter, August. “In my head, I was like, ‘You ugly f---er. You are not taking me away from my daughter’, and I twisted myself around and I just started punching it over and over and over again.



“It was like fighting a dinosaur. It was so big. It was like punching a brick wall. “I must have got a really good one in and so it let me go.” “It was the hardest thing in the world, but I fought my way out of there.” She had beaten back the shark, but Stewart’s fight was not over. A crew of rescuers, including champion paddleboarder Charlie Verco and off-duty lifeguard Ben Heenan got Stewart to shore before a team of clinicians at St Vincent’s Hospital worked to miraculously save a patient who was barely conscious, hardly breathing and with an undetectable pulse. It’s a condition medical professionals artfully describe as “not compatible with life”.



Incompatibility aside, Stewart is alive, to be with her daughter and to give her gratitude to the people who saved her. Leah Stewart, pictured with her daughter before she was attacked by a great white shark at Coogee in June. Stewart’s first thoughts were again for her daughter more than a week after the attack when she emerged from an induced coma, her brother Joshua previously revealed. Her incredible tale of survival is one she plans to tell August some day. “Not anytime soon … she’ll understand the full story a bit when she’s much older,” Stewart said.



“I thought maybe I’ll just write her a little children’s book, and I’ll work very carefully on the wording and how it goes. “Along the lines of: ‘Mummy loved you so much that, even when the scariest, scariest thing could happen … she loved you so much that she was able to conquer that’.” It’s a story she can tell with props. A broken-off piece of the shark’s tooth. “It’s a symbol of what I survived,” Stewart said. “I took home something from him. He took a lot away from me, but I got a tooth,” Stewart said.



Nine is also the publisher of this masthead. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘I did think she was going to die’: How strangers saved shark attack victim Leah Stewart
World.content:
NationalNSWSharks ‘I did think she was going to die’: How strangers saved shark attack victim Leah Stewart Jack Gramenz August 30, 2026 — 8:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dragged underwater by a great white shark at a Sydney beach, Leah Stewart thought she was going to die. Later, the heroes who brought her to shore and the ones who operated on her, thought so too. “I’m here. I’m alive,” Stewart told Nine’s 60 Minutes program on Sunday night. Leah Stewart can recall coming face-to-face with the great white shark. 60 Minutes “It was the hardest thing in the world, but I fought my way out of there.” Stewart was swimming at Coogee Beach on a Saturday morning in June, about to head back to shore to play with her baby daughter August, when she came face to face with a four-metre great white shark.



About 100 metres away, world champion paddleboarder Charlie Verco was training for an upcoming race. Normally, coming into Coogee was a relief. Close to the shore, and with people around. Charlie Verco rescued Stewart from the water. Sitthixay Ditthavong “That day, it was so nice that there were swimmers all around me,” Verco told the Nine program. Nine is also the publisher of this masthead. Then Verco saw a big shadow in the water, and he realised there was a big shark accompanying it.



The water clouded with blood as Stewart fought off the shark, which had ripped away her arm and dragged her underwater. “There was a lot of thrashing and that was around the time where I actually saw the shark come out of the water,” Verco said, as he recalled being shocked by “the volume of it”. “I kind of realised this thing’s actually just not going to be scared of me,” he said. He signalled lifeguards to sound the alarm and started paddling. “There was so much blood in the water that I couldn’t see into it any more,” Verco said.



Stewart managed to swim towards Verco as he tried to pull her on to his board. Her fight with the shark had shredded her hands and she struggled to hold on as Verco desperately paddled, backwards, towards the beach. Related Article Sharks ‘You are not taking me from my daughter’: Coogee shark attack survivor tells of desperate fight for life “Thank goodness, I got the world record holder for paddling,” Stewart said. Surf lifesaver Ben Heenan was coming out to meet them. He and Verco carried Stewart onto the sand as Heenan’s partner, doctor Kassandra McGregor phoned triple zero. Police patrols had been stepped up in Sydney’s east after the Bondi Beach terror attack in September and officers joined with doctors on the scene, making desperate efforts to stem Stewart’s bleeding.



“It was just luck that it was the riot squad … and they have a tourniquet on their uniform,” Heenan said. Trauma specialist Ian Ferguson was on hand to help, but he didn’t hold much hope. “Having seen the amount of blood that was in the water and seeing the extent of her wounds … she was pretty close to [bleeding to death],” Ferguson said. McGregor had applied the tourniquets, but Stewart’s veins were “completely flat” so Ferguson drilled into the bone marrow of Stewart’s shoulders to deliver fluids and blood, before she was rushed to hospital. Emergency specialist Nikki Woods was leading the emergency department at St Vincent’s Hospital when Stewart arrived, barely conscious and incredibly pale.



“My priority was to stabilise her, but get her up to theatre as soon as possible,” Woods said. Seventeen minutes later, Stewart was heading into surgery. Surgeon Kim Isaacs was doing the same. “I did think that she was going to die,” Isaacs said. “It doesn’t mean I’m not going to try.” A soaking wet sheet that ended up in the operating theatre carried in “half the sand from Coogee Beach” as surgeons worked to control Stewart’s bleeding. Her left arm could not be saved and was amputated below the elbow. Stewart remained in an induced coma for another 10 days, undergoing multiple further surgeries.



Since regaining consciousness, Stewart has been learning to walk again and rehabilitating her severely injured right hand with therapist Meredith Rogers. Rogers said Stewart, after fighting off a shark, spurred by the thought of her daughter growing up without her mum, had “constantly exceeded everyone’s expectations” on her recovery. While there were many doubts she could survive, Woods said she had a feeling Stewart would pull through. “There’s a power of being young and a mum, and you’re resilient, and you’ve got all that family support,” Woods said when she and Stewart met recently. Woods is just one of the many people Stewart has since thanked for saving her life.



“They’ve all played such an important piece in getting me to here now, and I’m very, very grateful for everything they’ve done for me,” Stewart said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Inside Reddam House, the Sydney private school trying to break the mould
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s just after 8.30am on an August Friday morning outside Reddam House North Shore. At the school gate, a mother chats with a staff member about anxiety. Do students have a reason to be anxious? Friday at Reddam is cycle test day, where every pupil from year 3 upwards sits a 50-minute test on a range of subjects including English, mathematics and science. After 8.50am, in a classroom on the upper floors of the school’s North Sydney building, year 9 science students sit at separate desks in rows. Teacher Steve Centra has soothing background music playing. He appears to be reading from a script. Inhale for four counts, exhale for six counts, he says. There’s also a message for the students. Teacher Steve Centra tells students their performance does not define their worth. Steven Siewert “This test measures your performance today,” he says. “It does not measure your worth. Your result doesn’t define your intelligence, does not define your potential, and certainly, it doesn’t define who you are.” In the 18 months since the North Sydney school opened, student numbers have grown from 498 to 875. Next year’s expected enrolment is 1100 students, with capacity of 1350 to be reached in 2028. The school’s first cohort of HSC students will start year 12 studies later this term.



Reddam North Shore is part of the Inspired Education group, a for-profit company that runs 125 schools in 30 countries. Students sit the cycle tests every Friday. Steven Siewert Some in the education sector are critical of high-stakes tests, which they regard as narrowing the focus of education and stressing students unnecessarily. At Reddam, cycle testing is the school’s main pillar. The school mantra could be: It’s cool to be clever. It’s cool to be kind. Kylie Chacon, head of primary, says tests go beyond academic benefits. “The main thing is that we’re teaching them to push themselves to be their personal best,” she says. Parents enrol their children because they like the amount of data the school uses, teachers say. Steven Siewert Every teacher tutors before and after school to help underperforming students improve. Chacon says testing helps provide teachers with data so they can reflect on how they have taught the content. It is also an enrolment drawcard. “Parents are choosing our school for our systems, and especially the cycle test,” she says.



Where other schools have sprawling campuses, Reddam North Shore is a converted Harry Seidler building, once six-storey office block. There are specialised mathematics, science and English teachers in years 5 and 6. Melissa Coombes, head of K-6 mathematics, says students get a strong foundation before entering year 7, where the curriculum steps up to more challenging concepts such as algebra. Mathematics is “not everyone’s cup of tea” and a subject some primary teachers might shy away from, she says. Having taught at another independent school, for girls, she regards Reddam North Shore as having a distinct academic culture. “I think the difference here is that students are quite motivated,” she says. “They do get excited about tricky maths problems and new topics.” Students conduct a science experiment. Steven Siewert Midmorning in a science laboratory, year 5 student Jordan Ma is keen to tell the Herald about a science experiment he’s poised to conduct. “Back in my old school, I didn’t really get to do any experiments. I only just sat in class and just listened.” Nearby, English teacher Sarah Burnham-King sits with a year 6 class in a public speaking lesson. A boy tells a story about the world’s ugliest fish, his arms by his side, steadily scanning classmates to make eye contact with everyone, and doing it without notes.



Students then give him feedback on his performance, noting two things he did well. They also note one weakness he could improve – one boy says he could make better use of his hands while speaking. A student gets feedback from his peers and teacher Sarah Burnham-King. Steven Siewert Public speaking is a central part of Reddam’s high school curriculum, with a one-hour public speaking class every week for students in years 7 to 9. Actor Rose Chachko, who now also teaches public speaking at Reddam North Shore, said she was mortified at the prospect of talking in front of her peers when she attended the high school’s eastern suburbs campus. “We were all frightened, scared, going up in front of an audience, in front of teenagers that we don’t know,” she says. Years later, it paid dividends into job interviews, including on one particular occasion at Channel Seven. “I remember the interviewer saying to me: ‘I actually noticed that you don’t say ‘um’ and ‘like’ a lot like I do.’



“I said to him: ‘It’s so interesting because for three years back in high school, I was trained to eliminate those words as much as possible in my public speaking class.’ “When you go out in the real world, when you communicate with your teachers, when you communicate with your friends, with your parents, later on in life when you’re going to be applying for jobs and things like that, it’s an absolute life skill to be able to communicate properly.” Annual fees for Reddam range from $30,000 for kindergarten to $49,000 for year 12, placing it among long-established high-fee independent schools. For deputy principal Nick Jolly, previously at Cranbrook, Reddam breaks the Sydney private school mould. As other schools might focus on ties and blazers, Reddam is simpler with plenty of room for individuality. Blue hair is fine. As others play on tradition, Reddam sees itself as outward-looking. Reddam does not have the focus on tradition of other private schools and does not have the sprawling grounds. Steven Siewert “For us, school is preparation for life, and we do our best to prepare kids for entry into that world,” he says.

World.title: Catholic schools warn of fee hikes as teachers negotiate pay
World.content:
NationalVictoriaHigh school Catholic schools warn of fee hikes as teachers negotiate pay Alex Crowe August 30, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Families can expect to pay more for potentially less at some Victorian Catholic schools next year, amid warnings that teacher salary increases could mean fee hikes and subject cuts. About 40,000 Catholic school staff, who are negotiating a workplace agreement for the next four years, anticipate an increase in line with the 28.3 per cent increase public school teachers are expected to endorse by October. Catholic schools are warning of fee increases in response to higher teacher wages. Brook Mitchell Catholic teachers, who have had pay parity with public colleagues since the 1990s, have received a commitment from employers to match the government offer, alongside a warning that it will have consequences. Melbourne Archdiocese Catholic Schools, the state’s largest employer of Catholic school teachers, wrote to employees saying it hoped to avoid “significant fee increases” due to wages going up.



“While these changes will be government-funded in state schools, Catholic schools will not receive additional funding commensurate with the additional cost,” wrote MACS general manager Marwin Austerberry and director Mary Oski. “They need to be supported through our usual budget and planning process.” Victorian Catholic Education Authority boss Elizabeth Labone. Flavio Brancaleone Mater Christi College, an all-girls secondary school in Melbourne’s outer east, warned that low-enrolment subjects might not run next year while some camps and excursions might be cancelled due to budget constraints. Principal Maria Haggett said the federal government, which provides up to 80 per cent of public funding for private schools, would not increase funding to cover the pay rise.



Haggett said the federal government’s decision was unprecedented in her career and left non-government schools with few options but to raise fees. Editor's pick Education ‘Historic milestone’: Third strike called off as teachers back pay deal “We don’t want to price anyone out,” she said. “We also want people to understand that there’s not a profit motive here. This is about operations and sustainability.” Haggett said the school of about 680 students, which receives more than $900,000 in annual government funding and charges about $12,690 a student, was still finalising its 2027 fee increase. “It certainly won’t be less than last year, and last year was around 7½ per cent,” she said.



Victoria’s more than 490 Catholic schools will share in $3.2 billion from the federal government this year. A federal Education Department spokesperson said the Australian government provided recurrent funding to all schools, including Catholic schools, calculated with reference to the Schooling Resource Standard. “The SRS is increased annually to reflect changes in wages and other costs, with its indexation formula giving a 75 per cent weighting to the Wage Price Index, reflecting the fact that teacher and staff salaries are a significant part of school costs,” the spokesperson said. The financial viability of more than 100 Victorian Catholic schools could be tested due to the pay rises, with total enrolments at Catholic schools failing to keep pace with independent schools. MACS has confirmed St Pius X Primary in Heidelberg and Ss Peter and Paul’s School in Doncaster East will close at the end of the year due to low enrolments. It says fewer than 20 of its almost 300 schools have fewer than 100 students.



However, 47 Catholic schools in Melbourne have fewer than 150 students, and 105 schools have fewer than 150 students when Catholic regional schools are included. Victorian Catholic Education Authority chief executive officer Elizabeth Labone said Catholic schools were planning 2027 budgets to accommodate the changes from the new enterprise agreement. “This is about investing more of our school budgets directly in teachers and staff so they can be among the best-paid educators in the country, with leading workload conditions,” she said. “As a sector, we’re mindful of the pressures facing families and are committed to keeping fees as low as possible while continuing to provide a high-quality Catholic education.” The warning over program cuts comes as Catholic school teachers push for increased bargaining power, including the right to strike, through an application currently before the Fair Work Commission.



The Independent Education Union Victoria Tasmania, which represents about 14,000 Catholic school members in the state, has applied to the commission on behalf of 24 of the state’s 35 Catholic employers. MACS, the biggest employer with more than 18,000 staff, blocked its employees from being part of the application by arguing the union didn’t have majority support because it had underestimated the number of Catholic staff in the workforce. The union intends to bring blocked MACS and regional diocese staff into the Fair Work process after going back to the Catholic schools that mounted a legal challenge and establishing majority support. Union general secretary David Brear said this was about giving Catholic education staff the bargaining power they needed to win a fair deal. “What’s deeply frustrating is that Catholic employers have spent enormous time and resources fighting their own employees’ right to bargain collectively, when they could have spent that time sitting down with us and negotiating a fair agreement,” Brear said.

World.title: Privacy laws target AI, smart glasses right to erase Australians’ data
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPrivacy Privacy laws target AI, smart glasses right to erase Australians’ data James Massola August 30, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The federal government will unveil a raft of changes to Australia’s privacy laws designed to keep pace with new technologies including smart glasses and artificial intelligence. Attorney-General Michelle Rowland will on Monday release the draft legislation, which will also include new online safeguards for identity documents, called IDLock, and a right to have personal information destroyed by social media and search companies. Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses in a Ray-Ban eyewear store in Rome. Bloomberg Smart glasses look like normal glasses but can also photograph or film what the user sees, potentially without the consent or knowledge of other people. The Greens are already proposing new laws that would ban the import of the glasses for the next 12 months because of privacy concerns. The rise of AI, meanwhile, has seen tech companies shovel huge volumes of data into their systems to help “train” their AI models, with little regard for people’s privacy or copyright.



The law changes will include a right to erasure, so people can ask social media and search companies to have their personal information destroyed, rather than it being retained. The right to erasure will not apply to media organisations publishing news articles. Rowland said Australians deserved to have control over how their personal identity information, such as their driver’s licence or passport, is used to verify their identity online. “As data breaches, scams and cyber-enabled crime continue to evolve, Australia’s approach must evolve with them. With the launch of IDLock, our government is taking the next step towards a stronger, more robust identity verification framework that expands the focus from responding after identity credentials have been compromised, to enabling Australians to protect themselves before identity crime occurs,” she said. Attorney-General Michelle Rowland during question time at Parliament House in Canberra on Wednesday. Alex Ellinghausen “Whether their driver licence details have been exposed in a data breach or they are concerned about scams and identity theft, IDLock will give Australians an accessible and simple way to have greater visibility, control and confidence in how their identity documents are used.”



After an initial trial, IDLock will be added to Australians’ myGov accounts in 2027 and will allow people to block, unblock and monitor the use of their ID documents. It will help people ensure they do not have their ID stolen or misused in scams and other identity crimes, while also allowing them to see whether their data has been subject to a data breach or hacking incident. IDLock builds on the Credential Protection Register, created in 2022 by the government, which is supposed to stop compromised identity documents from being used to falsely establish an individual’s identity. The register has blocked over 830,000 fraudulent identity verification attempts since it was established. After the release of the proposed new laws, the government will consult industry and look to introduce the laws into parliament by the end of 2026. World.title: ‘Broken’: Anthony Mundine reacts to father and boxing great Tony Mundine’s death
World.content:
Breaking SportVale ‘Broken’: Anthony Mundine reacts to father and boxing great Tony Mundine’s death Sally Rawsthorne Updated August 30, 2026 — 9:56pm ,first published 9:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains images and the name of a deceased Indigenous person. Australian boxing great Tony Mundine has died, age 75. The boxer, who is also the father of professional boxer and rugby league player Anthony Mundine, died at the weekend, sources close to the family have confirmed to this masthead. Three generations of the Mundine family, Anthony, Rahim and Tony in 2022. Jessica Hromas Mundine was the only Australian boxer to compete professionally across four weight divisions and held four different Australian titles.



On Sunday night, Anthony Mundine said he was “broken” in an Instagram post. Anthony Mundine gets his hands taped by his father. Tony Mundine pictured at home in 1972. Antony Matheus Linsen/Fairfax Media “Dad I love you man my Allah bless your soul. I’m on my way home to say goodbye one last time til we meet again... there’s only one Tony Mundine.” In 2024, Anthony Mundine described his father as his “biggest inspiration” in and out of the ring.



“You’ve shown me what it means to be a man of strength and integrity, and for that, I’m forever grateful. I wouldn’t be who I am without your sacrifices, your wisdom, and your unwavering support,” he wrote at the time. Tony Mundine retired from professional boxing in 1984 and became a member of the Order of Australia in 1986 for services to sport, particularly boxing and Aboriginal youth. Anthony Mundine speaking at a press conference promoting his next fight with his father Tony Mundine next to him. A Bundjalung man from Baryulgil, just north of the NSW town of Grafton, Mundine moved to Sydney in the mid-1960s with the hope of becoming a first grade footballer. He played with the Redfern All Blacks and it was while doing some off-season training at a local boxing gym his talent was discovered.



Mundine had his first fight in Sydney in 1969 - competing in 96 bouts in a career that spanned till 1984 that also saw him travel the world and challenge unsuccessfully once for the World Middleweight belt in 1974. Upon his retirement from boxing, Mundine was heavily involved in a gym in the neighbourhood known as The Block in Redfern, on the corner of Eveleigh and Vine Streets. Mundine, the middleweight champion, did not raise a sweat as he disposed of Filipino Rapalo in two rounds in 1970. The gym had been set up inside an old shoe factory that had been acquired by the Aboriginal Housing Company and Mundine’s work had a positive impact on young Aboriginal people as the venue became a popular place for the community to spend time.
