World.title: The plastic pushing people
World.content:
Helen Kershaw of Killara is over the plastic hassle: “I was appalled to read ‘The Ooshies campaign has been a big winner for Woolworths’. Not a big winner for the environment, unfortunately – more plastic in landfills and more plastic in our oceans. Shame on you, Woolworths.”

“As a regular visitor to Parkes, we inevitably end up at one of the Chinese restaurants for dinner,” says Robert McElhone of Roseville. “This year, we knew it was the same restaurant as last year. When we sat down with our BYO bottle of wine, the waitress said the same thing as last year: ‘Would you like some glasses?’”

The licensing law-friendly culinary delights at the Chatswood Charles (C8) compares with that at the Decline Wine Bar (appropriately named The Decline Of Human Civilisation As We Know It) in Kingsford, usually full of UNSW students,” recalls Frans Boot of Gregory Hills. “At 8pm, staff brought out paper plates with tinned spag bol, sometimes even warmed up. You got a plate whether you wanted one or not. That must have added to the job of cleaning-up.”

“I’m chuffed to see the well-deserved accolades coming Boyd Exell’s (C8) way,” declares Keith Mayoh of Tathra. “He’s a graduate of Bega Public School where he learnt little about Four-In-Hand carriage driving but did very well in the more traditional subjects. His introduction to the sport came from the late, great Max Pearce, who was well known in the horsey world. As far as I know, the duke did not contribute to his success. Onya, Boydie!”

“My cousin, Mary Willsallen, was judging a Four-In-Hand driving competition in Britain where Prince Philip’s team suffered an equipment malfunction,” writes Katrina Watts of Murwillumbah. “The British judges also marked him down for, as a royal, swearing in public while encouraging the horses. Mary was insistent that he be judged on skill, not social status, and won the day.”

World.title: ‘You are not taking me from my daughter’: Coogee shark attack survivor tells of desperate fight for life
World.content:
NationalNSWSharks ‘You are not taking me from my daughter’: Coogee shark attack survivor tells of desperate fight for life Jack Gramenz August 30, 2026 — 8:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Shark attack survivor Leah Stewart has told of her terrifying battle with a great white shark at a Sydney beach, and how thoughts of her daughter growing up without her spurred her on as she “fought like hell” to stay alive. A little over two months after losing part of her left arm and a “catastrophic” amount of blood, Stewart told Nine’s 60 Minutes program on Sunday she could feel her life slipping away as she lay on the sand of Coogee Beach on a weekend morning in June. Leah Stewart can recall coming face to face with the great white shark. 60 Minutes “It just felt like everything was leaving my body and I was going somewhere,” Stewart said. But then she thought of her baby daughter, August, growing up without her mum.



“I just knew I couldn’t leave her … I know it sounds strange but I sort of willed myself back,” Stewart told the Nine program. It was the middle of a winter’s day and Stewart had been swimming between the flags in clear waters under blue skies at a beach that had not reported a shark attack in more than a hundred years. A beach closure sign at Coogee Beach in the hours after Leah Stewart was attacked on June 13. Sitthixay Ditthavong She was just about to head in to shore to play with August on the beach. “I heard a girl behind me … a shrill shriek. I turned and there was a huge, huge fin behind her. It was massive,” she said.



“I looked at the size of it and I realised that’s not a dolphin.” She began to swim to shore but felt movement in the water nearby. “I turned around, and it was right there … and it just was getting closer and closer and closer.” Stewart said she thought briefly about which limb she was willing to lose as she looked into the looming shark’s beady black eyes. “I’m right-handed, so I thought ‘let’s do a left hook’,” she said.



“I just kind of throw my left arm and it just grabs onto my forearm and rips, rips away my skin, my muscle, everything … there’s a big gap between my forearm and the hand.” But the shark wasn’t done. Leah Stewart has recounted how she fought off a shark at Coogee Beach in June. 60 Minutes Stewart took a deep breath as the four-metre great white grabbed onto her leg and pulled her under the water. She thought this was how she would die. But then she thought of daughter, August. “In my head, I was like, ‘You ugly f---er. You are not taking me away from my daughter’, and I twisted myself around and I just started punching it over and over and over again.



“It was like fighting a dinosaur. It was so big. It was like punching a brick wall. “I must have got a really good one in and so it let me go.” “It was the hardest thing in the world, but I fought my way out of there.” She had beaten back the shark, but Stewart’s fight was not over. A crew of rescuers, including champion paddleboarder Charlie Verco and off-duty lifeguard Ben Heenan got Stewart to shore before a team of clinicians at St Vincent’s Hospital worked to miraculously save a patient who was barely conscious, hardly breathing and with an undetectable pulse. It’s a condition medical professionals artfully describe as “not compatible with life”.



Incompatibility aside, Stewart is alive, to be with her daughter and to give her gratitude to the people who saved her. Leah Stewart, pictured with her daughter before she was attacked by a great white shark at Coogee in June. Stewart’s first thoughts were again for her daughter more than a week after the attack when she emerged from an induced coma, her brother Joshua previously revealed. Her incredible tale of survival is one she plans to tell August some day. “Not anytime soon … she’ll understand the full story a bit when she’s much older,” Stewart said.



“I thought maybe I’ll just write her a little children’s book, and I’ll work very carefully on the wording and how it goes. “Along the lines of: ‘Mummy loved you so much that, even when the scariest, scariest thing could happen … she loved you so much that she was able to conquer that’.” It’s a story she can tell with props. A broken-off piece of the shark’s tooth. “It’s a symbol of what I survived,” Stewart said. “I took home something from him. He took a lot away from me, but I got a tooth,” Stewart said.



Nine is also the publisher of this masthead. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘I did think she was going to die’: How strangers saved shark attack victim Leah Stewart
World.content:
NationalNSWSharks ‘I did think she was going to die’: How strangers saved shark attack victim Leah Stewart Jack Gramenz August 30, 2026 — 8:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dragged underwater by a great white shark at a Sydney beach, Leah Stewart thought she was going to die. Later, the heroes who brought her to shore and the ones who operated on her, thought so too. “I’m here. I’m alive,” Stewart told Nine’s 60 Minutes program on Sunday night. Leah Stewart can recall coming face-to-face with the great white shark. 60 Minutes “It was the hardest thing in the world, but I fought my way out of there.” Stewart was swimming at Coogee Beach on a Saturday morning in June, about to head back to shore to play with her baby daughter August, when she came face to face with a four-metre great white shark.



About 100 metres away, world champion paddleboarder Charlie Verco was training for an upcoming race. Normally, coming into Coogee was a relief. Close to the shore, and with people around. Charlie Verco rescued Stewart from the water. Sitthixay Ditthavong “That day, it was so nice that there were swimmers all around me,” Verco told the Nine program. Nine is also the publisher of this masthead. Then Verco saw a big shadow in the water, and he realised there was a big shark accompanying it.



The water clouded with blood as Stewart fought off the shark, which had ripped away her arm and dragged her underwater. “There was a lot of thrashing and that was around the time where I actually saw the shark come out of the water,” Verco said, as he recalled being shocked by “the volume of it”. “I kind of realised this thing’s actually just not going to be scared of me,” he said. He signalled lifeguards to sound the alarm and started paddling. “There was so much blood in the water that I couldn’t see into it any more,” Verco said.



Stewart managed to swim towards Verco as he tried to pull her on to his board. Her fight with the shark had shredded her hands and she struggled to hold on as Verco desperately paddled, backwards, towards the beach. Related Article Sharks ‘You are not taking me from my daughter’: Coogee shark attack survivor tells of desperate fight for life “Thank goodness, I got the world record holder for paddling,” Stewart said. Surf lifesaver Ben Heenan was coming out to meet them. He and Verco carried Stewart onto the sand as Heenan’s partner, doctor Kassandra McGregor phoned triple zero. Police patrols had been stepped up in Sydney’s east after the Bondi Beach terror attack in September and officers joined with doctors on the scene, making desperate efforts to stem Stewart’s bleeding.



“It was just luck that it was the riot squad … and they have a tourniquet on their uniform,” Heenan said. Trauma specialist Ian Ferguson was on hand to help, but he didn’t hold much hope. “Having seen the amount of blood that was in the water and seeing the extent of her wounds … she was pretty close to [bleeding to death],” Ferguson said. McGregor had applied the tourniquets, but Stewart’s veins were “completely flat” so Ferguson drilled into the bone marrow of Stewart’s shoulders to deliver fluids and blood, before she was rushed to hospital. Emergency specialist Nikki Woods was leading the emergency department at St Vincent’s Hospital when Stewart arrived, barely conscious and incredibly pale.



“My priority was to stabilise her, but get her up to theatre as soon as possible,” Woods said. Seventeen minutes later, Stewart was heading into surgery. Surgeon Kim Isaacs was doing the same. “I did think that she was going to die,” Isaacs said. “It doesn’t mean I’m not going to try.” A soaking wet sheet that ended up in the operating theatre carried in “half the sand from Coogee Beach” as surgeons worked to control Stewart’s bleeding. Her left arm could not be saved and was amputated below the elbow. Stewart remained in an induced coma for another 10 days, undergoing multiple further surgeries.



Since regaining consciousness, Stewart has been learning to walk again and rehabilitating her severely injured right hand with therapist Meredith Rogers. Rogers said Stewart, after fighting off a shark, spurred by the thought of her daughter growing up without her mum, had “constantly exceeded everyone’s expectations” on her recovery. While there were many doubts she could survive, Woods said she had a feeling Stewart would pull through. “There’s a power of being young and a mum, and you’re resilient, and you’ve got all that family support,” Woods said when she and Stewart met recently. Woods is just one of the many people Stewart has since thanked for saving her life.



“They’ve all played such an important piece in getting me to here now, and I’m very, very grateful for everything they’ve done for me,” Stewart said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: One Nation win hastens our Trumpification
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters One Nation win hastens our Trumpification August 30, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Badiucao To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. BYELECTION RESULT One Nation’s victory on Saturday in the byelection for the West Australian lower-house seat of Secret Harbour, south of Perth, marks a major step in what I call the Trumpification of Australian politics — the process by which a party utilises opposition to immigration and, despite lacking the experience and competence to govern, gains power and undermines the institutions and values of liberal democracy.

We must now contemplate the possibility of a political tidal wave at forthcoming state elections — Victoria on November 28 and New South Wales on March 27 — and at the next federal election in 2028, with Pauline Hanson emerging as a real contender for the prime ministership.

In Secret Harbour, this disturbing result was enabled in part by the WA Liberal Party’s decision to preference One Nation ahead of Labor. That strategy is likely to backfire. Rather than strengthening the Liberals, it risks helping to establish One Nation as Labor’s principal opponent, further eroding the Liberal Party’s own electoral base.

Drastic action is needed if One Nation is to be prevented from capturing state and federal governments.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese needs to institute some bold, eye-catching reforms that will rapidly improve life for most Australians.

And the Liberal Party needs to find ways to win back conservative and other voters who are now under Hanson’s spell.

Edmund Doogue, Crawley, WA PM’s positivity won’t dent Hanson’s appeal

In the wake of One Nation’s stunning victory in WA, the prime minister’s reported ″⁣pivot to positivity″⁣ looks increasingly like a fool’s errand.

No amount of selling how positive the government’s policies are will work on an electorate who are convinced they stink.

Principal among these policies for One Nation voters is immigration, which the government seemingly cannot handle, being pulled by both business and the Labor Party’s left to maintain a virtual status quo – in other words, a mess.

Greg Gardiner, Brunswick



Albanese must change priorities, fast

With Labor’s huge majority, it would ordinarily be unthinkable for it to lose government at the next federal election. But in Western Australia, One Nation defeating Labor’s candidate, a Woodside lobbyist of all things, means that in 2028, Labor’s reign could be cut short.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese can change his priorities and start governing for people not corporations, or he can ignore Secret Harbour’s loud and clear warning at his peril.

The nation is watching.

Margaret Callinan, Hawthorn PM’s losing bet on GST stand

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese promising to leave the unfair distribution of GST to WA in place didn’t work. He gambled and sacrificed all the other states for a loss on Saturday when One Nation won the Secret Harbour byelection.

No wonder Albanese’s polling is looking so bad. You win some, you lose more.

Jenny Callaghan, Hawthorn Cutting immigration key to winning votes

Your correspondent (Letters, 30/8) says migrants are vilified and blamed for all our woes. A more apt description is that the federal government is allowing too much immigration, which is placing pressure on house prices and rents.

Voters are deserting the major parties because of this obvious issue, and One Nation has filled that vacuum.

Until Labor and the Liberals cut immigration to sustainable levels, the situation will continue to worsen.

The fact is houses cannot be built fast enough to accommodate the current rate of immigration.

Christo Krousoratis, Templestowe THE FORUM IDF participation

Penny Wong and the ALP may stand up and condemn the IDF and Israeli government over the death of Zomi Frankcom, yet we know that nothing will be done. Meanwhile our government allows a group of about 40 Israelis, including military veterans, to participate in the Sydney Marathon and to raise money for an Israeli charity.

Settler violence in the West Bank continues, homes are destroyed, Gaza is still being bombed, yet the UN and our government just come out with meaningless words.

Dean Virgin, Strathmore



The value of advice

The state government has announced it will abolish Infrastructure Victoria, with the feeble excuse that this is to “end duplication and find efficiencies”. That agency’s role is to provide independent advice to parliament on infrastructure priorities, to assist with cost-efficient forward planning.

As its CEO Dr Jonathan Spear has said, “Independence is what makes our advice worth having”.

Infrastructure Victoria does not cost money; it saves the state millions of dollars. Nothing that Premier Carroll has done so far changes the fact that for the past decade, Melbourne and Victoria have had no transport plan to guide road and public transport investments. Instead, we have had a collection of big project announcements.

One reason the Suburban Rail Loop is a financial and transport planning disaster is because there was no initial independent evaluation of it or viable options, before it was announced prior to an election. Infrastructure Victoria must be retained, and its advice sought far more often.

Rob Morgan, traffic engineer, Bulleen Learn from past

With hindsight, the decisions to close the outer circle railway in the 1890s and the inner circle rail in 1981 were arguably misguided, given the then unforseen growth of Melbourne.

By 2050, Melbourne will need a first class rail network. The long-term potential of the inner and outer circle railways did not eventuate. The city cannot afford to not proceed with the SRL and the airport rail link.

Jim McLeod, Sale Victoria’s bumpy ride

Regarding potholes (″⁣What our drive along the Hume showed ...″⁣30/8). We recently undertook a road trip westwards through South Australia and Western Australia. We found the roads in WA to be excellent and those in SA not far behind.

However, on our way home Victoria provided an immediate, stark comparison. Bumpy, narrower, quite dangerous roads strewn with potholes. It is a similar experience entering NSW with an immediate improvement in road conditions.

Stephen Dinham, Metung Children before profit

“Commercial childcare operators are struggling to remain viable – and children and carers are paying the price″⁣ (29/8).

I’m left wondering when governments will understand the folly of privatisation of services that should be run in the public interest rather than for a profit motive. Community-based childcare provided a terrific model for delivering high-quality childcare, and yet governments let it be taken over by a profit-driven sector.

This is not to say that all for-profit centres are bad – financial sustainability is essential in providing consistency of delivery – but rather that we should ensure that the primary motive for operating should be the welfare of the children. This is most likely when generating a profit is not part of the equation.

Jenny Macmillan, Clifton Hill Female GP demands

Dr Ellie Goodsall’s piece (″⁣There’s one key reason female GPs like me are quitting″⁣, 28/8) is heartbreaking and a must-read for everyone, especially our politicians and those determining funding of general practice medicine. If you’re looking for someone who listens, cares and gives time, a female GP is the natural choice for women and many men.

The stripping back of mental health services has meant GPs are more in demand and it’s the female GPs filling the gaps and ″⁣doing the profession’s invisible emotional labour″⁣.

How long can they keep it up (for a fraction of the remuneration)?

Mary Stephen, Fitzroy



Time’s running down

The tragic events in Nepal and Tibet are harbingers of what’s to come in this rapidly warming world. For decades warnings of mountain glacier and lake collapse have gone unheeded. Millions live at extreme risk of cataclysm. Wildfires in Europe and North America, hellish temperatures in India and Pakistan, and Australia’s increasing vulnerability to catastrophic bushfires and floods present clear and present dangers to our way of life.

And yet, our major political parties continue to deny there’s a problem, or present hopeful solutions that are more than cancelled out by spending billions of our money supporting fossil fuels. At what point will Australians demand action, and vote for politicians who will meet this critical moment? It’s never too late to do better.

Guy Abrahams, Fairhaven God’s plans

I understand why survivors of natural disasters thank God. But spare a thought for the loved ones of those who were not so lucky. Why was God’s plan for them so different?

Nick Carr, Richmond What can we do?

I wonder how the biblical idea (Matthew 5.5) that “the meek shall inherit the Earth” stands up against the activities of despots around the globe.

Surely, many of the humbler humans would be appalled at what’s happening in the Ukrainian and Middle Eastern wars, and with the unbridled grab for climate-changing, fossil fuel energy sources such that Donald Trump has orchestrated in Venezuela. What can the consciously considerate, careful humans who constitute most of our population do?

Andrew Smith, Leongatha Do try this at home

Many of your correspondents bemoan the dire situation in relation to the climate crisis, which is clearly visible in daily news stories. It sometimes feels overwhelming and leads to a sense of hopelessness.

However, on recent dog walks around my local neighbourhood, I have been reminded that the transition to cleaner technologies continues at pace. The electric bus goes past, as do many electric and hybrid vehicles. I even spot a large tradesman’s ute – fully electric. The recently installed chargers are in regular use and there is yet another installation of solar panels on a nearby home.

These observations would have been unthinkable only a few years ago. Now, they are common. While global crises need to be met with global responses, it is important to remember that smaller actions at the local level are important too. We can all play our part.

Judy Williams, Beaumaris Lanes for everyone

As a long-term resident of Fitzroy and Clifton Hill, I have minimal sympathy for the company that has seemingly used a public right of way (ROW) to enhance its business income.

The bluestone ROWs of the inner-city built environment are largely heritage protected and form an integral and valued part of the inner-city history.

The ROWs are a public amenity frequently used by local residents, trades people, utility providers etc who require rear access to properties.

I hope the Supreme Court finds in favour of the City of Yarra and an enforceable order is made for the company to remove the concrete flooring and reinstate and/or repair any original bluestone removed or damaged.

Carol Jasen, Clifton Hill



Medicalised boredom

Cherie Gilmour’s delightful piece “A squishy is not a therapy tool, it’s just overpriced gunk” (30/8) has its scary side. Her seven-year-old daughter needed a “dumpling squishy” because “it helps me regulate”. I loved Gilmour’s comment that “when a dumpling squishy becomes a tool to ‘regulate’, even in the eyes of kids who don’t need it, we are medicalising boredom”.

Kevin Burke, Sandringham Consumers R Us

Fidget toys for everyone are not just “medicalising boredom”. They are training our kids to consume in order to fix your mood. They are the opposite of self-regulation.

Lesley Walker, Northcote ScoMo surprises

In 2018, Cathy Wilcox heard Scott Morrison say that “voting independent is like a box of chocolates – you never know what you would get”, upon which she drew a box of assorted “Coalition” chocolates, which included “leadership brittle”, “religious nut cluster”, “royal knighthood surprise” among many hilarious others.

This single, brilliant cartoon set a standard for Australian cartoonists who have emulated this method of social observation since. A well-deserved feather in her cap. Hopefully, she will bob up somewhere soon.

Julian Guy, Mount Eliza Wilcox’s wry perspective

It is hard to put into words how much the cartoons by Cathy Wilcox will be missed. Over the years, the first thing that I do when I open The Age is to look for Cathy’s cartoon.

They sum up what a thousand words by other contributors cannot do. They offer readers a different perspective on life, wry, succinct and carry a sometimes sublime message on the frailties of the leaders in our society. A truly, wonderful member of The Age and , dare I say, part of our family over the years.

Bruce MacKenzie, South Kingsville AND ANOTHER THING



How petty have Victorians become – scrapping a statute of Dan Andrews who guided us through the COVID-19 epidemic? There was no rule book. The government had to negotiate through an unknown minefield. Take politics out of it. Let the statue be erected.

Alan Symington, Mt Martha So there will not be a statue for our former premier. The pigeons will be furious.

Tim Brow, Flemington Bravo on cancelling the Dan Andrews statue. A more appropriate statue could depict an ″⁣unknown youth″⁣, in the vein of the unknown soldier, to represent those who died as a consequence of mental health and lockdowns.

Miranda Lewis, Camberwell Americaland

Donald Trump is trying to change the name Lake Ontario to Lake America on his side of the Canadian/American border. It’s really no different to the French and the English. The French never call it “the English Channel”. It is La Manche (″⁣the Sleeve”). Bonne chance, Monsieur Trump.

Sally Holt, Balwyn Have you heard the latest? We’re to be called South Trumpland.

Paul Drakeford, Kew



Do your worst, Mr Trump; Lake Ontario still laps the shores of Canada. What you have is half-pint Lake America.

Vincent O’Donnell, Ascot Vale I hereby proclaim that from this date on, the United States

of America will be known as Fairyland.

Roger Le Mesurier, Paris, France AFL

I was there on Friday night and it looked like a final, smelt like a final, sounded like a final, and was a final. Go Pies.

Felix Patton, Mt Martha Despite the closeness of the “extra” finals week, it only emphasised the fact that the bottom four sides of the top 10 aren’t capable of winning the premiership. The AFL will laud its success, but it is only a revenue raiser, and rewards mediocrity. Go back to a final six, and have an interstate competition mid-season to satisfy that need.

Rob Prowd, Box Hill South The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Inside Reddam House, the Sydney private school trying to break the mould
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s just after 8.30am on an August Friday morning outside Reddam House North Shore. At the school gate, a mother chats with a staff member about anxiety. Do students have a reason to be anxious? Friday at Reddam is cycle test day, where every pupil from year 3 upwards sits a 50-minute test on a range of subjects including English, mathematics and science. After 8.50am, in a classroom on the upper floors of the school’s North Sydney building, year 9 science students sit at separate desks in rows. Teacher Steve Centra has soothing background music playing. He appears to be reading from a script. Inhale for four counts, exhale for six counts, he says. There’s also a message for the students. Teacher Steve Centra tells students their performance does not define their worth. Steven Siewert “This test measures your performance today,” he says. “It does not measure your worth. Your result doesn’t define your intelligence, does not define your potential, and certainly, it doesn’t define who you are.” In the 18 months since the North Sydney school opened, student numbers have grown from 498 to 875. Next year’s expected enrolment is 1100 students, with capacity of 1350 to be reached in 2028. The school’s first cohort of HSC students will start year 12 studies later this term.



Reddam North Shore is part of the Inspired Education group, a for-profit company that runs 125 schools in 30 countries. Students sit the cycle tests every Friday. Steven Siewert Some in the education sector are critical of high-stakes tests, which they regard as narrowing the focus of education and stressing students unnecessarily. At Reddam, cycle testing is the school’s main pillar. The school mantra could be: It’s cool to be clever. It’s cool to be kind. Kylie Chacon, head of primary, says tests go beyond academic benefits. “The main thing is that we’re teaching them to push themselves to be their personal best,” she says. Parents enrol their children because they like the amount of data the school uses, teachers say. Steven Siewert Every teacher tutors before and after school to help underperforming students improve. Chacon says testing helps provide teachers with data so they can reflect on how they have taught the content. It is also an enrolment drawcard. “Parents are choosing our school for our systems, and especially the cycle test,” she says.



Where other schools have sprawling campuses, Reddam North Shore is a converted Harry Seidler building, once six-storey office block. There are specialised mathematics, science and English teachers in years 5 and 6. Melissa Coombes, head of K-6 mathematics, says students get a strong foundation before entering year 7, where the curriculum steps up to more challenging concepts such as algebra. Mathematics is “not everyone’s cup of tea” and a subject some primary teachers might shy away from, she says. Having taught at another independent school, for girls, she regards Reddam North Shore as having a distinct academic culture. “I think the difference here is that students are quite motivated,” she says. “They do get excited about tricky maths problems and new topics.” Students conduct a science experiment. Steven Siewert Midmorning in a science laboratory, year 5 student Jordan Ma is keen to tell the Herald about a science experiment he’s poised to conduct. “Back in my old school, I didn’t really get to do any experiments. I only just sat in class and just listened.” Nearby, English teacher Sarah Burnham-King sits with a year 6 class in a public speaking lesson. A boy tells a story about the world’s ugliest fish, his arms by his side, steadily scanning classmates to make eye contact with everyone, and doing it without notes.



Students then give him feedback on his performance, noting two things he did well. They also note one weakness he could improve – one boy says he could make better use of his hands while speaking. A student gets feedback from his peers and teacher Sarah Burnham-King. Steven Siewert Public speaking is a central part of Reddam’s high school curriculum, with a one-hour public speaking class every week for students in years 7 to 9. Actor Rose Chachko, who now also teaches public speaking at Reddam North Shore, said she was mortified at the prospect of talking in front of her peers when she attended the high school’s eastern suburbs campus. “We were all frightened, scared, going up in front of an audience, in front of teenagers that we don’t know,” she says. Years later, it paid dividends into job interviews, including on one particular occasion at Channel Seven. “I remember the interviewer saying to me: ‘I actually noticed that you don’t say ‘um’ and ‘like’ a lot like I do.’



“I said to him: ‘It’s so interesting because for three years back in high school, I was trained to eliminate those words as much as possible in my public speaking class.’ “When you go out in the real world, when you communicate with your teachers, when you communicate with your friends, with your parents, later on in life when you’re going to be applying for jobs and things like that, it’s an absolute life skill to be able to communicate properly.” Annual fees for Reddam range from $30,000 for kindergarten to $49,000 for year 12, placing it among long-established high-fee independent schools. For deputy principal Nick Jolly, previously at Cranbrook, Reddam breaks the Sydney private school mould. As other schools might focus on ties and blazers, Reddam is simpler with plenty of room for individuality. Blue hair is fine. As others play on tradition, Reddam sees itself as outward-looking. Reddam does not have the focus on tradition of other private schools and does not have the sprawling grounds. Steven Siewert “For us, school is preparation for life, and we do our best to prepare kids for entry into that world,” he says.

World.title: Garage blaze spreads to two homes on Kapiti Coast
World.content:
Firefighters are battling a blaze that has jumped from a garage to two homes on Kapiti Coast.

Fire and Emergency said it was called to reports of a garage fire in Otaki shortly before 8pm on Sunday.

A FENZ shift manager said crews arrived to find the garage fire had spread to a house, which was engulfed in flames, and was also threatening a neighbouring property.

The fire was escalated to second alarm, pulling in crews from Otaki, Waikanae, and Paraparaumu, they said.

They said the fire at the second property has since been extinguished and the blaze was now contained.

World.title: SH2 north of Wellington closed by serious crash
World.content:
A two-vehicle crash on State Highway 2 at Silverstream north of Wellington has shut both southbound lanes.

Police say the crash was reported about 7.15pm this evening.

Two people are reported to be seriously injured.

The northbound right turn lane into Silverstream is also closed.

Police said diversions were in place and motorists should expect delays.

Further north, a slip has also closed State Highway 2 through Waioweka Gorge.

The NZ Transport Agency said the road linking Gisborne and Opotiki is shut in both directions just south of the Goldsmith site.

World.title: Taiarahia documentary captures kotahitanga in action
World.content:
"Ko te wawata o te ngākau, kia mau te maunga i tana kākahu tawhito i mahue iho e o tātou matua, tātou koroua."

Our earnest wish is that the mountain should maintain her ancient raiments left since the days of our forebears.

Hiki Toko, 1985 (Te Māhurehure, Tūhoe)

For generations of Tūhoe, Taiarahia mountain in the Bay of Plenty settlement of Ruatoki Valley has stood as a sentinel landmark watching over them and welcoming them home.

Her cliffs once held the ancient pā of Tūhoe tūpuna, her presence sheltering the marae and hapū below, her dense forest sustains and protects native species.

As forestry plans loomed, the native forest of the maunga came under threat, galvanising a unified vision voiced by Te Mahurehure, Ngāi Tūhoe kaumātua Hiki Toko from the summit of Taiarahia.

"Ko te wawata o te ngākau, kia mau te maunga i tana kākahu tawhito i mahue iho ai e o tātou matua, tātou koroua.Ko tērā kākahu tawhito o te ngahere, kaua hoki e tangohia tērā kia whakamau i te kākahu hou anō mōna."

Our earnest wish is that the mountain should maintain her ancient raiments , left since the days of our forebears , that she should not be made to wear these new clothes.

Taiarahia, Te Kākahu Tawhito Docu Series Taiarahia, Te Kākahu Tawhito

In 1985, Tasman Forestry began earthworks as part of plans to clear hundreds of hectares of native forest and replace it with pine.

The proposal, which was approved by the Tūhoe-Waikaremoana Māori Trust Board, triggered a six-month occupation that united and divided whānau, placing relatives on opposing sides of the argument.

Harata Day (Te Māhurehure. Ngāi Tūhoe) and Tame Iti Te Māhurehure Ngāi Tūhoe) - instigators of the occupation of Taiarahia. Taiarahia, Te Kākahu Tawhito

Harata Day and Tame Iti initiated a unified response when the reality of the threat became stark - bulldozers were already tearing up the earth and felling trees on the maunga.

Their coordinated campaign combined direct action with strategic advocacy. Iti and others confronted the forestry operation on the maunga, while Harata worked behind the scenes, writing to ministers, politicians and organisations including Greenpeace and Forest & Bird to raise awareness and rally support.

In the months that followed, an enduring committment to kotahitanga overcame overwhelming odds to succeed in protecting the maunga.

Harata Day and two of her daughters Wikitoria Day and Ngarimu Daniels. Taiarahia, Te Kākahu Tawhito

Taiarahia: Te Kākahu Tawhito chronicles the experiences of those caught up in the occupation in a seven-part documentary series co-directed by Harata's daughter, Wikitōria Day.(Te Māhurehure, Ngāi Tūhoe)

Day said one of its unique strengths was capturing the vastly different memories and emotions of generations who experienced the same event.

"Most documentaries are centred around a handful of kaikōrero. In contrast, this kaupapa captures at least 15 different perspectives, and what's quite fascinating is the difference in recollections across generations ."

The series includes the voices of those who experienced the occupation as children and are now pakeke with mokopuna of their own.

"Tamariki were very involved in the occupation, but they were sheltered from the confrontational aspects,and still quite naive to the significance of what was happening, "

"They saw it as a time of adventure and playing with their cousins, despite the emotional impact of the events, they were allowed to maintain that sense of naivety children often have around kaupapa like this."

In stark contrast to the perspectives shared by tamariki the series also captures the painful reality of whānau finding themselves on opposing sides of the argument. The impact still resonates with those involved.

Forestry provided employment when decent paying jobs were hard to come by and some of the Tasman Forestry workers sent to the maunga found themselves in stand-offs with whanaunga.

On one side was Tame Iti and his 'puna kiore' (rat pack) who were focused on protecting and upholding their obligation to the maunga, while on the other were whānau trying to protect jobs and feed their families.

Day described the result as an emotional rollercoaster.

"You hear anger, frustration and sadness. It's a real concoction of emotions, and that's what makes it really unique."

Beyond the occupation Te Māhurehure demonstrated the value of combining whakapapa, tikanga, strategy and collective action to build a movement around an extraordinarily complex issue.

Forty years after the occupation, Day said its enduring lesson was clear.

"The biggest and strongest lesson this provides is the power of kotahitanga."

"Kotahitanga can be achieved no matter how complex the argument, and the power of unity and kotahitanga can make a genuine and real difference."

After six months, the occupation ended in favour of tangata whenua and the native forest remained standing.

The feature-length version of Taiarahia: Te Kākahu Tawhito won the People's Choice award for best documentary at the Māoriland Film Festival.

World.title: Person critically injured after fight in Lower Hutt
World.content:
One person is in hospital with critical injuries following a fight in Lower Hutt overnight.

Police were called to Waterloo Road just after 2am.

One person was taken to hospital with critical injuries.

Several other people suffered minor injuries during the fracas.

A 45-year-old man has been arrested after he handed himself in at the Wellington Central Police Station just before 5pm.

World.title: Auckland and Canterbury university enrolments rise as trades training struggles
World.content:
Auckland and Canterbury have seized most of the growth in university enrolments this year, while trades training numbers continue to slide.

A Tertiary Education Commission report to Tertiary Education Minister Penny Simmonds said in April this year 354,695 people were enrolled in tertiary education and training, 1 percent fewer than the same time last year.

A 5 percent drop in the number of people enrolled in vocational education and training caused the fall, while the number in higher education increased 4 percent.

The individual enrolments were equivalent to 203,918 full-time students, 2 percent more than last year.

The report said the number of full-time equivalent students increased at universities, but some gained more than others.

"Based on the number of EFTS delivered, the largest increases in higher education were at the University of Auckland (8 percent, 2165 EFTS) and the University of Canterbury (8 percent, 1254 EFTS)," the report said.

"These two universities accounted for nearly half of the total growth in higher education delivery. With a minimal decline of six EFTS, Lincoln University was the only university to see a decrease in delivery."

The decline in vocational education and training was concentrated in work-based apprenticeships and training enrolments, which dropped 10 percent compared to April last year.

"Most subject areas saw a decline in work-based EFTS between April 2025 and April 2026, with Architecture and Building (-17 percent, -706 EFTS) and Engineering and Related Technologies (-9 percent, -413 EFTS) seeing the greatest decreases," the report said.

"These subject areas accounted for 63 percent of all work-based vocational education provision April 2026, contributing to a notable impact on work-based provision."

The report said the number of work-based learners had dropped for four consecutive years and was 28 percent lower than in April 2021 on an equivalent full-time student basis.

World.title: Warriors at top of NRL table after 14-point win over Knights
World.content:
Jacob Laban's try double has powered NZ Warriors to a 46-32 shootout win over Newcastle Knights, regaining the NRL competition lead with one week remaining in the regular season.

Needing to win by 14 points to sneak past Penrith Panthers on countback, the Warriors did exactly that, but the result looked unlikely as they lurched out of the starting blocks to trail 16-0 early.

Newcastle scored three tries in the opening quarter hour, before the home side could find the scoreboard, through second-rower Laban, sporting a new bleached hairdo for the occasion.

The Warriors were forced into late changes to their selected line-up with halves Te Maire Martin and Chanel Harris-Tavita dropping out through injury.

Jett Cleary - youngest son of former Warriors player/coach Ivan and younger sibling of NRL superstar Nathan - was handed his first-grade debut and played a major hand in several of the eight tries scored by his team.

After Laban's opening try, they piled on three more to hooker Wayde Egan, lock Erin Clark and forward Demitric Vaimauga before halftime to lead 22-20 at the break.

They have not lost a game from that advantage this season and were next to score after the restart, through centre Ali Leiataua, as Laban chased another Cleary kick and offloaded in midair to his teammate.

Wing Luke Laulilii also made his Warriors debut, but left the game in the first half, after he copped a high tackle from prop Jacob Saifiti, who was sent off as a result, leaving his team undermanned for the next 67 minutes.

Adam Pompey replaced Laulilii and scored to stretch the Warriors lead to 34-20 10 minutes into the second half.

Back-to-back tries to Knights wing Greg Marzhew threatened to spoil the Warriors party, but wing Alofiana Khan-Pereira restored some order, leaving them needing a converted try to rise atop the ladder.

They got that from Laban in the dying moments, as he cut back against the grain for an offload from Cleary to score near the posts. Fullback Taine Tuaupiki missed the first conversion of the night, but slotted the next seven - many from near touch - including the decisive kick for the 14-point margin.

The Warriors now host Manly Sea Eagles at Go Media Stadium next Saturday with a minor premiership crown very much on the line.
