Tech.title: Why the Hottest New Wearables Want to Be Ignored
Tech.content:
There’s a new kind of gadget on shelves, designed for you to ignore it 99 percent of the time—it only needs attention when its battery is low. I'm talking about the screen-free wearable. You rarely look at it or touch it, yet it collects health stats day and night so you can view them later on in an app, when you get the time—if you can find the time. No pressure.

They have been exploding of late and are only set to grab more attention in the coming months, with the promise of demanding less of your attention once you actually buy one. Today there’s the Garmin Cirqa, Google Fitbit Air, Polar Loop, the Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Whoop series, the original pioneer of this category. Apple is considering its own version of the concept, according to Bloomberg. One answer to that big question of why? Many of us are sick of attention-hoarding tech and social media, not least realizing it is probably doing us no good.

I have reviewed wearables since they went mainstream the first time around with the early waves of Fitbits from 2009 and onward. In some ways this new generation of trackers feels like a callback to those days. Back when I used the Fitbit Ultra, a 2011 tracker that clipped to your jeans, I paid so little attention to it that two days passed before I realized I’d lost it somewhere on the streets of Zagreb, Croatia. While, like many, I fell for the sub-Tamagotchi little cartoon faces of the 2012 Fitbit Zip’s screen, it—like a Fitbit Air—wasn't something you were meant to pay attention to more than a couple times a day, max.

Over the last few years, though, I’ve spent most days referring to a Garmin, Samsung, Fitbit, Coros—the list goes on—dozens or hundreds of times a day. WhatsApp messages and emails buzz on their little screens and my wrist reflexively raises to see what’s up. When I wear a Garmin watch, I’m also lulled into the rhythm of checking evening and morning “reports,” and pathologically looking at my sleep score as soon as I wake up. And let’s not even get into the move alerts, an eye-rolling nag wearables have had for years now.

What Wearables Have Become

Part of the sell-in of new-breed wearables is that they're, in some ways, the antithesis of what other watches have grown into. Fitness watches are more smartwatch-like than ever. OLED screens are near-ubiquitous even in health trackers; hardcore running wearables let you communicate with AI assistants. And this is all even though smartwatches have never really fulfilled the original promise of a life-changing app or feature beyond what people used the first Apple Watch for back in 2015: not much.

Sure, Apple Watches may have saved a life or two, but that’s not necessarily what you’re buying them for. I waited years to report on smartwatch apps that would change things and instead saw entire wearable app ecosystems wither like neglected houseplants. Screen-free wearables want to hit “reset” on the entire category.

The most interesting factor isn't that bands like the Fitbit Air exist now, but why this is all happening now, in 2026. These wearables are largely a case of design subtraction. They are much like a normal fitness tracker—heart rate sensor, battery, accelerometer, Bluetooth transmitter, and whatever other sensors are packed in on a per-case basis—with the display excised.

Tech.title: The Best Label Makers (2026): Brother, Niimbot, Dymo
Tech.content:
There’s not a whole bunch more the average person could want in a handheld label maker other than what the PT-n25bt offers, particularly at such an approachable price. With this device, even a label-making newbie should have no issue making a custom tag in less than a minute. After clicking the tape cartridge into place, simply close the back of the machine, power it on, and type directly onto the standard QWERTY keyboard. Press print, and then use the on-device cutting mechanism to get a clean, straight edge every time. If you’re not in a huge rush, you can putter around with three font options, seven font styles (think: bold, underline, italic), 15 text frames, and hundreds of symbols. The LCD screen lets you preview any edits you make to your label, minimizing unintended surprises you get when it, say, spits out a thick border design you really hate.

For even more design flexibility, you can opt for the Brother Design&Print 2 companion app that’s available on iOS and Android devices. It connects via Bluetooth and provides dozens of templates geared toward specific purposes, like gift tags, file folders, or food containers. You can also design your own custom label on the app without using a template. If you go this route, you’ll have way more font, frame, and design options at your disposal than if you design directly on the app.

The labels themselves offer a level of customization. Because the tape cartridges are available in 17 colors, you can choose to make your labels look all your own, particularly if you opt for a less-common color, like black print on green tape. The labels also hold up to the conditions. Brother markets its durability-minded laminated BTag label tapes—specifically for its P-touch line of label makers—as being water-, temperature-, and fade-resistant, along with microwave-, dishwasher-, and freezer-resistant. In my few weeks of testing, these claims held up.

For all of its wins, there are a few drawbacks of the PT-n25bt: It runs on a whopping six AAA batteries that aren’t included in the box. You can also power it with an AC adapter, but you have to buy that separately for $26. You’re also limited to labels that are 12 millimeters wide (roughly half an inch), so you’ll need to stack labels if you’re looking for a bigger visual.

Tech.title: How to Escape Group Chat Hell
Tech.content:
A specific cadence for contemporary group chats eludes me. The rapid-fire tempo of texts combined with custom stickers, often based on inside jokes, leaves me behind. My digital fate: the silent lurker. As I let the notifications wash over me, I am a ghostlike figure haunting the group chat, a silent watcher who rarely responds without a specific invocation.

Group chats are dominating the social lives of younger Americans. In a recent YouGov poll, 34 percent of adults under 30 said they are in at least four group chats, whether via text or other messaging app. Power texters are spending hours juggling multiple message threads—3 percent of adults under 30 said they are in more than 20 distinct group chats.

These group chats are not just for the young folk, though. All attempts at social interactions now spark a new group message. A WhatsApp thread for our monthly book club. An Instagram group for that weekend getaway. A bulbous iMessage chat with random cousins attempting to plan a family reunion. Group chat hell is everywhere you turn.

Here are a few tips for maintaining your sanity during the reign of the group chat, without becoming a textless social pariah. Hint: It’s all about boundaries.

Core Compromise

Maybe you thrive in the chaos of hundreds of notifications, but I don't. I started by choosing which text threads were most important to me. A text thread with my immediate family is nonnegotiable. A group message about a trip that's in one month is actually helpful for logistics. A random thread where people are throwing out Halloween ideas might be fun, but it's on the chopping block. Make a short list of what you actually want to participate in and stay there.

Walk Away

For the others, you can leave the chat. It really is that easy. Especially for event-based group chats, I’m quick to leave the conversation after it's all wrapped and any outstanding bills are settled. Much like I’m not going to be the last person to leave an afterparty, I’m walking away from group chats without hesitation. If there's a specific aspect of the conversation I want to keep going, I'll follow up with those people.

Mute It

You've picked your core group chats you don't want to give up, and you've walked away from the rest. Now is your time to play with the notification settings and see what your smartphone offers. It's worth looking into the settings overall, as well as the options for individualized threads inside apps, especially if some notifications rarely come through while other text threads are more active.

If you balk at the idea of notification distractions, consider Do Not Disturb settings. Be forewarned that being this unreachable can sometimes become a headache for those closest to you.

Get Creative

For those group chats you decide to stay in, why not spruce up the place a bit? Whether you're on an iPhone or Android, there are plenty of options for making your group chats more specific to your context and potentially just more fun to use. Right now I'm watching Game of Thrones from the beginning for the first time. I have a group chat with friends to process some of our reactions and update the background image to whatever character I’m currently rooting for.

Go Direct

I mentioned earlier that when I leave a group thread and I want to keep some aspect of the conversation going, I'll follow up directly with people. This seems to be the better direction to take overall. While you may get a dopamine rush from shooting off hilarious memes and receiving reaction emojis in the group chat, cultivating relationships often happens best with one-on-one moments. Directly texting someone feels like a worthwhile compromise to escape from group chat hell, without fully excluding yourself from modern messaging. Though a face-to-face chat always feels best.

Tech.title: Scientists Create the Littlest Big Bang to Study the Universe's Origins
Tech.content:
In the very first moments of the universe, matter didn’t exist as we know today. A millionth of a second or so after the big bang, the universe was a dense, hot soup scientists call quark-gluon plasma (QGP). For several years, particle colliders—which smash molecules together at nearly the speed of light—have been able to replicate this state, but often using heavy elements like lead.

Now, a recent experiment by the European Organization for Nuclear Research (also known as CERN from its French acronym) has demonstrated this plasma can be produced by much smaller collisions. Since there’s no longer an accessible natural source of this primordial sludge, these micro big bangs can help reveal what happened in the first few minutes of our universe.

First, a little context. Quarks are what make up protons and neutrons, which, in turn, are the building blocks of atoms and thus all matter. Meanwhile, gluons—as their name suggests—stick quarks together.

During the first microseconds of the universe, quarks and gluons were not yet confined within protons and neutrons but instead formed an extremely hot plasma. As the universe expanded, the matter cooled, and the quarks condensed into larger particles.

After decades of studying QGP in large nuclear collisions, physicists are now trying to understand the limits of this strange state of matter. In particular, they are exploring just how much they can scale down a collision and still observe a collection of particles that behaves like a drop of fluid.

According to a recent article in Physical Review Letters, CERN and an international team of collaborators were able to generate the substance using oxygen-16 and neon-20. Both are less than a tenth of the weight of a lead atom, which was previously considered one of the lightest elements capable of generating QGP.

“We have pushed the boundary for how small the atomic nuclei can be while still re-creating this primordial matter—what you could call a ‘little big bang.’ We now know more about the fundamental conditions required for matter to transition into this extreme state,” You Zhou, a researcher at the Niels Bohr Institute in the Netherlands and a coauthor of the study, explained in a press release.

The scientists found that, despite the small size of the oxygen and neon nuclei, the collisions produced signals consistent with the behavior they expected to find in QGP. For an instant, the generated matter appeared to expand collectively like a fluid before cooling and reverting to particles.

“Hopefully, this will help us better understand how the plasma behaved during the first moments of the universe—and how it later evolved into the forms of matter that everything around us is made of,” Zhou added.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

Tech.title: Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Review: Master of Phone Calls
Tech.content:
The Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro did something I wasn't expecting: It made me call my family more.

Here's my problem: I have aging parents who are losing their hearing, and I like to mumble. That's a bad combination for catching up over the phone during my New York City commute. I almost always have to talk loudly and repeat myself way more often than I would like. It makes the whole conversation feel unnatural, so much so that a little part of me dreads making that phone call.

I've tested over 50 pairs of wireless earbuds in my career as a headphones expert, and none of them have totally solved this problem. That is, until I started reviewing the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro, with its Guinness World Records claim of “highest speech quality score.” And what sounded like pure marketing at first turned into something else—earbuds that are probably my new daily carry.

Put a Screen on It

Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz

The Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro has a new design from its predecessor. The buds have a larger, flat pill shape (similar to the second-gen Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds) and are bigger and heavier than stem-shaped buds like Apple AirPods Pro 3. While they are a little big, they are very comfortable—I wore them for multiple hours without any irritation or fatigue. In the box, there are multiple alternative ear tips and wing-tip sizes to find your ideal fit.

Tech.title: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope Has a Hidden Technological Leap
Tech.content:
Two mirrors, each small enough to fit in the palm of your hand, are set to change how we understand the cosmos.

The launch window for NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is about to open. The telescope’s primary instrument is due to inform practically every area of astrophysics, but also tucked inside the telescope is a specialized coronagraph, an experimental apparatus that will attempt to directly capture starlight reflected off a planet’s surface for the first time. It’s an ambitious project that NASA hopes will pave the way for a space telescope that can one day provide a glimpse of an Earthlike planet orbiting a sunlike star.

That’s a feat far beyond the power of current engineering—hence taking the basic technique for a spin on Roman. “We’ll test them in space for the first time, and we’ll understand what work still is left to go,” says Vanessa Bailey, an astrophysicist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory and instrument scientist for the coronagraph.

At its core, a coronagraph is just a science-minded sunshade that can block out the light of a bright star and reveal a fainter object otherwise lost in the glare. Such instruments have flown in space before—both the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes carry coronagraphs. But Roman’s is light-years more sophisticated than its predecessors, thanks largely to technology called adaptive optics, which deforms a telescope’s mirror to cancel out these light distortions. It still faces a monumental challenge, though: NASA compares the task of Roman’s coronagraph to photographing a firefly perched next to a floodlight—from across the country.

“Any little bit of starlight that gets in the wrong place could just destroy a whole portion of the image,” says Margaret Turnbull, an exoplanet scientist at the SETI Institute, a nonprofit research organization in California, who leads a Roman coronagraph science team.

Tech.title: The Cybersecurity Apocalypse Is Coming in ‘Months,’ AI Giants Warn
Tech.content:
Meta settled a massive multistate lawsuit over child safety issues this week and has agreed to make substantial changes to its social media platforms. It will pay up to $16.7 billion to participating US states and territories—with some of the money contingent on competitors adopting the same practices.

Also, local prosecutors in Illinois shared sensitive personal information about immigrants with the Department of Homeland Security, despite a state law that is supposed to prevent local law enforcement from assisting with federal deportation efforts. Finally, a California-based WIRED reporter tried exercising their legal right to request data from 100 companies … only to find that companies started deleting the requested data instead.

And there’s more. Each week, we round up the security and privacy news we didn’t cover in depth ourselves. Click the headlines to read the full stories. And stay safe out there.

Following a seemingly endless parade of rogue AI agent hacking incidents, OpenAI, Anthopic, and more than 100 companies have cosigned a letter saying that everyone else has mere months to prepare for AI-enabled cyberattacks.

The letter calls for a “collective response,” suggests that every organization should make cyber defense an “immediate leadership priority,” and calls on governments to give hospitals, water utilities, and local governments access to capable defensive AI, as well as to “impose costs” on attackers.

Axios notes that the letter doesn’t include any specific commitments, deadlines, or investments. Good luck!

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency says that it observed “malicious cyber activity” targeting over 100 water and wastewater systems across the United States. According to CISA, the attacks have mostly targeted programmable logic controllers, or PLCs, which can monitor or control equipment. Some communities have hooked up those devices to the internet so that they can be accessed remotely. According to TechCrunch, CISA has also said that hackers are using AI to help generate scripts to attack the devices. In July, WIRED reported on a leaked industry memo that tied the “unprecedented wave” of cyberattacks to Iran.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement is set to spend over a million dollars on robot dogs from Boston Dynamics, according to 404 Media. The agency’s announcement says the bots will “improve officer safety,” in part because they can be remotely operated. This follows another recent announcement that the agency will be purchasing electric shock gloves for its officers. In April, DHS requested nearly $100 billion in discretionary spending.

A West Virginia man who went by the name “MrChildPorn” online has been charged with possession of material depicting minors engaged in sexually explicit content. According to a criminal complaint filed against him, the man “boasted” about having a large collection of child sexual abuse material on Discord. In an interview with state troopers, the man claimed that he was “trolling” and “rage-baiting,” but the complaint also alleges that the man would individually message CSAM to people on Discord and attempted to use the chat app’s AI feature to search for explicit images of infants.

Tech.title: Our Research Shows How Just One Security Camera Cuts the Risk of Break-Ins
Tech.content:
Home security doesn’t have to begin with a complicated fleet of cameras or multidevice security kit (although I’ve found some very good ones). When I looked into the data around the effects of security cams, I was pleasantly surprised to find only a single home security camera or a device such as a video doorbell has a big impact — and that’s coming from burglars themselves.

The best study on the subject, titled “Understanding Decisions to Burglarize from the Offender’s Perspective,” was conducted by the University of North Carolina at Charlotte, along with other colleges and organizations, including the Electronic Security Association, offering support. This project interviewed over 400 burglars to learn more about their habits and motives.

One finding caught my eye: The majority of burglars said they considered warning signs when selecting a target and specifically called out not only alarm signage but also outdoor cameras, surveillance equipment and increased security in general. Overall, 83% of interviewees said they tried to find out if the home they were targeting had a security alarm, and 60% said they would choose another if they noticed the alarm (down to 50% if they noticed an alarm halfway through breaking-in).

While the questions specified a security alarm, I think today’s outdoor security cameras and video doorbells — with their lights, sirens, audio and alerts — qualify. Most burglars are aware of how only a single device can give them away.

However, note that it’s important that the doorbell or camera be visible. Research confirms that burglars need to notice the security device for it to prevent crime, so think twice before hiding cameras.



Other statistics back up these findings

Blink’s Outdoor 4 camera isn’t just easy to use — it also lasts a ridiculously long time per charge. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

It’s difficult to find high-quality studies on the effects of home security devices because accounting for variables and measuring residential property crime can be very challenging. Most studies in this area focus on commercial camera systems, like city CCTVs, which is less useful for people buying security equipment.

One additional standout study, called “Public Area CCTV and Crime Prevention: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis,” showed noticeable reductions in general areas but a large 51% drop in crime when cameras were added to car parks and lots. I like this particular research because searching out parked vehicles to look for easy, lucrative break-ins is similar to burglars scouring a residential neighborhood, so related effects are likely.

And if you want to go back further in time, a study examined England and Wales crime rates in the 1990s when household security devices were growing more common. The study found even basic security upgrades, like proper lighting, decreased the chance of burglary, while seemingly increasing the chance of burglary for homes that didn’t have any precautions.

Remember, today’s cams are better than ever

Modern security cameras are far more effective at guarding your home. Eufy/CNET

Here’s a big caveat: Most of these studies are a decade old or more. But that could work in your favor because today’s security cameras have grown far more advanced, including human recognition, better accuracy, two-way audio and faster alerts right to your phone so you can take immediate action.

I’d like to see newer studies about the impact of advanced cameras on burglar decisions, but in general, the data still shows the trend. One security device capable of alerting owners or responders has a highly significant impact on reducing the chance of crime and stopping break-ins before they begin.

Keep in mind, as security devices have become more high-tech, so have burglars’ responses, including spying with cameras of their own and even attempting to use Wi-Fi jammers to cut off cameras. Those methods don’t really work against high-quality security from the best brands, but it’s always helpful to be aware of current risks.

Tech.title: A Folding iPhone at Last? What to Expect From Apple’s Surprise and Shine Fall Event
Tech.content:
After months of leaks and rumors, Apple is set to reveal its fall hardware lineup on Wednesday, Sept. 9, at its Surprise and Shine event. And from everything we know so far, the event will be unlike most others.

For one, this year’s event is a bit sentimental for the Cupertino company. Tim Cook announced in April that he is stepping down from his role as CEO, a job he has held for nearly 15 years after legendary Apple co-founder Steve Jobs stepped down in 2011. John Ternus, the company’s hardware engineering chief, will be stepping into the top role just days before the event.

Apple is also heavily rumored to break with its usual routine by holding off on releasing a base iPhone 18 until next year, meaning only the more expensive Pro models will be revealed in September. That would give another highly anticipated release center stage: the foldable device expected to be called the iPhone Ultra.

We’ll be keeping a close eye on the price tags. Apple raised prices across its computer and home devices this summer, attributing the cost increases to memory chip supply chain issues, largely driven by the AI race. Additional price hikes on Apple Music and Apple TV subscriptions aren’t helping cash-strapped consumers, either.



New iPhone 18 models, joining the foldable fun

Apple’s iPhone 18 lineup is likely going to look a little different this year. One of the biggest rumors is that Apple is going to do an extended rollout. This September, we expect to see the foldable iPhone Ultra, the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, but we likely won’t get the base iPhone 18, iPhone 18E and a possible iPhone Air 2 until spring 2027.

The iPhone Ultra, as Apple’s much-rumored first foldable phone is tentatively named, has a book-style design, according to analyst leaks. Think more Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, which opens like a book into a mini tablet — not like an OG 90s flip phone.

But the possible $2,000 price tag means the Ultra likely won’t be a replacement for the base iPhone 18. More likely, it will be more of a luxury option. That may be one reason why a majority of US adults (75%) don’t care about foldable phones, a recent CNET survey found.

We had CNET’s creative director show us what we could expect from the new potential iPhone 18 colors. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max models are rumored to have bigger batteries, variable-aperture cameras and run on the new Apple A20 processor. More satellite connectivity, a smaller Dynamic Island and tweaked back camera islands are also possibilities. And these new phones could come in colors such as light blue, dark cherry and dark gray.

Running on all these devices is the already announced new family of operating systems. iOS 27, with the anticipated Siri AI revamp, is likely to be released this fall, along with MacOS Golden Gate, Apple TVOS 27 and more. Since we learned about these at WWDC in June, we’ve been playing around with the public betas to see what’s inside.

Apple Watch Series 12: Apple Health and Touch ID?

A Series 12 Watch is “all but guaranteed,” CNET wearables expert Vanessa Hand Orellana says. Less likely are a new Apple Watch SE and Ultra model since they were refreshed in 2025. But any new watches, the Series 12 and Ultra 4, are likely to come with a new processor, which should extend their life and usefulness for you.

The biggest design change expected is largely mechanical, not aesthetic. A more energy-efficient screen technology could be included to extend the watches’ battery life without sacrificing screen brightness. A new processor — probably named the S12 to match the line-up’s naming, despite “S11” being next in line — would also help with this.

The next Apple Watch Series 12 may bring back TouchID. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

Another potential addition could be biometric authentication — in other words, a Touch ID for Apple Watch. Some internal code leaks suggest Apple is working on integrating this tech into its wearables, but it’s unclear when it will be publicly available. Health features, like blood pressure monitoring, are also rumored to be in progress, but again, no guarantees. The Apple Health App’s AI overhaul has also reportedly run into issues.

Our early testing shows WatchOS 27 with Siri AI will bring a big boost to devices — at least, for the ones it’s compatible with, which isn’t all of them. Watches were excluded from Apple’s summer price hike, but similar raises from watches by Google and Samsung mean a higher starting price isn’t out of the realm of possibility.

AirPods with or without cameras

Possibly the biggest Apple rumor has been that the next generation of Apple AirPods will be equipped with a new, tiny infrared camera — not to take photos, but to scan its physical environment to power its visual intelligence, or AI, answers.

The AirPods 5 could look similar to the AirPods 4 (shown) but have performance upgrades. David Carnoy/CNET

These rumored “AirPods Ultra” sparked a lot of concern and outrage from tech enthusiasts, who have spent most of the summer criticizing other AI-and-camera-enabled wearables, like Meta’s smart glasses. Apple is known to tout its focus on privacy, so it will be interesting to see if Apple ultimately comes out with these earbuds and, if so, how it defends them.

AirPods are generally on a two-year refresh cycle, so we may get the AirPods 5 and AirPods 5 Pro this year. The previous model, the AirPods 4 with active noise canceling, is “something of a technological marvel,” CNET headphones expert David Carnoy said. Effective noise canceling is hard to achieve with an open-earbud design, but Apple’s previous success sets the foundation for even more progress here. The Apple-owned Beats 360 headphones could also get refreshed this fall.

For more, check out the best iPhones and best MacBooks for 2026.

Tech.title: Equifax Class Action: Last Change to Claim Part of the $2.2M Settlement
Tech.content:
If you used Equifax’s consumer credit reports service in 2022, you may be eligible to claim part of a $2.2 million settlement payout. The case centered on allegations that Equifax violated the Fair Credit Reporting Act, a federal statute that dictates credit reporting companies must “follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of the information concerning the individual about whom the report relates.”

The class action lawsuit, Bradberry v. Equifax Information Services LLC, alleged that Equifax “wrongfully reported duplicates of negative accounts” on certain consumer reports, and that these duplicated debt tradelines are a result of the company having inadequate datakeeping policies and procedures. The lawsuit alleges that Equifax “negligently and recklessly disseminated false and damaging information” regarding the credit of certain customers.

Essentially, the lawsuit alleges that Equifax’s negligent reporting made some customers’ debts appear larger than they actually were, potentially creating situations where affected individuals couldn’t secure loans, credit cards, mortgages and other lines of credit.

The plaintiff, Charmayne Bradberry, filed the suit in the US District Court for the Northern District of Georgia. Bradberry said that she received a report showing the same $305 collection account twice, and that each instance showed separate “opened” and “reported” dates for the debt. She alleges that her credit score dropped severely following this report, which may have prevented her from securing a vital mortgage application.

Bradberry is one of 37,651 customers Equifax identified as having received reports with duplicate debt tradelines.

Equifax has denied any wrongdoing and denied that settlement class members were harmed by its actions, and the court has not ruled in favor of either side. The settlement was agreed upon by both parties, and the court has preliminarily approved the $2.2 million payment, subject to a final approval hearing.

The settlement website is live now. The hearing is scheduled to take place on Oct. 6, during which the court will confirm the settlement sum, allocate funds for attorneys’ fees and create a plan to distribute money to the affected class members.

While some class action lawsuits automatically pay out from the agreed-upon sum, that isn’t the case with Bradberry v. Equifax. Affected individuals need to file a claim and provide valid payment information by Sept. 1 to receive a share of the funds.

If you wish to opt out of or object to the settlement, you must do so by the same Sept. 1 deadline. Failure to do so will mean you remain part of the settlement class and forfeit your right to separately sue Equifax for this incident.

Who can be part of the Equifax settlement?

Not every Equifax customer is automatically eligible to claim part of the settlement. The money is reserved for people who received reports with duplicated collection account information that reflected larger sums of debt than existed in reality.

In order to join, you must meet the following qualifications:

Be a living individual in the US or its territories. Received one of the identified Duplicate Reporting Letters from Equifax between August and September 2022.

The settlement class in this case is extremely well-defined. Equifax identified 37,651 people who received duplicated reports. These individuals are the qualifying settlement class members.

Affected class members need to file a paper claim or log in through the settlement website in order to receive a payout. In order to file a claim online, you need to use the unique settlement member ID number included within the initial communication sent to affected individuals. This communication was sent out via postcard and email.

How much will the Equifax settlement pay out?

The total payment for each claimant is capped at $600, but actual payouts will depend on how many settlement class members file claims and how much money the court sets aside for attorney and administrative fees.

Whether or not settlement class members file a claim, they will receive six months of Equifax Complete credit monitoring services, including credit reports, credit score monitoring and up to $500,000 insurance for identity theft-related expenses.

During the claims process, class members must select a valid payment method for their share of the settlement funds. According to the paper claim form, you can choose to have the money sent to a PayPal, Venmo or Zelle account, a virtual prepaid card or a check.

If you’re eligible to claim a piece of the settlement sum, you must file by Sept. 1. Payments will be distributed after the court’s final approval hearing, assuming there are no appeals.

Tech.title: Apple Might Skip the iPhone 18 This Year. Is the iPhone 17 Still Worth It?
Tech.content:
The iPhone 17 closed the gap between Apple’s entry-level phone and the pricier Pro models last year with long-overdue display upgrades, alongside nifty camera and durability improvements. Apple also made new features like Center Stage (its new selfie camera) and Dual Capture available across the entire lineup, making the iPhone 17 an even better value.

A year later, it has become the most affordable entry-level flagship across brands, thanks to Samsung and Google raising the prices of their entry-level models due to a surge in RAM prices driven by AI and data centers.

August is usually when we suggest to avoid buying a new iPhone and to wait for the next one. But things are looking different in 2026.

As we inch closer to the next-generation iPhone announcement on Sept. 9, the iPhone 17 is holding strong against its Android rivals. And it will have to compete with newer models till March 2027, since the iPhone 18 won’t launch until then alongside the iPhone 18E, according to the rumors.

So what if you need a new iPhone before March or don’t want to pay $1,100 or more for an iPhone 18 Pro? I charged up my iPhone 17 and revisited Apple’s standard model this week to find out if it’s still worth buying.

Display, durability and camera upgrades keep it strong

Reading on the iPhone 17 is a pleasant experience. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

The iPhone 17 arrived last year with multiple major upgrades, many of which you’ll appreciate daily.

The screen is finally on par with Apple’s Pro models and every other Android counterpart. It runs at a smooth 120Hz refresh rate, which also adapts to the on-screen content to save battery. I compared it to the iPhone 15 and the smoother visuals were immediately noticeable when scrolling through the home screen. It makes the phone feel faster and more responsive.

The display is also brighter and less reflective than its predecessor. It is immediately noticeable when you’re navigating outdoors or need to do anything on your phone under bright lights. I put it against the new Pixel 11, which is equally bright, but iPhone 17’s smaller bezels make its screen more pleasing to look at.

Apple said its 2025 iPhones were more durable than ever. While I haven’t used the iPhone 17 for a year straight, I have daily driven the iPhone 17 Pro Max without a case for 10 months. (Yes, I’m that guy.) Compared to my 2024 iPhone 16 Pro, the 17 Pro has fared better against scratches and drops thanks to its Ceramic Shield 2 glass, the same found on the iPhone 17.

The auto framing feature, combined with better stabilization, has been a godsend for recording myself using the front camera. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

Some might dismiss it as a minor feature, but the 17’s selfie camera is the best upgrade, in my opinion. The new 18-megapixel square sensor is more of a quality-of-life upgrade than just a mere number bump because it lets you shoot landscape selfies without needing to rotate your phone. The viewfinder automatically repositions its framing based on the number of people in the photo.

I love the camera for two reasons. First, it enables Center Stage, which tracks you (even if you’re moving) on video calls (both on FaceTime and third-party apps like WhatsApp). It’s a handy feature for when I need to move around doing chores, but the camera keeps me in the frame and helps me be less annoying for my girlfriend.

Second, the square sensor improves stability in selfie video recording. I live with a condition that causes constant hand tremors, which makes it difficult to record myself on phones. The iPhone 17 has been helpful as I’m less self-conscious and more confident that I’ll get stable footage instead of a blurry video.

As for the two cameras on the back, they are far more capable than its predecessor. The iPhone 17 has two rear cameras: a 48-megapixel wide-angle camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide, which is an upgrade over the 12-megapixel ultrawide camera on the iPhone 16. You’ll get sharp photos, better indoor shots and a smooth video experience. It misses out on a telephoto camera that the 17 Pro has, so there’s no optical zoom, but these are all the cameras most people would ever need.

iOS 26 has its flaws — I can’t wait for iOS 27

iOS 26 (left) displaces the Control Center settings in landscape orientation. The upcoming iOS 27 (right) has fixed this issue. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

The iPhone 17 runs iOS 26, which offers more translucent controls, customization options and Apple Intelligence features. However, my experience has been buggy since the beginning. On multiple occasions, I’ve missed calls and alarms because my iPhone automatically lowered its system volume to a minimum. I didn’t put it in Do Not Disturb or Focus modes. Other times, the keyboard starts lagging out of nowhere, and whenever I need to access the Control Center while watching a video in landscape mode, my controls are all over the place.

Some of these issues have already been fixed on the iOS 27 Public Beta, which I’ve been running on my iPhone 17 Pro Max.

For starters, I can set different volume levels for the call ringer, alarms and media. The Control Center is now better optimized for horizontal orientation, keeping my customizations right where I want them. Then there are smart features, like spatial reframing in Photos for using generative AI to “change” the camera’s position when an image was taken. There’s also an all-new Siri mode in the Camera app.

In CNET’s 45-minute endurance test, which includes streaming, scrolling through social media, joining a video call and playing games, Apple’s entry-level iPhone went from full to 98%, which matches the results of the iPhone 17 Pro. It has the second-longest battery life of any phone CNET has tested in the past 12 months, tied with the OnePlus 15 and Motorola Razr (2026); behind the first-place phone is the iPhone 17 Pro Max.

However, subsequent iOS 26 updates along with continued use have had an impact on the battery life of my personal iPhone 17, causing more overnight idle drain. That’s why I’m looking forward to the upcoming iOS 27 update. If the beta is any indication, it should only improve the iPhone 17 experience with smarter features and better stability.

It has fared well, but what about six months from now?

The iPhone 17 has aged well and stacks well against its 2026 Android rivals. Prakhar Khanna/CNET

The baseline model stacks well against the competition. The iPhone 17 was launched at $799, which is $100 less than the $899 Samsung Galaxy S26 and the new Google Pixel 11. But with phone prices increasing across the board and new rumors pointing to higher iPhone prices, the iPhone 17’s current price is good if you are looking for a phone upgrade.

Those notable upgrades make it worth the $799 price, which might not remain the same in a few days from now, when Apple announces the iPhone 18 Pro and its first-ever foldable iPhone Ultra.

While the iPhone 18 is tipped to be announced next year, the Pro series could get a price hike, resulting in a wider price gap between the entry-level and top-of-the-line models.

To compensate, Apple could push the ceiling of its base iPhone and make it more expensive, even before the iPhone 18 launches. This is just speculation right now, based on Apple’s recent price hikes. But the base iPhone has remained at $799 ($829 without a carrier discount) since 2020, and after the new pricing on Macs, iPads and several other products, it makes much more sense to raise the barrier to a new entry-level model than ever.

As for those willing to wait for the iPhone 18, it is unlikely to be a major upgrade. Apple is expected to reserve the most prominent changes like a reduced Dynamic Island and newer cameras for its Pro models. Moreover, a recent rumor on Weibo suggests that the iPhone 18 could align more closely with a lower-cost iPhone 18E model. It might not receive a similarly powerful chip as its Pro siblings, for instance. It’s a similar move Google has made with its base Pixel 11 and budget Pixel 10A.

Given the lukewarm rumors regarding the upcoming model and iPhone 17’s current price tag (and the looming price hike), I think last year’s model is still an excellent deal. And for the first time in my career, I’d say if you want a new iPhone before Sept. 9, it is totally fine to get the iPhone 17 now rather than wait and see what the 18 Pro may bring.

Tech.title: This Website Is the Most Reliable Tool for Looking Up Flock Cameras Near You
Tech.content:
Flock Safety’s AI surveillance cameras, drones and listening devices get plenty of attention these days as they continue to expand across the US — but they can still can catch us by surprise. I’ve seen many people and even city councils surprised that local law enforcement or private organizations have signed Flock contracts. That’s a major reason I created a guide on exactly how to recognize a Flock camera, as opposed to other devices. But there’s also another tool I highly recommend using if you’re worried about Flock and don’t know where to start.

Maintained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation and the Reynolds School of Journalism at the University of Nevada, Reno, this database tracks police surveillance technology deployments across the US using public records, news reports, community submissions and a whole truckload of research.

In South Carolina, officials have been sparring over whether to install 25 new cameras, a dispute that reflects broader questions about cost, oversight, and how much surveillance communities are willing to accept. The city of Los Angeles recently broke its contract with Flock Safety, though Flock’s CEO argues that the suspension should be temporary while the police department revises its rules.

Public opposition has fueled many of these cancellations, reflecting concerns that the system facilitates mass surveillance and can lead to harms such as discriminatory policing and privacy infringements. It’s also led to a concerning rise in police officers getting arrested for using the systems to stalk exes.

To track such surveillance, journalists and researchers are increasingly turning to a free tool called the Atlas of Surveillance, a collaboration between the renowned digital privacy group Electronic Frontier Foundation and the University of Nevada, Reno. The site has become a go‑to source for mapping police technology — which also includes drones, facial-recognition cameras and body cameras — with a searchable database that’s often more dependable than alternatives.

Atlas searches only take seconds to get started. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

With the Atlas of Surveillance tool, you enter a city, county, state, law enforcement agency or vendor in the US and select which technology you’re interested in tracking. You’ll get a list of details based on your search, including links to public records or news articles.

A major advantage of this tool, besides its reliability compared to other apps, is that it covers all kinds of surveillance technology local governments and police have adopted, not just ALPR cameras but drones, databases, bodycams and other tools, by Flock and a variety of competitors such as Axon.

“We frequently run into situations where local councilpeople don’t even know that a certain tool is in use,” said Beryl Lipton, Electronic Frontier Foundation senior investigative researcher. “Learning about a technology we have logged in the Atlas of Surveillance is meant to help people have conversations [about] whether that tool is appropriate for local use, start asking questions, and advocate for standards around how their police can or can’t use this equipment.”

Surveilling surveillance

While other tools for tracking Flock cameras and similar surveillance systems exist, I prefer the EFF’s approach, which uses reliable crowdsourced data from specific volunteers, including University of Nevada students and staff, as well as experienced researchers. These volunteers use a variety of information, including government documents, press releases, news stories and confirmed social media posts, to create lists of exactly which surveillance technologies local police or sheriff departments are using, as well as when they were adopted.

Deflock, another popular crowdsourced app for reporting Flock camera locations, has an open-source design that leaves it vulnerable to false reports from people who only think they’re seeing a surveillance device. Self-reports are also becoming less reliable as surveillance cameras are being hidden in speed signs and cacti.

The Atlas provides sources for its information and includes records dating back years. EFF

I tried the Atlas tool with several location searches, including Albany, Georgia, where five police officers were fired and arrested in July on charges of misusing the city’s Flock system. Sure enough, I could see exactly when Albany began its Flock program, among other details about the technology it uses.

“While we may know that a police department has a tool, we may not know that they don’t have a governing policy or what is in the policy they have, like how long the data is retained,” Lipton told me.

Lipton recommends that users pair the Atlas tool with the EFF’s Street-Level Surveillance hub, which offers deeper documentation, including details on third‑party vendors that collaborate with law enforcement.

The Atlas database isn’t perfect, and the volunteers can do only so much. In my own searches, I found that my home city offered accurate listings for traffic cameras, but didn’t mention the period when it adopted Flock automated license plate readers last year, before removing them after public complaint. I’ve seen similar patterns in other cities with comparable histories, suggesting the database may emphasize active programs or exclude portions of older records.

Resources like the Atlas of Surveillance give residents a clearer view of the technologies their police departments use, information that can otherwise be difficult to obtain. As I’ve covered before, some cities will carefully omit the name “Flock” when announcing new surveillance or monitoring programs, even if they are using the brand’s drones or ALPR cameras.

If you’d like to volunteer for the Atlas of Surveillance, you can select the Collaborate option to submit a datapoint for consideration.

Tech.title: I Stopped My Mindless Scrolling Using This iOS 27 Shortcut
Tech.content:
How many times did I pick up my phone and get sucked into the endless scroll? Too often to count, thanks to the compulsion to open Threads and TikTok at all hours of the day. But I discovered a way to retrain my brain using a new iOS 27 feature.

I’m beta testing the upcoming operating system and its refreshed Shortcuts app, which lets you program your iPhone to do things using ordinary language. It’s called Describe a Shortcut. I speak my wishes into the app, and it obeys.

So in this One More Thing video, which you can watch embedded above, I found out what happens when you tell Shortcuts to not let you open Instagram (or Threads or TikTok) during work hours.

This is probably not what Apple developers had in mind for Shortcuts. After all, the Apple Screen Time app already has plenty of ways to help curb a social media addiction. But reprogramming my phone to turn it into a brick is more fun than paying for another company to “Brick” my phone. (Yes, people do this.)

For more One More Thing, subscribe to our YouTube page to catch Bridget Carey breaking down the latest Apple news and issues every Friday.

Tech.title: What Meta’s All-New Social Media Guidelines Promise to Change for Teen Users
Tech.content:
The fallout of an $18 billion lawsuit against Meta, announced on Wednesday, is already here. A new announcement from Meta is designed to meet the terms of the settled lawsuit while helping to prevent teen social media addiction.

In its post, Meta outlined a series of changes to both Instagram and Facebook that will apply only to those under 18. Most of the changes were required as part of the lawsuit settlement, notably the creation of daily limits and night mode controls for teens, as well as the adoption of age-assurance measures to help prevent cheating the system. As part of the agreement, Meta has denied any wrongdoing.

There’s been worldwide pushback against teens and children using social media, including the EU restricting access to social apps for kids under 13, and Australia banning apps like Instagram for anyone under 16. But some advocates worry Meta’s changes won’t be enough to fully protect teens.

In an interview with Democracy Now on Thursday, attorney and co-director of the AI Now research institute, Amba Kak, said the changes don’t address the platform’s architecture, which is designed to addict teenagers with features like infinite scroll. “It’s the business model of surveillance advertising, where it is the optimization of engagement and attention at any cost,” Kak said. “And I think if we don’t get at those root cause fixes, we’re going to be stuck playing whack-a-mole.”

A representative from Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Time limits for kids

Chief among the upcoming changes to Instagram and Facebook are time limitations for teens. A new default time limit will set the social media scrolling time to 2 hours a day for those under 18, and it can only be extended by parents.

An additional night mode will block most access to content such as feeds, stories, explore mode and reels between midnight and 6 a.m. and a school mode will mute notifications between 8 a.m. and 3 p.m.

Meta is also adding a feature to give 15-minute warnings to teens if they’ve been on the apps for an extended period of time, as well as 60-minute and 90-minute warnings they’re daily allotment is running down. To further reduce constant scrolling, autoplay for videos and clips will also be turned off by default, but like most features, it can be adjusted by parents.

Protection against toxic content

Meta is also implementing a number of changes intended to reduce toxicity and obsession with social media. By default, teens won’t see likes and reactions on posts, including their own. They’ll also be restricted from seeing certain content, such as cosmetic surgery and “extreme makeup” filters, although it’s not clear how far those limitations will extend (for example, a filter that adds dog ears).

Meta is adding age-appropriate content restrictions, but it remains vague on the details. While using movie ratings and parent feedback to build filters, the company fails to explain how this applies to social media posts or provide examples of blocked content.

In addition, teens will have the option to choose a non-algorithm version of their feeds that won’t be personalized by any Meta recommendations (which I also want for my own account).

Hazy tools for age verification

A new age-assurance strategy is also coming to Instagram and Facebook, but it’s unclear how it will work.

“We’re investing in even stronger technology to proactively catch accounts that may belong to under-13s,” Meta said on its blog. “We’re also strengthening the technology we use to identify accounts that may be between the ages of 13 and 17.”

Meta didn’t provide any details on how this tech would work, what it would look for or how it would flag accounts. I also asked about any appeals process for those incorrectly tagged, but Meta didn’t respond to my request.

It’s possible Meta will be using AI scan to profile context, account activity and visual cues to raise red flags, but there’s not much clarity otherwise.

Rolling out changes

The proposed changes were approved by a judge on Thursday, and Meta will roll out the first protections in the coming months, with the rest to follow afterward, although the exact timeline isn’t clear. As required by the agreement, Meta will also establish an independent social media research foundation to share “consented” user data in an effort to support teen well-being.

In its post, Meta said, “The fact is that teens move fluidly between dozens of apps a day. All platforms should empower parents and support teens by putting the same measures in place … we urge TikTok and YouTube to join us and state attorneys general in adopting this new standard.”

Other platforms have not responded to this call-out.
